sources.source_report_limitations: This is a narrative review and expert opinion, not an original empirical study, systematic review, or quantitative meta-analysis. Many cited-study claims are reported without endpoint numerators, denominators, confidence intervals, or exact site-level counts; study cohort size in Table 1 is not treated as an endpoint denominator. Cited studies are not independently reviewed here, and source-level attribution is preserved as reported. The body describes de Ribaupierre et al. (2012) speech arrest in three patients, while Table 1 lists eight subjects for that study; the source does not reconcile the narrative subset with the table total. The locked filename contains "2016," but the PDF title page and citation identify Aron et al. (2021), published 10 March 2021. The article concerns stimulation-evoked language responses and postoperative naming rather than spontaneous ictal seizure semiology, and its laterality statements are often task-, site-, or cohort-specific.
sources.source_report_methods_population: This is not an original cohort or pooled analysis. The review discusses published sEEG/ECS, subdural ECS, intraoperative ECS, intracranial recording, fMRI, and surgical-outcome studies; Table 1 lists 16 reviewed depth-electrode studies with study-level subject counts ranging from 1 to 172, including pediatric and adult populations. The source does not define one aggregate analysis population, does not report a pooled estimate, and states that no proper comparison has been made between resections with and without extra-operative or intra-operative language mapping. Stimulation protocols and language-task choices are described as methodological context; findings below retain study-specific populations and units where the review reports them.
sources.source_report_summary: Aron, Jonas, Colnat-Coulbois, and Maillard, "Language Mapping Using Stereo Electroencephalography: A Review and Expert Opinion," Frontiers in Human Neuroscience 15:619521, published 10 March 2021. This narrative review and expert opinion evaluates electrical cortical stimulation (ECS) and related intracranial language mapping with stereo-electroencephalography (sEEG) in epilepsy surgery, distinguishing indispensable anterior/posterior language cortex from dispensable basal temporal language cortex. Its in-scope contribution is language localization, language-dominance lateralization, stimulation-evoked language responses, and postoperative naming outcomes.

sources.source_report_limitations: The source is a retrospective, surgically selected cohort of patients evaluated with SEEG, not an unselected population with temporal or temporal-plus epilepsy. Only one typical seizure per patient entered the quantitative clinical analysis despite 607 SEEG-recorded seizures, and aura ascertainment could rely on event-time reports, post-ictal interview, or recent history. SEEG sampled targeted regions but did not explore most brain volume; the authors state that T+ subgroup assignment cannot be considered definitively error-free. The cohort excluded many patients with clear initial eloquent-cortex involvement, and the authors identify selection bias as a possible explanation for the reported seizure-lateralization difference. T+ subgroups were small. Table 2 percentages have no row-specific numerators or denominators, and the source does not provide confidence intervals or correction for multiple comparisons. Cluster analysis used 30 clusters from 72 non-zero events and is described by the authors as descriptive, with no well-established a-priori method for choosing the number of clusters. The rendered Table 1 lateralization cells (“4 L” and “20 L”) are not directionally concordant with the Results text's statement of left-side predominance in TL patients; this is retained as an unresolved source conflict rather than normalized. Cited-study statements remain unverified restatements and are not independent measurements of the present cohort.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The study was retrospective and included 80 of 212 consecutive patients with medically intractable seizures operated on after SEEG at Grenoble Hospital from 1990 to 1998. Eligibility required no detectable MRI lesion except hippocampal sclerosis, SEEG involvement of at least mesial and/or lateral temporal structures, SEEG-guided surgery, and at least 5 years of postoperative follow-up. The cohort comprised 42 females and 38 males; the reported mean age at SEEG was 29.3 ± 8.7 years, mean age at epilepsy onset 10.1 ± 7.9 years, mean epilepsy duration 19 ± 8 years, and mean seizure frequency 13.5 ± 17.5 per month. Sixty-six patients had unilateral hippocampal sclerosis; 14 had no clear MRI abnormality before surgery, with hamartoma or non-Taylor cortical dysplasia found in two of those at neuropathology. Long-term scalp video-EEG recorded 432 seizures in 79 patients; SEEG used 888 chronically implanted electrodes and recorded 607 seizures in 79 patients, with one patient not captured because the SEEG study was interrupted. The epileptogenic zone was defined by the first clear preclinical ictal SEEG change consisting of low-voltage fast activity or recruiting fast spikes and by the cortex considered for removal; 58 patients were classified TL and 22 T+, with T+ subgroups temporo-frontal (TF, n=9), temporo-sylvian (TS, n=7), and temporo-parieto-occipital (TPO, n=6). Clinical semiology was assessed on one typical seizure per patient, giving 80 analyzed seizures, because the number of recorded seizures per patient ranged from 1 to 44. The comparison used relative frequencies and contingency tables; Phi and Cramer V significance was set at P≤0.05. Scalp-EEG findings were classified by type, lateralization, and 10–20 localization; ictal onset included low-voltage fast activity, localized flattening, disappearance of localized interictal abnormalities, or rhythmic theta when the other patterns were absent. Tailored resections included at least the temporal pole and mesio-temporal structures; 18 of 22 T+ cases had extension outside the temporal lobe, and postoperative Engel classes were reported as context rather than as semiologic findings. The introduction also cites surgical outcome examples involving temporo-perisylvian, temporo-insular, temporo-parietal, and posterior basal temporal onsets; these cited reports are represented separately only where the outcome is inseparable from the localizing claim.
sources.source_report_summary: This is a retrospective primary empirical study of ictal clinical semiology and scalp-EEG findings differentiating SEEG-defined temporal lobe (TL) from temporal-plus (T+) epilepsies in 80 consecutive surgical patients. Its atlas relevance is the source-reported comparison of ictal auras, autonomic, motor, behavioural, post-ictal, interictal scalp-EEG, and ictal scalp-EEG features, including body-side and extra-temporal localization descriptors. The paper also reports cited-study restatements in its discussion; those are kept separate from the present cohort's results and are not verified against the cited sources here.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a narrative review with heterogeneous cited populations, qualitative language, and no single source-wide denominator or reference standard. Several localizing or lateralizing statements are explicitly qualified as usual, typical, reported, suggested, or disputed; those qualifiers are retained. The review warns that scalp-inaccessible onset or propagation into eloquent cortex can produce false localization, so semiology may represent propagation rather than seizure origination. The cited articles were not inspected, and no outside source, public atlas, registry, prior review, sibling report, or handoff was used. Pages 7–10 contain only the article’s bibliography after the review text; bibliography entries were not treated as findings. No page was unreadable or blocked.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The document reports a narrative review and does not report a systematic-search method, single enrollment cohort, eligibility criteria, pooled analysis, or source-wide reference standard. Population descriptors are claim-specific and heterogeneous, including temporal-lobe, mesial-temporal, neocortical-temporal, frontal-versus-temporal, childhood, older-adult, benign mesial-temporal, and cited study cohorts. The review discusses 31 Engel class 1 patients in one cited symptom-cluster analysis and a 50-patient sample in one cited facial-asymmetry result; those cohort descriptors are retained only with the corresponding findings. It also reports lesion/etiologic context, including mesial temporal sclerosis or hippocampal sclerosis as a common cause of TLE and HS evidence in benign mTLE, but those context statements are not treated as stand-alone semiologic findings. No source-wide analysis unit, surgery-outcome analysis, or mortality-outcome analysis is reported. Cited-study restatements remain unverified against the cited articles under this review boundary.
sources.source_report_summary: This 2012 Review Article by Robert D. G. Blair, “Temporal Lobe Epilepsy Semiology,” is a narrative review of temporal-lobe seizure semiology and its localization or lateralization, including temporal-versus-frontal differential features, auras, automatisms, motor, autonomic, speech, age-related, childhood, sleep/wake, symptom-cluster, orgasmic-aura, and benign-mesial-temporal patterns. It is relevant as a source-authored synthesis and as a container for cited-study restatements; it is not a single primary cohort or pooled analysis.

When discharge did not remain local, prefrontal or premotor onset propagated toward more caudal regions (premotor or precentral); caudal-to-rostral propagation was not observed.

findings.claim: Hierarchical clustering identified Group 1 (16 patients) with elementary motor signs including early clonic, contralateral tonic or versive, somesthetic localized aura, asymmetric tonic, and asymmetric facial signs, with gestural motor behavior and emotional features absent; rolandic BA4, low-BA4 rolandic operculum, parietal cortex, and other caudal or premotor regions were involved. Group 2 (23 patients) combined symmetric proximal or axial tonic posture or chapeau de gendarme with nonintegrated gestural motor behavior, often nonlocalized aura or vocalization, while integrated behavior, distal stereotypies, early clonic signs, and fixed facial expression were absent; premotor and lateral prefrontal regions were frequently co-involved, commonly with lateral-to-medial propagation. Group 3 (10 patients) showed integrated gestural behavior with distal stereotypies, fixed facial or positive emotional expression, proximal stereotypies, and speech production, with elementary motor signs absent; the early spread network involved rostral ventrolateral prefrontal BA47/12, BA10, BA11, BA46 and rostral cingulate BA32 or rostral BA24. Group 4 (5 patients) showed integrated fearful behavior, sometimes hyperkinetic, with fight or escape attempts, frightened expression, occasional screaming or swearing, and autonomic signs, with elementary motor signs absent; orbital or medial prefrontal BA14, BA32/24r, BA10 propagated to amygdala and anterior temporal regions but not lateral frontal cortex.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a selected presurgical SEEG cohort with hypothesis-driven electrode placement and frontal-lobe EZ, so the findings do not directly generalize to unselected epilepsy or unsampled networks. The early spread network includes propagation during emergence of signs and is not identical to the EZ; the study is observational and correlational. The source describes 20 sampled cortical regions in one methods passage but 24 brain-area variables in the analysis matrices, without reconciliation. PCA variance is reported as 42.36% in the Results and 44.36% in the Supporting Information notice; the online supporting material is not included in the locked PDF. Whole-group percentage denominators and several group-specific feature denominators are not stated, and no left/right hemisphere lateralization accuracy is reported. Cited-study restatements in F009-F013 were not verified against their cited sources.
sources.source_report_methods_population: Consecutive presurgical SEEG series from Timone Hospital, Marseille, February 2000-November 2010: 54 patients in whom SEEG-defined EZ was within the frontal lobe, selected from 180 SEEG explorations; patients with inconclusive intracranial recording (n=1) or a nonpredominantly frontal EZ were excluded. All patients had noninvasive presurgical assessment and video-SEEG after complete or partial antiepileptic-drug withdrawal; 374 seizures were recorded and analyzed. The cohort included 22 male and 32 female patients, mean age 24.9 +/- 9.5 years, mean epilepsy duration 16.9 +/- 8 years, and 27/54 with normal MRI. Three epileptologists independently reviewed VEEG and electrical data; 31 ictal signs and 24 brain-area variables were scored 0-1-2 per patient, with rank-based PCA, hierarchical clustering, correlation matrices, and Kendall tests at p < 0.05. The source describes sampling 20 cortical regions in one methods passage and distinguishes the SEEG-defined EZ from the source-defined early spread network.
sources.source_report_summary: Bonini et al., “Frontal lobe seizures: From clinical semiology to localization” (Epilepsia 2014;55:264-277; DOI 10.1111/epi.12490), an original empirical SEEG study relating ictal semiology to anatomic early-spread networks in a selected frontal lobe epilepsy cohort.

findings.claim: In this 54-patient frontal-lobe epilepsy series, hierarchical analysis identified four semiologic groups associated with different early spread/anatomic patterns: Group 1 had elementary motor signs with precentral/premotor involvement; Group 2 had elementary motor plus nonintegrated gestural behavior with premotor/prefrontal involvement; Group 3 had integrated gestural behavior with distal stereotypies and anterior lateral/medial prefrontal involvement; and Group 4 had fearful behavior with ventromedial prefrontal/anterior temporal paralimbic involvement.
findings.evidence_text: “Four main groups of patients were identified” and correlated with specific anatomic seizure-localization patterns.
findings.laterality_localization: Rostrocaudal anatomical organization from precentral/premotor through premotor/prefrontal and anterior lateral/medial prefrontal to ventromedial prefrontal/anterior temporal regions; no left/right hemisphere direction reported
findings.limitations: The anatomical measure is the early spread network, which includes activity during clinical-sign production and is distinct from the EZ.

findings.claim: In all recorded seizures, clinical signs began after SEEG ictal discharge. Electrical onset to completion of clinical semiology ranged from 1 to 12 s (median 4 s), and the electrical-to-clinical-onset interval ranged from 0.5 to 10 s (median 3 s); shorter values usually occurred with motor/premotor onset, longer values with prefrontal onset, and five patients had particularly long delays. When discharge originating in prefrontal or premotor regions propagated, it tended toward caudal premotor/precentral regions; caudal-to-rostral propagation was not observed.

findings.claim: The sign-area correlation matrix showed a diagonal posterior-to-anterior pattern. Early clonic signs, contralateral versive signs, contralateral tonic posture, and somesthetic localized aura correlated with more caudal areas such as primary motor cortex and rolandic operculum, whereas staring, speech arrest, manipulation behavior, and fixed facial expression correlated with more rostral/frontopolar areas. Early clonic signs and manipulation behavior were relatively region-specific, while hyperkinetic movements and impairment of consciousness were weaker, more distributed associations involving caudal and rostral prefrontal regions; the diagonal pattern remained for significant correlations.

findings.claim: Group 1 comprised 16 patients and was characterized by one or more elementary motor signs, including clonic signs, contralateral tonic posture, contralateral versive signs, asymmetric tonic posture, secondary generalization, or asymmetric facial contraction; somesthetic localized aura and tonic vocalization could also occur. Gestural motor behavior and emotional features were absent. Its early spread network showed significant involvement of rolandic cortex (BA 4), rolandic operculum (low BA 4), and parietal cortex, with other caudal and premotor regions also possible; discharge could begin in medial or lateral premotor regions or propagate lateromedially.

Nonlocalized aura and complex nonverbal vocalization were also frequent; integrated gestural behavior, distal stereotypies, early clonic signs, and fixed facial expression never occurred. Both premotor and lateral prefrontal regions were frequently co-involved; lateral-to-medial propagation was more frequent, although medial premotor onset could propagate laterally.

findings.claim: The authors interpret the four clusters as a continuum rather than rigid compartments: the most anterior prefrontal seizures showed the most integrated behavior, posterior prefrontal seizures progressively less integrated behavior, and still more posterior motor seizures exclusively elementary motor signs without a gestural component. Group 2 was described as a transition zone in which more anterior organization could show coordinated rocking and more posterior organization prominent tonic posturing that hindered gestural behavior.

They observed lateral prefrontal discharge tending to propagate to anterior cingulate and pre-SMA, and SMA/pre-SMA discharge tending to propagate to lateral areas 6 and 8; medial premotor and cingulate regions were proposed as a possible “final common pathway” for anterior frontal seizure organization.

sources.source_report_limitations: The cohort is a single-center, presurgical SEEG-selected population: 54 frontal-lobe cases from 180 explorations, with electrode sampling and clinical ascertainment determined by presurgical hypotheses. The early spread network is not the EZ, and many reported associations include propagation during clinical-sign production. Group membership resulted from a chosen hierarchical-clustering cut, and the authors themselves characterize the groups as a continuum. Several percentage results lack numerators and use “patients” versus “cases” inconsistently. The main text reports three PCA components explaining 42.36% of variance, whereas the Supporting Information notice reports 44.36%; the same notice lists online Table S1 and Figures S1–S2, which are not included in this 14-page PDF. Methods text also describes 20 sampled cortical regions and later reports 24 brain-area variables. Contralateral/ipsilateral sign terminology appears in the source, but no dedicated left/right hemisphere lateralization analysis or side-specific diagnostic accuracy is reported.
sources.source_report_methods_population: This single-center presurgical series included 54 patients whose SEEG-defined epileptogenic zone (EZ) predominantly involved the frontal lobe, selected from 180 SEEG explorations performed from February 2000 through November 2010; one inconclusive exploration and nonpredominantly frontal cases were excluded. The cohort included 22 male and 32 female patients, mean age 24.9 ± 9.5 years, mean epilepsy duration 16.9 ± 8 years, and 27/54 with normal MRI. Three epileptologists independently reviewed all seizures and scored presence/absence of 31 ictal signs; each patient's sign was assigned 0, 1, or 2 according to reproducibility. The “early spread network” was the cortical tissue involved from electrical onset through completion of clinical semiology and was explicitly distinguished from the EZ. SEEG sampling is described as 20 frontal cortical regions, while the later matrices are described as containing 24 brain-area variables. Analyses used correlation matrices, Kendall tests with p < 0.05, PCA on rank-transformed sign scores, hierarchical clustering, and value-test ≥ 2 to identify characteristic variables.
sources.source_report_summary: Bonini et al., “Frontal lobe seizures: From clinical semiology to localization” (Epilepsia 55(2):264–277, 2014; doi: 10.1111/epi.12490), is a full-length original research report. It examines whether semiologic subgroups in frontal lobe seizures correlate with anatomic organization using SEEG-recorded ictal clinical and electrical data.

findings.citation: Bancaud and Talairach 1965; McGonigal et al. 2007; Wendling et al. 2003
findings.claim: The review presents semiology as an evolving consequence of ictal electrical activity spreading through neural pathways in time and space: clinical signs appear after a variable lag and install more slowly in temporal than frontal seizures, and SEEG relates discharge timing and spread to clinical expression.
findings.evidence_text: Clinical signs evolve as discharge spreads in time and space; the review states that temporal seizures generally propagate more slowly than frontal seizures and that the onset lag may range from milliseconds to seconds.
findings.laterality_localization: Seizure-onset and propagation network; no fixed single-site assignment
findings.limitations: No unified cohort or pooled timing estimate
findings.locators: PDF p.1, abstract; PDF p.2, section 3
findings.measure: Time lag is described as variable from milliseconds to seconds; temporal versus frontal propagation is described qualitatively as slower versus faster
findings.phase: Electrical seizure onset through first clinical sign and full clinical expression
findings.population: Heterogeneous SEEG, stimulation, and clinical literature synthesized by the review; no single cohort
findings.source_term: seizure spread in time and space
findings.uncertainty: Source reports substantial variability; no summary distribution is reported

findings.citation: Talairach and Bancaud 1966; Bonini et al. 2013; Penfield 1958
findings.claim: The structures involved in producing semiology form an early spread network tightly linked to the epileptogenic zone; its anatomical extent and the frequencies developed immediately after onset can produce different clinical features even when seizures arise from the same region, and fast immediate invasion of sensory or cognitive areas can abolish conscious perception.
findings.comparator: Same onset region with different early spread extent or frequency
findings.evidence_text: The review calls the early spread zone the organic link between the epileptogenic zone and emergence of semiology and states that immediate fast invasion may produce no conscious perception.
findings.laterality_localization: Epileptogenic zone versus the anatomically distributed early spread network; no fixed body-side direction
findings.limitations: Mechanistic attribution between frequency and spread rate remains unresolved in the source
findings.locators: PDF p.1, abstract; PDF p.4, section 5
findings.measure: Qualitative relation of early spread extent and discharge frequency to clinical phenotype
findings.phase: Immediately after seizure onset and during early ictal spread
findings.population: Heterogeneous motor, sensory, and cognitive seizure observations synthesized by the review; no single cohort
findings.source_term: early spread network / early spread zone
findings.uncertainty: The review states that the relative roles of frequency and spread rate are not yet understood

findings.claim: Semiology is described as more elementary and directly sensory or motor when primary cortex is involved, whereas associative-cortex seizures produce more complex cognitive or behavioral signs through distributed cortical networks.
findings.evidence_text: The abstract contrasts direct primary-cortex relations producing visual or auditory hallucinations and elementary sensorimotor signs with associative-cortex involvement producing altered cognitive or behavioral signs.
findings.laterality_localization: Primary sensory or motor cortex versus distributed associative networks; no fixed side stated
findings.limitations: No quantitative boundary between primary and associative manifestations is reported
findings.locators: PDF p.1, abstract; PDF p.2, section 3

findings.uncertainty: Source describes a general organizational principle rather than a quantified rule

findings.citation: Ikeda et al. 2000; Tassinari et al. 1998; Shibasaki et al. 1994
findings.claim: The review states that discharge frequency changes the peripheral expression of a seizure: fast gamma activity tends to deactivate normal function, whereas slower theta activity can mimic physiological function; in the same motor region, lower-frequency or phasic activity can produce a jerk while higher-frequency oscillation can produce arrest of posture or voluntary movement.
findings.comparator: Fast gamma or higher-frequency discharge versus slower theta or phasic discharge
findings.evidence_text: The review links fast gamma activity with functional deactivation and slower theta activity with physiological mimicry, and contrasts a phasic discharge producing a myoclonic jerk with higher-frequency oscillation producing motor arrest.
findings.laterality_localization: Primary motor and other cortical regions; no fixed body-side direction
findings.limitations: No numeric frequency thresholds are reported
findings.locators: PDF p.1, abstract; PDF p.4, sections 4-5
findings.population: Heterogeneous motor-seizure and stimulation literature; no single cohort
findings.source_term: discharge frequency and positive or negative semiology
findings.uncertainty: Source presents frequency as a crucial determinant but does not define a universal cutoff

findings.citation: Manford et al. 1996; Ryvlin et al. 2006
findings.claim: The review cautions that many studies found no significant localizing value for isolated signs or symptoms when lesion or resection region was used as reference, and that assigning an entire ictal sequence to the area of seizure onset is also misleading; the relevant object is the evolving anatomo-electro-clinical network.
findings.comparator: Isolated-sign or onset-only interpretation versus full network analysis
findings.evidence_text: The review states that isolated signs often fail to show significant localizing value and that attributing an entire clinical sequence to paroxysmal activity at seizure onset is misleading.
findings.laterality_localization: Lesion or surgical-resection reference versus seizure-onset and propagated network; no fixed side
findings.limitations: This finding is a review-level methodological conclusion, not a new comparative analysis
findings.locators: PDF p.2, section 3; PDF p.8, section 10
findings.measure: Qualitative evidence appraisal; no pooled estimate
findings.phase: Isolated signs and complete ictal sequence across onset and spread
findings.population: Clinical-localization studies summarized by the review; study-specific populations and denominators are not reported here
findings.source_term: localizing value of isolated signs and complete ictal sequences
findings.uncertainty: Source describes the localizing value as complex and context-dependent

findings.citation: Panayiotopoulos 1999; Jobst et al. 2010; Williamson et al. 1992
findings.claim: The review reports that an elementary visual hallucination such as colored circles, twinkling stars, or moving flies in the left superior visual-field quadrant indicates discharge in the right infra-calcarine cortex, and that elementary hallucinations do not arise in spontaneous seizures beginning in structures distant from visual cortex.
findings.comparator: Elementary hallucination with visual-cortex onset versus spontaneous seizure onset distant from visual cortex
findings.evidence_text: The review gives the example of moving flies in the left superior visual-field quadrant indicating right infra-calcarine discharge and states that elementary hallucinations do not arise from distant onset structures.
findings.laterality_localization: Left superior visual field mapped to right infra-calcarine cortex; contralateral visual-field relation
findings.limitations: Cited restatement; the cited source was not independently reviewed

findings.population: Cited intracranial-stimulation, surgically treated, and spontaneous-seizure observations; cohort details are not reported in this review
findings.uncertainty: The cited source populations and diagnostic performance are not reported here

findings.citation: Bien et al. 2000; Halgren and Chauvel 1993; Manford and Andermann 1998
findings.claim: Complex visual phenomena such as dyschromatopsia or metamorphopsia are described as implying temporal or occipito-temporal seizure organization with discharge in visual associative areas rather than primary visual onset; the review distinguishes hallucination at the cortical entry from distortion or illusion at downstream interpreter sites.
findings.comparator: Elementary hallucination or primary visual entry versus complex visual distortion or associative visual involvement
findings.evidence_text: The review places altered color perception and metamorphopsia with temporal or occipito-temporal organization and visual associative discharge, distinguishing them from elementary primary-visual hallucinations.
findings.laterality_localization: Temporal or occipito-temporal associative visual areas versus primary visual cortex; side not reported

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a narrative review rather than a single primary cohort or quantitative meta-analysis. Its scientific content mixes review-authored synthesis, cited-study restatements, and illustrative case or figure observations; cited sources remain unverified cited restatements under this review boundary. The review reports percentages of 80% and 41–55% for the auditory-stimulation comparison without numerator or denominator, and reports statistically significant synchronization differences without p values, intervals, or sample sizes. It provides no unified denominator, no pooled estimate, and no universal sign-to-lobe rule. Pages 9–10 are reference pages and were inspected but do not add source-reported scientific findings beyond the cited-source identities used for attribution.
sources.source_report_methods_population: This is a narrative review with no single study cohort, unified eligibility population, or common comparator. The evidence discussed spans heterogeneous SEEG recordings, cortical stimulation observations, clinical/video studies, ictal SPECT, and cited cases or series. Finding-specific populations and analysis units are retained below; where the review does not report a denominator, it is marked NOT_REPORTED rather than inferred.
sources.source_report_summary: Chauvel and McGonigal, “Emergence of semiology in epileptic seizures” (Epilepsy & Behavior 38, 2014), is a narrative review of seizure semiology using anatomo-electro-clinical correlations, SEEG, electrical stimulation, video/clinical observations, cited case and series reports, and network physiology. It is relevant to the atlas because it describes sensory, motor, cognitive, emotional, language, consciousness, localization, and laterality relationships as dynamic network phenomena. It does not present one new cohort or one unified quantitative dataset.

findings.citation: Liou J-Y, Smith EH, Bateman LM, et al. A model for focal seizure onset, propagation, evolution, and progression. Elife 2020;9:e50927.
findings.claim: The review states that clinical signs evolve as seizures propagate and may be generated by slow activation of brain areas or faster disruption of connected networks; it contrasts an ictal wavefront of about 1 mm/s with a faster ictal discharge of about 300 mm/s detected by EEG, which does not necessarily mean the recruited cortex is firing.
findings.comparator: Slow ictal wavefront versus faster ictal discharge
findings.evidence_text: EEG detects rapid propagation into an area but does not establish that the area is firing; semiology can reflect activation or network disruption.
findings.laterality_localization: Symptomatogenic-zone and propagation anatomy; no body-side direction
findings.limitations: Rapid subcortical and network recruitment can make observed semiology reflect spread rather than seizure onset.
findings.locators: PDF p.1, Introduction; PDF p.2, Introduction
findings.measure: Ictal wavefront about 1 mm/s; faster ictal discharge about 300 mm/s
findings.population: NOT_REPORTED
findings.uncertainty: Source uses “about” for both propagation rates

findings.citation: Elwan S, Alexopoulos A, Silveira DC, et al. Lateralizing and localizing value of seizure semiology: comparison with scalp EEG, MRI and PET in patients successfully treated with resective epilepsy surgery. Seizure 2018;61:203–8.
findings.claim: In a cited series of patients successfully treated with epilepsy surgery, seizure semiology was correctly lateralising in 74% and correctly localising in 77%, which the review describes as on a par with scalp EEG and MRI.
findings.evidence_text: The review reports semiology as correctly lateralising in 74% and correctly localising in 77% of patients.
findings.laterality_localization: Correct hemispheric lateralization and anatomical localization; direction NOT_REPORTED
findings.limitations: The current review does not report the cited study’s cohort denominator or endpoint definitions beyond these percentages.
findings.locators: PDF p.2, Introduction
findings.population: Patients successfully treated with resective epilepsy surgery
findings.source_term: localising and lateralising value of seizure semiology

findings.claim: Table 2 contrasts frontal seizures as often daily, sleep-typical, abrupt, usually brief, rapidly evolving, less often automatistic, early and prominently complex-motor, commonly hypermotor, loud and nonspeech in vocalization, more often secondarily generalized, and followed by shorter or less prominent postictal confusion, versus temporal seizures as less frequent, less sleep-associated, gradual, usually longer, gradually evolving, more often and longer automatistic, later and less frequent complex-motor, rarely hypermotor, sometimes ictal speech in the nondominant hemisphere, less often secondarily generalized, and followed by longer or more prominent postictal confusion.
findings.comparator: Frontal lobe versus temporal lobe seizures
findings.evidence_text: Table 2 lists abrupt, brief, rapidly evolving frontal seizures versus gradual, longer temporal seizures, with the stated differences in automatisms, complex motor features, vocalization, generalization, and postictal confusion.
findings.laterality_localization: Nondominant hemisphere specified only for ictal speech; no general side direction
findings.limitations: The table footnote states that listed durations can be longer; rapid propagation can confound clinical distinctions.
findings.locators: PDF p.2, Frontal lobe seizures; PDF p.4, Temporal lobe seizures; PDF p.5, Table 2
findings.measure: Qualitative frontal-versus-temporal comparison across frequency, sleep, onset, duration, evolution, automatisms, complex motor features, hypermotor activity, vocalization, secondary generalization, and postictal confusion
findings.population: Focal seizure semiology; exact cohort NOT_REPORTED
findings.source_term: frontal lobe seizures versus temporal lobe seizures

findings.citation: Bonini F, McGonigal A, Trébuchon A, et al. Frontal lobe seizures: from clinical semiology to localization. Epilepsia 2014;55:264–77.; McGonigal A, Chauvel P. Prefrontal seizures manifesting as motor stereotypies. Mov Disord 2014;29:1181–5.
findings.claim: The review reports that intracranial stereo-EEG studies associate elementary clonic, tonic, and versive signs with precentral and premotor regions; more complex motor signs with more rostral frontal regions; non-integrated proximal stereotypies such as rocking and turning with premotor and posterior prefrontal regions; and integrated distal stereotypies such as manual automatisms with anterior prefrontal regions including orbitofrontal cortex, frontal pole, and anterior cingulate.
findings.comparator: Elementary versus complex and non-integrated versus integrated motor phenomena
findings.evidence_text: Intracranial studies are summarized as linking elementary motor signs to precentral/premotor regions and complex or stereotyped behaviors to progressively more rostral frontal regions.
findings.laterality_localization: Frontal regional localization; no body-side direction
findings.limitations: The review states that rapid propagation can confound these distinctions in clinical practice.
findings.locators: PDF p.2, Frontal lobe seizures
findings.measure: Qualitative regional comparison of motor and gestural semiology
findings.population: Patients in intracranial stereo-EEG studies; exact cohorts NOT_REPORTED
findings.source_term: elementary motor signs; complex motor signs; gestural behaviour

findings.citation: McGonigal A, Chauvel P. Frontal lobe epilepsy: seizure semiology and presurgical evaluation. Pract Neurol 2004;4:260–73.
findings.claim: Seizures from primary motor cortex comprise contralateral unilateral clonic, and sometimes tonic or myoclonic, activity that can spread to adjacent body parts in a Jacksonian march along the motor homunculus; the starting face, upper limb, or lower limb can distinguish lateral from medial precentral onset.
findings.evidence_text: Contralateral clonic activity may spread through the motor homunculus as a Jacksonian march.
findings.laterality_localization: Motor activity is contralateral to primary motor cortex onset; face, upper-limb, or lower-limb onset localizes along the precentral homunculus
findings.limitations: The source attributes the march to propagation through motor cortex, so the first observed sign and later spread are not interchangeable.
findings.locators: PDF p.2, Primary motor cortex; PDF p.3, Figure 1
findings.population: NOT_REPORTED

findings.claim: In the review’s video case 1, a 50-year-old man with a cystic lesion in the right middle frontal gyrus had an aura followed by behavioural arrest, left-face clonic movements spreading over the left arm, then left-arm extension in a fencing posture before secondary generalisation; the semiology and ictal EEG pointed to right frontocentral/right hemispheric onset.
findings.evidence_text: The case had left-face clonus spreading to the left arm, followed by left-arm extension, with right frontocentral ictal EEG onset.
findings.laterality_localization: Left face/arm signs contralateral to right frontocentral onset; left-arm fencing posture indicating supplementary motor area involvement
findings.limitations: Single illustrative case; the reported lesion, EEG, and clinical semiology are concordant but do not establish general diagnostic accuracy.
findings.locators: PDF p.3, Video case 1; PDF p.4, Figure 2 and Video case 1 description
findings.phase: Ictal onset, propagation, and secondary generalization
findings.population: Single case: 50-year-old man with focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures and a right middle frontal gyrus lesion

findings.citation: Ikeda A, Sato T, Ohara S, et al. “Supplementary motor area (SMA) seizure” rather than “SMA epilepsy” in optimal surgical candidates: a document of subdural mapping. J Neurol Sci 2002;202:43–52.; Werhahn KJ, Noachtar S, Arnold S, et al. Tonic seizures: their significance for lateralization and frequency in different focal epileptic syndromes. Epilepsia 2000;41:1153–61.; Sitthinamsuwan B, Usui N, Tottori T, et al. Seizures with tonic posturing: Semiologic difference between supplementary sensorimotor area (SSMA) origin and extra-SSMA origin. Epilepsia 2016;57:e39–44.
findings.claim: Supplementary motor area seizures are characterized by asymmetric bilateral tonic posturing, with or without impaired awareness, sometimes with contralateral upper-limb extension and ipsilateral upper-limb flexion in a fencing posture plus contralateral head and eye deviation; sensory tingling or tightness may precede the motor signs.
findings.evidence_text: The source describes asymmetric bilateral tonic posturing with contralateral extension, ipsilateral flexion, and contralateral head and eye deviation.
findings.laterality_localization: Upper-limb extension and head/eye deviation are described relative to the hemisphere of onset: extension and deviation contralateral, flexion ipsilateral
findings.limitations: Asymmetric tonic posturing can also arise from parietal or occipital seizures; extrafrontal seizures are more likely to have preceding aura or impaired awareness.
findings.locators: PDF p.3, Supplementary motor area; PDF p.4, Supplementary motor area
findings.population: NOT_REPORTED
findings.source_term: supplementary motor area seizure; fencing posture

findings.citation: Bonini F, McGonigal A, Trébuchon A, et al. Frontal lobe seizures: from clinical semiology to localization. Epilepsia 2014;55:264–77.; McGonigal A, Chauvel P. Prefrontal seizures manifesting as motor stereotypies. Mov Disord 2014;29:1181–5.; Chibane IS, Boucher O, Dubeau F, et al. Orbitofrontal epilepsy: case series and review of literature. Epilepsy Behav 2017;76:32–8.; Ikeda A, Hirasawa K-ichi, Kinoshita M, et al. Negative motor seizure arising from the negative motor area: is it ictal apraxia? Epilepsia 2009;50:2072–84.; Kovac S, Diehl B, Wehner T, et al. Gelastic seizures: incidence, clinical and EEG features in adult patients undergoing video-EEG telemetry. Epilepsia 2015;56:e1–5.
findings.claim: The review associates orbitofrontal seizures with impaired awareness, automatisms, occasional olfactory aura, ictal tachycardia, and complex motor evolution; frontopolar seizures with impaired awareness followed by motor features; ventromedial prefrontal/anterior cingulate seizures with forced thinking, fear, and hypermotor features; contralateral dorsolateral frontal seizures involving frontal eye fields with early head and eye version; dominant frontal or Broca-region seizures with dysphasia; and frontal operculum seizures with unilateral face clonus, laryngeal symptoms, hypersalivation, and articulation difficulty.
findings.comparator: Orbitofrontal, frontopolar, ventromedial prefrontal/anterior cingulate, dorsolateral frontal, dominant frontal, and frontal opercular regions
findings.evidence_text: The region-specific associations include orbitofrontal automatisms, frontal-eye-field head/eye version, dominant-hemisphere dysphasia, and frontal-opercular facial/laryngeal signs.
findings.laterality_localization: Frontal regional associations; head version is described for contralateral frontal eye-field involvement and dysphasia for dominant-hemisphere involvement
findings.limitations: Spread to the insula creates substantial overlap with insular semiology; rapid propagation may obscure the onset region.
findings.locators: PDF p.3, Figure 1; PDF p.4, Other frontal regions
findings.population: NOT_REPORTED

findings.claim: In video case 2, a 24-year-old man had hyperkinetic seizures from sleep, right orbitofrontal PET hypometabolism, stereo-EEG onset in the right orbitofrontal region, progression to bilateral tonic seizures with loss of awareness when the seizure spread to the supplementary motor area, and seizure freedom after right orbitofrontal resection.
findings.evidence_text: Stereo-EEG showed right orbitofrontal onset and tonic features after spread to supplementary motor contacts; the patient was seizure free after resection.
findings.laterality_localization: Right orbitofrontal onset; tonic features appeared when activity spread to the supplementary motor area
findings.limitations: Single illustrative case with concordant PET, stereo-EEG, and outcome; it does not establish that hyperkinetic seizures generally localize to orbitofrontal cortex.
findings.locators: PDF p.4, Video case 2; PDF p.5, Figure 3
findings.phase: Ictal onset, propagation, and postoperative outcome
findings.population: Single case: 24-year-old man with non-lesional hyperkinetic seizures

findings.citation: Blair RDG. Temporal lobe epilepsy semiology. Epilepsy Res Treat 2012;2012:1–10.
findings.claim: The review states that temporal lobes are the most frequent focal-seizure origin and that two thirds of people with refractory epilepsy assessed for potential surgery have temporal lobe seizures; temporal seizures typically include behavioural arrest, manual and oral automatisms in two thirds, variable loss of awareness, and postictal confusion.
findings.evidence_text: The source describes temporal seizures as commonly involving behavioural arrest, manual/oral automatisms, impaired awareness, and postictal confusion.
findings.laterality_localization: Temporal-lobe localization; no side direction
findings.limitations: The review does not provide endpoint numerators or denominators for either “two thirds” statement and notes overlap with frontal seizures.
findings.locators: PDF p.4, Temporal lobe seizures; PDF p.5, Temporal lobe seizures
findings.measure: Temporal lobe seizures in two thirds of the stated population; behavioural arrest and manual/oral automatisms in two thirds
findings.population: People with refractory epilepsy assessed for potential surgery

findings.citation: Henkel A, Noachtar S, Pfänder M, et al. The localizing value of the abdominal aura and its evolution: a study in focal epilepsies. Neurology 2002;58:271–6.
findings.claim: An abdominal aura, such as a rising epigastric sensation or abdominal discomfort, is reported as highly associated with temporal lobe epilepsy with a probability of 74%, and evolution of the abdominal aura into an automotor seizure increases the probability to 98%.
findings.comparator: Abdominal aura alone versus abdominal aura evolving into automotor seizure
findings.evidence_text: The review reports a 74% probability for temporal lobe epilepsy with abdominal aura and 98% when it evolves into an automotor seizure.
findings.laterality_localization: Temporal-lobe localization; no side direction
findings.limitations: The current review does not state the cited endpoint denominator or whether the probabilities refer to patients, seizures, or another analysis unit.
findings.locators: PDF p.5, Auras
findings.measure: Probability 74% for abdominal aura and 98% after evolution to automotor seizure
findings.phase: Aura and subsequent ictal automotor evolution
findings.population: Patients with focal epilepsies in the cited study; exact cohort NOT_REPORTED

findings.citation: Maillard L, Vignal J-P, Gavaret M, et al. Semiologic and electrophysiologic correlations in temporal lobe seizure subtypes. Epilepsia 2004;45:1590–9.
findings.claim: In a cited study of 187 temporal lobe seizures assessed by intracranial stereo-EEG, abdominal aura and experiential phenomena including fear, déjà vu, and jamais vu indicated mesiotemporal seizures, whereas elemental auditory aura indicated lateral onset involving Heschl’s gyrus or primary auditory cortex.
findings.evidence_text: The review contrasts abdominal/experiential auras for mesiotemporal seizures with elemental auditory aura for lateral onset in 187 intracranial stereo-EEG seizures.
findings.laterality_localization: Mesiotemporal versus lateral temporal onset; elemental auditory aura indicates lateral onset in Heschl’s gyrus/primary auditory cortex, without a hemisphere direction
findings.limitations: The review does not provide the cited study’s subgroup numerators, denominators, or uncertainty estimates.
findings.locators: PDF p.5, Auras
findings.population: 187 temporal lobe seizures assessed by intracranial stereo-EEG
findings.source_term: abdominal aura; experiential phenomena; elemental auditory aura

findings.citation: Du X, Usui N, Terada K, et al. Semiological and electroencephalographic features of epilepsy with amygdalar lesion. Epilepsy Res 2015;111:45–53.
findings.claim: The review states that early apnoea and tachycardia in mesial temporal lobe seizures indicate involvement of the amygdala.
findings.evidence_text: Early apnoea and tachycardia are described as indicating amygdala involvement.
findings.laterality_localization: Mesial temporal/amygdalar involvement; hemisphere direction NOT_REPORTED
findings.limitations: The review does not report the cited study’s endpoint denominator or the sensitivity or specificity of these signs.
findings.locators: PDF p.5, Mesial temporal lobe including hippocampus
findings.population: Patients with epilepsy and an amygdalar lesion in the cited study; exact cohort NOT_REPORTED
findings.source_term: early apnoea and tachycardia; amygdala involvement

findings.citation: Marashly A, Ewida A, Agarwal R, et al. Ictal motor sequences: lateralization and localization values. Epilepsia 2016;57:369–75.; Chabardès S, Kahane P, Minotti L, et al. The temporopolar cortex plays a pivotal role in temporal lobe seizures. Brain 2005;128:1818–31.
findings.claim: Mesial temporal seizures may have experiential or abdominal auras and early autonomic phenomena, then behavioural arrest, manual or oral automatisms, and impaired awareness; unilateral dystonic posturing is described as contralateral, and mesial seizures tend to be longer than lateral temporal seizures and less often evolve to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures.
findings.comparator: Mesial temporal versus lateral/neocortical temporal seizures
findings.evidence_text: The source links mesial temporal seizures to aura, autonomic symptoms, automatisms, impaired awareness, contralateral dystonia, longer duration, and less frequent bilateral tonic-clonic evolution.
findings.laterality_localization: Unilateral dystonic posturing is contralateral to the mesial temporal focus; mesial versus lateral temporal localization otherwise has no side direction
findings.limitations: Reciprocal mesial-neocortical connections produce semiologic overlap; no uniform cohort or endpoint denominator is given.
findings.locators: PDF p.5, Mesial temporal lobe including hippocampus; PDF p.6, Mesial temporal lobe including hippocampus
findings.phase: Aura, ictal evolution, and secondary generalization
findings.population: NOT_REPORTED

findings.claim: In video case 3, a 36-year-old right-handed man with a left amygdala/hippocampal-head cavernoma had déjà vu and epigastric rising followed by oral and manual automatisms and loss of awareness; before generalization, right head and eye version and a figure-of-4 posture with the left arm flexed and right arm extended lateralised onset to the left hemisphere, concordant with left temporal EEG onset.
findings.evidence_text: The case combined left-temporal EEG onset with right version and a left-flexed/right-extended figure-of-4 posture before generalization.
findings.laterality_localization: Right head/eye version and right-arm extension with left-arm flexion indicated left-hemispheric/left-temporal onset
findings.limitations: Single illustrative case; the case does not establish the general performance of the figure-of-4 sign.
findings.locators: PDF p.6, Video case 3 and Figure 4
findings.population: Single case: 36-year-old right-handed man with a left mesiotemporal cavernoma
findings.source_term: psychic and abdominal aura; figure-of-4 sign

findings.citation: Maillard L, Vignal J-P, Gavaret M, et al. Semiologic and electrophysiologic correlations in temporal lobe seizure subtypes. Epilepsia 2004;45:1590–9.
findings.claim: Auras are less common in lateral temporal seizures and may be auditory or vertiginous; elementary sounds suggest primary auditory cortex, complex sounds or distortions auditory association areas, unilateral elementary auditory aura contralateral onset, and early ictal dysphasia dominant-hemisphere involvement. Compared with mesial temporal seizures, lateral temporal seizures are shorter, have earlier loss of awareness, more frontal propagation with complex motor features, and more frequent bilateral tonic-clonic evolution, although reciprocal connections create overlap.
findings.evidence_text: The review associates elementary auditory aura with primary auditory cortex and unilateral elementary auditory aura with contralateral onset, while describing shorter and earlier-evolving lateral temporal seizures.
findings.laterality_localization: Unilateral elementary auditory aura is contralateral to onset; ictal dysphasia suggests dominant-hemisphere involvement; auditory localization includes primary and association cortex
findings.limitations: Reciprocal mesial-neocortical connections limit the distinction; ictal dysphasia is a localizing as well as lateralizing clue only when its clinical context is clear.
findings.locators: PDF p.6, Lateral/neocortical temporal lobe
findings.population: NOT_REPORTED

findings.claim: In video case 4, a 27-year-old woman with a psychic aura and occasional ear noise had ictal dysphasia; she could follow visual but not verbal commands, with expressive-language and reading impairment, and PET, statistical analysis, and ictal EEG indicated a left temporal neocortical onset extending toward the temporoparieto-occipital junction.
findings.evidence_text: The patient followed visual but not verbal commands during stereotypical seizures, with left temporal PET and ictal EEG findings.
findings.laterality_localization: Left temporal/neocortical onset involving the superior temporal gyrus and temporoparieto-occipital junction; dominant-language impairment described
findings.limitations: Single illustrative case; the source notes that lateral and mesial temporal semiology overlaps.
findings.locators: PDF p.6, Video case 4; PDF p.7, Figure 5
findings.population: Single case: 27-year-old woman with non-lesional seizures

findings.citation: Salanova V. Parietal lobe epilepsy. J Clin Neurophysiol 2012;29:392–6.
findings.claim: Parietal lobe epilepsy is described as rare, accounting for 5% of epilepsies, and difficult to diagnose because subjective symptoms and rich connections can place the symptomatogenic zone distant from the seizure-onset zone; the review notes that few surgical localization data are available.
findings.evidence_text: The review states that parietal lobe epilepsy accounts for 5% of epilepsies and may be misdiagnosed or underdiagnosed because of subjective symptoms and network connections.
findings.laterality_localization: Parietal localization; symptomatogenic zone may be distant from seizure-onset zone; no side direction
findings.limitations: The review emphasizes sparse surgical data and does not provide the cited denominator for 5%.
findings.locators: PDF p.6, Parietal lobe seizures; PDF p.7, Parietal lobe seizures
findings.population: Patients with parietal lobe epilepsy; exact cohort NOT_REPORTED

findings.citation: Asadollahi M, Sperling MR, Rabiei AH, et al. Drug-Resistant parietal lobe epilepsy: clinical manifestations and surgery outcome. Epileptic Disord 2017;19:35–9.; Francione S, Liava A, Mai R, et al. Drug-Resistant parietal epilepsy: polymorphic ictal semiology does not preclude good post-surgical outcome. Epileptic Disord 2015;17:32–46.
findings.claim: In two of the larger surgical series of patients with parietal lobe epilepsy, the most commonly reported aura was a contralateral somatosensory aura, reported in 38% in both series.
findings.evidence_text: The review reports contralateral somatosensory aura in 38% of patients in both of two larger parietal surgical series.
findings.laterality_localization: Somatosensory aura contralateral to the epileptogenic zone
findings.limitations: The review does not state the endpoint denominators or whether the 38% values use the same ascertainment and analysis unit in both series.
findings.locators: PDF p.7, Parietal lobe seizures
findings.measure: 38% in each of two cited series
findings.population: Patients in two surgical series of parietal lobe epilepsy

findings.citation: Salanova V. Parietal lobe epilepsy. J Clin Neurophysiol 2012;29:392–6.; Yang Y, Wang H, Zhou W, et al. Electroclinical characteristics of seizures arising from the precuneus based on stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG). BMC Neurol 2018;18:110.; Perumal MB, Chinnasami S, Shah A, et al. Epileptic kinetopsia localizes to superior parietal lobule and intraparietal sulcus. Neurology 2014;83:768–70.
findings.claim: Primary sensory cortex seizures tend to begin with contralateral tingling or numbness that may spread through the sensory homunculus, sometimes with pain or altered thermal sensation; non-dominant parietal association seizures may distort body image, superior parietal/precuneus seizures may produce macrosomatognosis or microsomatognosis, superior parietal/intraparietal seizures may produce kinetopsia, precuneus seizures macropsia or micropsia, and dominant parietotemporal seizures language impairment.
findings.comparator: Primary sensory cortex versus parietal association regions
findings.evidence_text: The source maps contralateral tingling/numbness to primary sensory cortex and several body-image or visual illusions to named parietal association regions.
findings.laterality_localization: Primary sensory signs are contralateral; non-dominant and dominant parietal associations are specified; named regional associations include superior parietal lobule, intraparietal sulcus, and precuneus
findings.limitations: Rich parietal connections allow propagation to sensorimotor, supplementary motor, or temporal regions, so later manifestations may not identify onset.
findings.locators: PDF p.7, Primary sensory cortex; PDF p.7, Parietal association areas
findings.population: NOT_REPORTED
findings.source_term: primary sensory cortex; parietal association areas

findings.citation: Blume WT, Wiebe S, Tapsell LM. Occipital epilepsy: lateral versus mesial. Brain 2005;128:1209–25.; Kuzniecky R. Symptomatic occipital lobe epilepsy. Epilepsia 1998;39(Suppl 4):S24–31.; Salanova V, Andermann F, Olivier A, et al. Occipital lobe epilepsy: electroclinical manifestations, electrocorticography, cortical stimulation and outcome in 42 patients treated between 1930 and 1991. surgery of occipital lobe epilepsy. Brain 1992;115(Pt 6):1655–80.
findings.claim: Occipital lobe seizures are usually characterized by visual aura in 40%-75% of patients, or less commonly oculomotor features, and primary visual cortex seizures produce brief elementary visual auras, usually less than 2 minutes; in most patients the visual phenomena are lateralized and contralateral to seizure onset, but up to 30% have more diffuse visual changes.
findings.evidence_text: The review reports visual aura in 40%-75% of occipital patients and usually contralateral visual phenomena, with up to 30% more diffuse.
findings.laterality_localization: Visual phenomena are usually contralateral to the hemisphere of seizure onset; up to 30% are more diffuse
findings.limitations: True ictal visual-field loss or amaurosis is rare and may be postictal, particularly when long lasting.
findings.locators: PDF p.8, Occipital lobe seizures; PDF p.8, Primary visual cortex
findings.measure: Visual aura in 40%-75% of patients; primary visual aura usually <2 min; up to 30% diffuse visual changes
findings.population: Patients with occipital lobe epilepsy; exact cohort NOT_REPORTED
findings.source_term: occipital lobe seizures; elementary visual aura
findings.uncertainty: Source uses “usually” and “up to” qualifiers; exact denominators NOT_REPORTED

findings.citation: Salanova V, Andermann F, Olivier A, et al. Occipital lobe epilepsy: electroclinical manifestations, electrocorticography, cortical stimulation and outcome in 42 patients treated between 1930 and 1991. surgery of occipital lobe epilepsy. Brain 1992;115(Pt 6):1655–80.; Lee S-U, Suh H-I, Choi JY, et al. Epileptic nystagmus: a case report and systematic review. Epilepsy Behav Case Rep 2014;2:156–60.
findings.claim: In a cited large series, 20% of patients had eye blinking at seizure onset; the review also states that eye version can occur with occipital-localized ictal discharges and that epileptic nystagmus typically has its fast phase contralateral and slow component ipsilateral to the seizure-onset hemisphere.
findings.comparator: Fast versus slow nystagmus components; eye blinking versus eye version
findings.evidence_text: The source reports 20% eye blinking at onset and describes the fast and slow directions of epileptic nystagmus relative to onset.
findings.laterality_localization: Eye version may occur with occipital onset; nystagmus fast phase contralateral and slow component ipsilateral to seizure onset
findings.limitations: Eye version may represent propagation; the review notes that the cited nystagmus evidence includes a case report and systematic review.
findings.locators: PDF p.8, Parieto-occipital junction
findings.measure: Eye blinking at onset in 20% of the cited series
findings.population: Patients in the cited occipital epilepsy series and reported nystagmus cases; exact cohorts NOT_REPORTED

findings.citation: Bancaud J, Talairach J. Clinical semiology of frontal lobe seizures. Adv Neurol 1992;57:3–58.
findings.claim: Anterior cingulate seizures are described as intense fright, screaming or vocalization, autonomic signs, and complex gestural automatisms or hypermotor activity, whereas posterior cingulate seizures are described as variable and dependent on propagation, with some series showing temporal-lobe-like auras.
findings.comparator: Anterior cingulate versus posterior cingulate onset
findings.evidence_text: The review characterizes anterior cingulate seizures by fear, vocalization, autonomic signs, and hypermotor or gestural behavior, while posterior cingulate semiology is variable.
findings.laterality_localization: Anterior versus posterior cingulate localization; no hemisphere direction
findings.limitations: Most data are from case series of lesional cases, and posterior-cingulate signs depend on spread.
findings.locators: PDF p.8, Cingulate gyrus
findings.population: Mostly lesional case series; exact cohort NOT_REPORTED

findings.citation: Alkawadri R, So NK, Van Ness PC, et al. Cingulate epilepsy: report of 3 electroclinical subtypes with surgical outcomes. JAMA Neurol 2013;70:995–1002.
findings.claim: A later cited case series including anterior and posterior cingulate seizures identified two anterior-cingulate groups: typical hypermotor seizures with fear and autonomic features and infrequent generalization, and a subgroup with simple motor features and frequent generalization in which all cases had infiltrating astrocytomas; all posterior-cingulate cases in that series had temporal-lobe-like auras such as psychic, abdominal, or gustatory auras.
findings.comparator: Two anterior-cingulate subgroups versus posterior-cingulate cases
findings.evidence_text: The cited series is summarized as having two anterior-cingulate groups and temporal-like auras in all posterior-cingulate cases.
findings.laterality_localization: Anterior versus posterior cingulate; no hemisphere direction
findings.limitations: The review does not provide the cited series’ subgroup counts or denominators and notes the astrocytoma association only for the simple-motor subgroup.
findings.locators: PDF p.8, Cingulate gyrus
findings.population: Cited cingulate epilepsy case series; exact cohort NOT_REPORTED

findings.citation: Enatsu R, Bulacio J, Nair DR, et al. Posterior cingulate epilepsy: clinical and neurophysiological analysis. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2014;85:44–50.
findings.claim: Another cited study reported that posterior cingulate seizure semiology varied with spread: spread to frontal areas produced motor manifestations including bilateral asymmetric tonic or hypermotor seizures, whereas spread to temporal areas produced dialeptic or automotor seizures.
findings.evidence_text: Frontal spread was associated with asymmetric tonic or hypermotor manifestations and temporal spread with dialeptic or automotor seizures.
findings.laterality_localization: Posterior cingulate onset with frontal-versus-temporal propagation; no hemisphere direction
findings.limitations: The cited observation concerns spread patterns and should not be treated as a direct one-to-one onset signature.
findings.locators: PDF p.8, Cingulate gyrus
findings.population: Patients with posterior cingulate epilepsy in the cited study; exact cohort NOT_REPORTED

findings.citation: Isnard J, Guénot M, Sindou M, et al. Clinical manifestations of insular lobe seizures: a stereo-electroencephalographic study. Epilepsia 2004;45:1079–90.; Peltola ME, Trebuchon A, Lagarde S. Anatomoelectroclinical features of SEEG-confirmed pure insular-onset epilepsy. Epilepsy Behav 2020;21:105.
findings.claim: Insular seizures are rare and heterogeneous, with viscerosensory, somatosensory, autonomic, language, complex auditory, automotor, hypermotor, tonic, or clonic manifestations; deep location and often non-localising scalp EEG can make them resemble temporal or frontal seizures and go unrecognized.
findings.comparator: Insular versus temporal or frontal seizure appearance
findings.evidence_text: The review describes heterogeneous visceral, sensory, autonomic, language, auditory, and motor signs with frequently non-localising scalp EEG.
findings.laterality_localization: Insular localization; no hemisphere direction
findings.limitations: Rapid propagation and overlap with temporal or frontal semiology limit clinical localization from any single sign.
findings.locators: PDF p.8, Insular seizures; PDF p.9, Insular seizures
findings.population: NOT_REPORTED

findings.citation: Jobst BC, Gonzalez-Martinez J, Isnard J, et al. The insula and its epilepsies. Epilepsy Curr 2019;19:11–21.
findings.claim: Viscerosensory symptoms such as abdominal aura and laryngeal constriction and autonomic signs such as nausea, hypersalivation, and sweating are suggested to arise from anterior insula, whereas painful burning, electric-shock, or tingling sensations are more likely posterior insular; insular sensory responses may involve a larger skin territory including perioral regions, be bilateral or ipsilateral, and more often evolve to complex motor phenomena than primary or secondary somatosensory responses.
findings.comparator: Anterior versus posterior insula and insula versus primary/secondary somatosensory cortex
findings.evidence_text: The source contrasts anterior-insular visceral/autonomic symptoms with posterior-insular painful sensations and describes larger, sometimes bilateral or ipsilateral insular sensory territories.
findings.laterality_localization: Anterior versus posterior insula; responses can be bilateral or ipsilateral rather than strictly contralateral
findings.limitations: The review presents probabilistic associations and emphasizes heterogeneity rather than a definitive sign-to-region rule.
findings.locators: PDF p.8, Insular seizures
findings.population: Stimulation-study and review literature; exact cohorts NOT_REPORTED
findings.source_term: anterior versus posterior insula; insular sensory territory

findings.citation: Jobst BC, Gonzalez-Martinez J, Isnard J, et al. The insula and its epilepsies. Epilepsy Curr 2019;19:11–21.
findings.claim: The review states that seizures arising from hippocampus almost always propagate to the insula, so abdominal aura is also common in mesiotemporal seizures; nevertheless, the combination of complex visceral and somatosensory auras points toward insular onset.
findings.comparator: Isolated abdominal aura in mesiotemporal seizures versus combined complex visceral and somatosensory aura
findings.evidence_text: The review cautions that hippocampal seizures commonly propagate to the insula but says combined complex visceral and somatosensory auras favor insular onset.
findings.laterality_localization: Hippocampal-to-insular propagation; combined complex visceral and somatosensory aura points toward insular onset without a hemisphere direction
findings.limitations: Shared abdominal aura and rapid propagation make hippocampal, insular, temporal, and frontal localization difficult from aura alone.
findings.locators: PDF p.8, Insular seizures; PDF p.9, Insular seizures
findings.population: NOT_REPORTED
findings.source_term: hippocampal propagation to insula; complex visceral and somatosensory aura
findings.uncertainty: Source uses “almost always” and “points toward” qualifiers

findings.citation: Kovac S, Diehl B, Wehner T, et al. Gelastic seizures: incidence, clinical and EEG features in adult patients undergoing video-EEG telemetry. Epilepsia 2015;56:e1–5.
findings.claim: Gelastic seizures typically arise from hypothalamic hamartomas, but the review states that a cited case series found one third of cases with hypothalamic hamartomas, one third temporal, and one third frontal; hypothalamic-hamartoma seizures usually begin in early childhood, are brief, stereotyped, and very frequent with mirthless laughter and common autonomic signs, whereas non-hypothalamic and especially temporal gelastic seizures usually present in adulthood as more complex automotor seizures with loss of consciousness.
findings.evidence_text: The cited case-series distribution is summarized as one third hypothalamic hamartoma, one third temporal, and one third frontal.
findings.laterality_localization: Hypothalamic, temporal, or frontal localization; no hemisphere direction
findings.limitations: The review does not report the cited case-series denominator or the extent to which age and semiology were ascertained uniformly.
findings.locators: PDF p.9, Gelastic seizures
findings.measure: One third hypothalamic hamartoma, one third temporal, and one third frontal in the cited series
findings.population: Cases in the cited gelastic-seizure series; exact denominator NOT_REPORTED
findings.uncertainty: Source uses “typically” and “usually”; exact counts NOT_REPORTED

findings.claim: In video case 5, an 18-year-old right-handed man had gelastic seizures beginning at age 2, imaging-confirmed hypothalamic hamartoma, typical gelastic seizures without mirth, and loss of awareness in some seizures.
findings.evidence_text: The case had childhood-onset gelastic seizures, a hypothalamic hamartoma, mirthless laughter, and occasional loss of awareness.
findings.laterality_localization: Hypothalamic hamartoma; hemisphere direction NOT_REPORTED
findings.limitations: Single illustrative case; occasional impaired awareness is not presented as universal for hypothalamic-hamartoma gelastic seizures.

findings.citation: Hayakawa I, Kubota M. Ictal pouting: Kabuki visage or chapeau de gendarme? Pract Neurol 2018;18:410–2.; Tan Y-L, Muhlhofer W, Knowlton R. Pearls and Oysters: the chapeau de gendarme sign and other localizing gems in frontal lobe epilepsy. Neurology 2016;87:e103–5.
findings.claim: The chapeau de gendarme or ictal pout sign is a downturned mouth caused by bilateral lip and chin contraction and, when seen early in a seizure, is described as highly localising to frontal onset, particularly anterior cingulate, orbitofrontal, mesio-prefrontal, or premotor cortex.
findings.comparator: Early versus later appearance in the seizure
findings.evidence_text: The sign is defined by a downturned mouth from bilateral lip and chin contraction and is highly localising to specified frontal regions when early.
findings.laterality_localization: Frontal localization, particularly anterior cingulate, orbitofrontal, mesio-prefrontal, or premotor cortex; no hemisphere direction
findings.limitations: The source’s “highly localising” statement is citation-based and a later case in the article had non-localising ictal EEG.
findings.locators: PDF p.9, Chapeau de gendarme
findings.population: NOT_REPORTED
findings.source_term: chapeau de gendarme; ictal pout sign

findings.citation: Italiano D, Ferlazzo E, Gasparini S, et al. Generalized versus partial reflex seizures: a review. Seizure 2014;23:512–20.
findings.claim: The review links photosensitive focal epilepsy to possible occipital onset, musicogenic seizures to mesial or neocortical temporal lobe, startle-induced tonic or atonic seizures triggered by auditory stimuli to onset in or near the supplementary motor area, and eating-induced seizures to temporal or extratemporal perisylvian regions.
findings.comparator: Photosensitive, musicogenic, startle-induced, and eating-induced triggers
findings.evidence_text: The source maps specific triggers to occipital, temporal, supplementary motor, or perisylvian regions and notes that spontaneous seizures may also occur.
findings.laterality_localization: Occipital, temporal, supplementary motor area, or perisylvian localization as specified; no hemisphere direction
findings.limitations: These are trigger-associated localizing suggestions, not exclusive onset rules.
findings.locators: PDF p.9, Reflex seizures; PDF p.10, Reflex seizures
findings.population: Patients with reflex focal epilepsies; exact cohorts NOT_REPORTED
findings.uncertainty: Source states that spontaneous seizures can also occur

findings.citation: Marashly A, Ewida A, Agarwal R, et al. Ictal motor sequences: lateralization and localization values. Epilepsia 2016;57:369–75.
findings.claim: The review describes unilateral clonic movements, unilateral tonic or dystonic posturing, and early head version as robust lateralising motor signs with positive predictive value greater than 80%, all contralateral to onset; it also states that before secondary generalization the extended arm in a figure-of-4 sign is contralateral, the last clonic jerk is ipsilateral, and postictal Todd’s paresis is contralateral to seizure onset.
findings.comparator: Contralateral versus ipsilateral motor direction relative to onset
findings.evidence_text: The review reports positive predictive value greater than 80% for several motor signs and specifies the contralateral or ipsilateral direction of each sign.
findings.laterality_localization: Unilateral clonic/tonic/dystonic signs and early head version contralateral; last clonic jerk ipsilateral; Todd’s paresis contralateral
findings.limitations: These features lateralise onset but do not differentiate frontal from extrafrontal onset.
findings.locators: PDF p.10, Lateralising signs
findings.measure: Positive predictive value >80% for the listed robust motor signs
findings.phase: Ictal onset, pre-generalization, generalized phase ending, and postictal period
findings.population: Patients with focal seizures in the cited motor-sequence literature; exact cohort NOT_REPORTED
findings.source_term: robust lateralising motor signs; figure-of-4 sign; Todd’s paresis
findings.uncertainty: Exact confidence interval and endpoint denominator NOT_REPORTED

findings.claim: In video case 7, a 33-year-old man with left temporal hypometabolism had head version to the right followed by right-arm extension in a figure-of-4 posture, indicating left hemispheric onset; in one seizure the last clonic jerk was on the left, also pointing to left onset, while ictal EEG was non-localisable in one seizure and lateralised left in another.
findings.evidence_text: Right head version and right-arm extension were interpreted as left onset; the last jerk was left in one seizure, with EEG non-localisable in one and left-lateralised in another.
findings.laterality_localization: Right head version and right-arm extension, plus left last clonic jerk, pointed to left hemispheric onset
findings.limitations: Single illustrative case showing that semiologic lateralization and ictal EEG localization can vary by seizure and that lateralization does not equal precise localization.

findings.population: Single case: 33-year-old man with focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures and left temporal PET hypometabolism
findings.source_term: head version; figure-of-4 sign; last clonic jerk

findings.citation: Blair RDG. Temporal lobe epilepsy semiology. Epilepsy Res Treat 2012;2012:1–10.; Lee GR, Arain A, Lim N, et al. Rhythmic ictal nonclonic hand (RINCH) motions: a distinct contralateral sign in temporal lobe epilepsy. Epilepsia 2006;47:2189–92.
findings.claim: Ictal or postictal dysphasia lateralises to the dominant hemisphere but has poor localising value and must be distinguished from non-lateralising speech arrest; formed nonsensical ictal speech and preserved awareness during ictal automatisms point to the nondominant hemisphere, while rhythmic ictal non-clonic hand motions may be contralateral in temporal lobe epilepsy and peri-ictal drinking, spitting, vomiting, or urge to urinate point to a nondominant focus.
findings.comparator: Dominant versus nondominant hemisphere; contralateral RINCH direction
findings.evidence_text: The review separates dominant-hemisphere dysphasia from nondominant ictal speech and preserved awareness, and lists contralateral RINCH motions and nondominant peri-ictal behaviors.
findings.laterality_localization: Dysphasia to dominant hemisphere; ictal speech, preserved awareness during automatisms, and listed peri-ictal autonomic/behavioral signs to nondominant focus; RINCH motions contralateral
findings.limitations: Speech arrest is non-lateralising and dysphasia is poorly localising; clinical context is required.
findings.locators: PDF p.10, Lateralising signs
findings.population: NOT_REPORTED
findings.source_term: ictal/postictal dysphasia; ictal speech; preserved awareness; RINCH motions
findings.uncertainty: Dysphasia is explicitly qualified as poor localizing value

findings.citation: Salanova V, Andermann F, Olivier A, et al. Occipital lobe epilepsy: electroclinical manifestations, electrocorticography, cortical stimulation and outcome in 42 patients treated between 1930 and 1991. surgery of occipital lobe epilepsy. Brain 1992;115(Pt 6):1655–80.; Benbadis SR, Kotagal P, Klem GH. Unilateral blinking: a lateralizing sign in partial seizures. Neurology 1996;46:45–8.; Lee S-U, Suh H-I, Choi JY, et al. Epileptic nystagmus: a case report and systematic review. Epilepsy Behav Case Rep 2014;2:156–60.
findings.claim: A hemifield visual aura has good lateralising value to the contralateral occipital lobe; unilateral eye blinking lateralises to the hemisphere ipsilateral to the blinking eye; the fast component of epileptic nystagmus is contralateral to seizure onset; and a simple unilateral auditory aura, which the review notes is rare, is contralateral.

findings.laterality_localization: Hemifield visual aura and simple unilateral auditory aura contralateral; unilateral eye blinking ipsilateral; nystagmus fast component contralateral
findings.limitations: These signs lateralise the hemisphere but do not by themselves establish the seizure-onset zone or distinguish propagation from onset.
