findings.population: NOT_REPORTED
findings.source_term: hemifield visual aura; unilateral eye blinking; epileptic nystagmus; unilateral auditory aura
findings.uncertainty: Simple unilateral auditory aura is described as rare

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a narrative review rather than a single primary cohort or systematic quantitative synthesis. Cited studies, case series, and the seven illustrative cases have different populations, ascertainment methods, reference standards, phases, and analysis units; many percentages and probabilities have no endpoint denominator in the review. The source repeatedly cautions that symptomatogenic cortex may differ from seizure-onset or epileptogenic cortex, that propagation and network disruption can produce later signs, and that deep sources may have non-localising scalp EEG. Lesions may be incidental, and the review does not establish universal one-to-one sign-to-onset rules or a pooled effect estimate. All native pages 1-12 and their text/rendering representations were readable; no page was blocked.
sources.source_report_methods_population: Narrative review; the authors summarize literature on focal seizures and present illustrative cases from their centre using clinical history, videotelemetry, scalp or intracranial stereo-EEG, MRI/PET, and surgical outcome where stated. No single review cohort, systematic eligibility set, pooled analysis, or uniform endpoint denominator is reported. Populations, analysis units, and reference standards are therefore retained at finding level; source-reported reference standards include ictal EEG, imaging, lesion location, clinical semiology, and seizure freedom after resection.
sources.source_report_summary: Chowdhury FA, Silva R, Whatley B, and Walker MC, “Localisation in focal epilepsy: a practical guide,” Pract Neurol 2021;21:481-491, doi:10.1136/practneurol-2019-002341. This is a narrative review of focal-seizure semiology for localization and lateralization in presurgical evaluation, combining literature synthesis, two summary tables, a regional figure, and seven illustrative video cases. Cited-study restatements below are not independent primary observations.

sources.source_report_limitations: The review may have publication bias, and its proportions and comparisons are tentative because it narratively summarized heterogeneous literature without comparative statistical testing. AP subtype definitions varied across studies (CH sometimes included MH/VH and I sometimes included HD); cortical-stimulation brain-region labels and electrode localization varied, afterdischarges were often not reported, and stimulation may produce network-wide or remote effects. AS was not always the first ictal symptom, so some localized structures may reflect propagation rather than generation; Table 2 may count cases multiple times for multiple structures or AS types, and the authors sometimes interpreted SOZ localization across investigations. The paper refers readers to online supplementary data for exact type-specific counts, but no supplement was included in the authorized 12-page source package. The abstract reports right-hemisphere SOZ frequency as 38%, whereas Table 2 reports 77/200 (39%); the discrepancy is retained rather than resolved.
sources.source_report_methods_population: PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar were searched without language or date restrictions through 11 December 2022. The review narratively summarized auditory-network anatomy and compiled encountered cortical-stimulation studies reporting auditory phenomena (AP) plus case reports/series with AS-like phenomena and enough information to determine seizure-onset-zone (SOZ) lateralization and/or localization; acute symptomatic seizures and cases without evident auditory semiology were excluded. Level A evidence comprised seizure freedom after surgery with more than 1 year follow-up, seizures demonstrated from a SOZ on intracranial EEG, a concordant structural MRI lesion, or a concordant MEG cluster of at least 6 spike sources within 1 cm; Level B used MEG scatters, scalp EEG, PET/SPECT, and/or other clinical features. Localization and lateralization were analyzed for Level A, but only lateralization for Level B; data were tabulated as count (frequency), missing data were pairwise-deleted, and no comparative statistical tests were performed.
sources.source_report_summary: Perspective and narrative literature review of the localizing and lateralizing value of auditory phenomena in focal seizures, combining cortical-stimulation reports with case reports and series of auditory seizures (AS).

sources.source_report_limitations: The report is a single case plus a heterogeneous review of case reports, with no controlled comparator and no seizure captured during the index palinacousis. The index EEG was obtained after symptoms ceased, and intraoperative stimulation occurred after phenytoin. Several review percentages and subset summaries lack explicit denominators. Table 2's printed lesion-aetiology counts sum to 37 although the review states 36 cases; the printed tumour-subtype counts also do not reconcile with the Table 2 tumour total. The source refers to online supplemental table E1 and figure E1, but those materials are not part of this five-page locked package and were not used.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The index report concerns one 24-year-old Caucasian right-handed woman with a ruptured left temporal cavernous malformation. The review searched PubMed for the word “palinacousis,” found 26 reports including 3 reviews, cross-referenced all publications, excluded reports without perseveration of previously heard sounds or words and all review articles, and retained 22 articles with 35 cases; the authors added their own case. No year or primary-language exclusions were applied. The source does not state a diagnostic reference standard or provide complete denominators for several review percentages; the index EEG was performed after symptoms had ceased.
sources.source_report_summary: Veilleux C, El-Hage G, L'Ecuyer N, Bojanowski MW, “Palinacousis: an eloquent symptom of temporal lobe lesion,” BMJ Case Reports 2021;14:e236615. This is a case report of palinacousis after a left temporal cavernous-malformation haemorrhage plus a systematic review of 22 articles reporting 35 cases, to which the index case was added for a total of 36 cases. It addresses auditory perseveration, structural localization, ear/lesion laterality, and the unresolved ictal, postictal, or non-ictal mechanism.

sources.source_report_limitations: The source is retrospective and restricted to a highly selected group rendered completely seizure free and aura free after resection confined to one anatomical lobe; it states that applicability to patients rejected for surgery or with non-intractable epilepsy is unknown. Parietal and occipital subgroups were small, sublobar analysis was limited, and PET was available only in 40/73 clinically selected patients; ictal SPECT was performed in 20/73. The study did not correlate semiology with intracranial EEG because of electrode-placement bias and lack of stereo-EEG before 2008, and EEG/MRI/PET were not subjected to the same inter-observer analysis as semiology. The article reports unresolved internal numerical discrepancies, including 20/27 versus 21/27 for frontal lateralization and localization, 54/73 in text/Table 2 versus the Figure 1 semiology-lateralization label of 53, and differing displayed Figure 1 counts versus Table 4 values. Cited-study restatements in F025–F032 are claims made by the current article and were not independently verified against the cited sources. No page was blocked; page 6 contains the reference list and no additional primary result beyond the cited targets named in the report.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The cohort comprised consecutive patients operated between 1999 and 2007: temporal lobe epilepsy (30 patients, 63 seizures), frontal lobe epilepsy (27 patients, 51 seizures), parietal lobe epilepsy (8 patients, 14 seizures), and occipital lobe epilepsy (8 patients, 18 seizures). Patients were at least 12 years old, had one focal resection without hemispherectomy or multilobar resection, and had Engel class Ia outcome for at least 1 year; the study population was 73 patients and 145 seizures. Three investigators independently reviewed one or two best video examples of each seizure type while blinded to clinical details, with charted auras supplied by an unblinded investigator. A positive result required agreement of at least two of three raters; the same rule defined presence of a sign, correct lateralization, and correct lobar or sublobar localization. The surgical resection and lasting seizure freedom were used as the reference for the epileptogenic zone. Free Marginal Kappa and positive predictive value were calculated. Noninvasive EEG, MRI, and PET had been reviewed in the presurgical conference; PET was available for 40/73 patients and ictal SPECT for 20/73.
sources.source_report_summary: Elwan, Alexopoulos, Silveira, and Kotagal report a retrospective original empirical study of the lateralizing and lobar-localizing value of seizure semiology in 73 patients rendered Engel class Ia seizure free after focal resective epilepsy surgery. Three blinded investigators reviewed seizure videos and charted auras, then compared semiology with scalp interictal and ictal EEG, MRI, and clinically indicated PET.

sources.source_report_limitations: The source is an image-based scan/photo excerpt; the V30 package marks fresh page text for all three pages as NONE_REQUIRES_VISION with zero extracted characters, so no text extraction was available as an aid. PDF p.3 has visible page wear and water/stain damage and includes a partial neighboring-page edge at left; the table entries remain visually readable in the packaged rendering. No source citations, study attributions, sample sizes, denominators, numerical values, uncertainty estimates, methods, or population details are visible in the reviewed pages. The p.2 and p.3 tables are not identical: p.2 includes asterisk reliability qualifications and p.3 includes the additional compound subentry Versive and the page-specific entry Immediate postictal speech.
sources.source_report_methods_population: NOT_REPORTED. The excerpt is an educational handbook table and reports no study design, setting, cohort, analysis population, ascertainment method, comparator, reference standard, sample size, or statistical analysis.
sources.source_report_summary: This source is a 3-page scanned institutional Epilepsy Fellow Handbook excerpt, with the UTHealth and McGovern Medical School identity visible on the title page. PDF p.1 is a title page; PDF pp.2-3 are tables headed "Lateralizing signs" and "Localization". The tables provide qualitative seizure-semiology side, hemisphere, and anatomical localization pairings and do not report primary-study methods or quantitative results.

findings.claim: Among the recorded seizures, the LTL group had 54 CPS and 19 PE seizures, whereas the RTL group had 50 CPS and 4 PE seizures.
findings.evidence_text: “Seventy-three seizures were recorded in 9 patients with LTLE: 54 (74%) were CPS and 19 (26%) were partial evolving to generalized”; “Fifty-four seizures were recorded in 10 patients with RTLE: 50 (93%) were CPS and 4 (7%) were PE.”

findings.limitations: Only CPS and secondarily generalized/PE seizures were analyzed.

sources.source_report_limitations: The study is a retrospective review of medical charts, videotapes, and EEG recordings. The patient count was relatively small despite the larger number of seizure events; participants were selected surgical candidates with precise localization, and patients with unclear localization were excluded. Speech arrest, aphasia, and rapid return to baseline required specific testing that was not performed universally, particularly for seizures occurring at night. The source reports unequal seizure counts and a mixture of patient- and seizure-level wording in discussion paragraphs; this report preserves the stated units and does not calculate conversions. Table 5 states that percentages are relative to automatisms involving extremities for the relevant subrows, but does not provide every row-specific denominator. There is also an unresolved internal PET description: the prose says PET scans were abnormal in all patients except 2 with RTLE, while Tables 3-4 display missing PET entries for LTL patients 8-9 and RTL patient 19 and a normal PET entry for RTL patient 10. Cited-study restatements above were not independently verified against their cited targets.
sources.source_report_methods_population: Patients were admitted to an epilepsy unit over 30 months and underwent 5-14 days of scalp and sphenoidal EEG-CCTV monitoring with antiepileptic-drug discontinuation; all had head MRI, 16 had PET, 18 had neuropsychological testing, 16 had Wada testing, and 6 had repeat monitoring with implanted subdural grids. The 19 patients were divided by unilateral temporal onset using interictal discharges, ictal EEG onset, MRI lesions including mesiotemporal sclerosis, PET hypometabolism, neuropsychological testing, Wada testing, preoperative evaluation, and surgical outcome; 10 patients had RTL onset and 9 had LTL onset, yielding 54 and 73 recorded seizures, respectively. Only complex partial seizures (CPS) and secondarily generalized or partial-evolving-to-generalized (PE) seizures were analyzed. Clinical features were compared with chi-square or Fisher's exact tests.
sources.source_report_summary: This original empirical study retrospectively reviewed EEG/closed-circuit-TV-recorded seizures in 19 consecutive patients with medically intractable temporal lobe epilepsy undergoing preoperative evaluation, comparing clinical features of left temporal lobe (LTL/LTLE) and right temporal lobe (RTL/RTLE) seizure onset. Its purpose was to assess seizure semiology with potential lateralizing value, especially auras, automatisms, motor signs, ictal language, and postictal manifestations.

findings.source_term: frontopolar and dorsolateral frontal seizure semiology

findings.claim: Opercular seizures are described with gustatory hallucinations, salivation, mastication, swallowing, speech arrest, and autonomic signs; focal clonic activity and Todd's paralysis are described with seizures involving the perirolandic area.
findings.evidence_text: The source lists opercular autonomic/oral/speech phenomena and perirolandic focal clonic activity with Todd's paralysis.
findings.laterality_localization: Opercular versus perirolandic frontal region; Todd's paralysis is described without a stated side in this general passage
findings.limitations: No frequency or side-specific comparison is reported.
findings.locators: PDF p.5, Frontal lobe epilepsy, paragraph on opercular and perirolandic regions
findings.population: Patients with frontal lobe epilepsy

findings.claim: In one large series, interictal spiking was bilaterally synchronous in 37%, lobar in 32%, multilobar in 24%, focal in 12%, and hemispheric-independent in 9% of cases; epileptiform activity occurred exclusively outside the frontal lobes in 20%-50%, was restricted to the frontal lobes in only 25%, and spiking was absent in 20%-70%.
findings.comparator: interictal distribution categories and frontal versus outside-frontal restriction
findings.evidence_text: The source provides the five-category interictal-spiking distribution and the separate ranges for outside-frontal, frontal-restricted, and absent spiking.
findings.laterality_localization: Bilateral synchronous, lobar, multilobar, focal, hemispheric-independent, outside-frontal, and frontal-restricted distributions
findings.limitations: The chapter does not report the cohort denominator or uncertainty and combines several cited statements.
findings.locators: PDF p.6, Frontal lobe epilepsy, interictal EEG paragraph
findings.measure: 37% bilateral synchronous; 32% lobar; 24% multilobar; 12% focal; 9% hemispheric-independent; 20%-50% exclusively outside frontal; 25% frontal-restricted; 20%-70% absent
findings.population: One large series of patients with frontal lobe epilepsy; exact cohort not reported

findings.claim: Approximately one-third of frontal lobe seizures were not accompanied by EEG changes, another one-third showed nonlateralized slowing, rhythmic activity, or repetitive spiking, and focal ictal onsets were less common in frontal than temporal seizures.
findings.comparator: frontal versus temporal focal ictal onset; EEG-visible versus absent/nonlateralized patterns
findings.evidence_text: The source describes two roughly one-third groups with absent or nonlateralized EEG and contrasts focal frontal onset with temporal onset.
findings.laterality_localization: Frontal ictal activity may be absent or nonlateralized on scalp EEG; focal onset is less common than in temporal seizures
findings.limitations: Denominators and the basis for the frontal-temporal comparison are not reported.
findings.locators: PDF p.6, Frontal lobe epilepsy, paragraph beginning "Frontal lobe complex partial seizures"
findings.measure: approximately one-third without EEG changes; another one-third with nonlateralized patterns
findings.population: Patients with frontal lobe complex partial seizures; exact cohorts not reported

findings.claim: Lateralized or localized ictal patterns were reported in 33%-50% of frontal epilepsy cases; the chapter also describes secondary bilateral synchrony and a paradoxical ictal lateralization pattern when a generator near the interhemispheric fissure projects an obliquely oriented dipole to the opposite hemisphere.
findings.comparator: lateralized/localized versus nonlateralized patterns; apparent versus true side of origin
findings.evidence_text: The source reports a 33%-50% range and explains paradoxical ictal lateralization as projection from a generator in the interhemispheric fissure.
findings.laterality_localization: Frontal lateralized/localized patterns; paradoxical apparent contralateral onset from an interhemispheric generator projecting to the opposite hemisphere
findings.limitations: The source does not quantify the paradoxical-lateralization subgroup or provide denominators.
findings.locators: PDF p.7, Frontal lobe epilepsy, paragraph before "Electroencephalography in Parietal Lobe Epilepsy"
findings.measure: 33%-50% lateralized or localized ictal patterns; paradoxical contralateral appearance described qualitatively
findings.population: Patients with frontal lobe epilepsy; exact cohorts not reported
findings.source_term: lateralized or localized ictal patterns in frontal epilepsy

findings.claim: Parietal lobe seizures comprise 5%-6% of focal epilepsy cases in medical and surgical series. SPS commonly involve contralateral extremity or facial somatosensory symptoms, sometimes bilaterally, including paresthesias, numbness, pain, or cold/burning sensations; parietal CPS may show asymmetric tonic limb posturing, unilateral clonic activity, and contralateral version, with frontal activation or temporal spread producing the stated motor or awareness/automatisms patterns.
findings.comparator: parietal seizure semiology and propagation patterns
findings.evidence_text: The source gives the 5%-6% prevalence and lists contralateral somatosensory, asymmetric tonic, unilateral clonic, and contralateral-versive manifestations with propagation effects.
findings.laterality_localization: Contralateral extremity or face relative to parietal origin; frontal activation and temporal spread are stated propagation directions
findings.limitations: The source does not give the series denominators or frequencies for individual symptoms.
findings.locators: PDF p.7, Electroencephalography in Parietal Lobe Epilepsy, clinical semiology paragraphs
findings.measure: 5%-6% of focal epilepsy cases; semiologic features qualitative
findings.population: Medical and surgical series of parietal lobe epilepsy
findings.source_term: parietal lobe seizure somatosensory and motor semiology

findings.analysis_unit: structured cases, patients, and seizures as source-reported
findings.claim: Parietal interictal EEG may be normal or show lateralized/generalized slowing, while epileptiform activity is often multiregional and may suggest areas distant from the epileptogenic zone; centroparietal activity as the sole interictal abnormality was reported in 5%-20%, secondary bilateral synchrony in one-third, SPS often had no EEG correlate, and localized ictal onsets occurred in 6% of a large surgical series.
findings.comparator: interictal versus ictal EEG; parietal-localized versus multiregional or absent correlates
findings.evidence_text: The source combines the qualitative limitations of parietal EEG with reported 5%-20%, one-third, and 6% rates.
findings.laterality_localization: Centroparietal, multiregional, lateralized/generalized, nonlateralized, and localized parietal patterns; distant areas may be implicated by multiregional activity
findings.limitations: The chapter reports different source units and does not provide denominators or uncertainty for the ranges.
findings.locators: PDF p.7, Parietal lobe epilepsy, interictal paragraph; PDF p.9, continuation before "Electroencephalography in Occipital Lobe Epilepsy"
findings.measure: 5%-20% centroparietal-only interictal activity; one-third secondary bilateral synchrony; 6% localized ictal onsets; frequent absence of SPS EEG correlate
findings.population: Patients with parietal lobe epilepsy and a large surgical series; exact cohorts not reported

findings.claim: Occipital lobe epilepsy comprises 8% of focal epilepsy cases. SPS may involve elementary visual phenomena, ocular movement sensations, nystagmus, eye flutter or forced blinking, ictal amaurosis, and versive head or eye movements; elementary visual hallucinations were the most common manifestation in 50%-60% of cases. Infrasylvian spread to temporal regions was associated with altered awareness and automatisms, suprasylvian spread to mesial frontal regions with contralateral tonic posturing, and lateral spread with focal motor or sensory seizures; multiple seizure types occurred in one-third to one-half of patients.
findings.comparator: infrasylvian versus suprasylvian versus lateral propagation
findings.evidence_text: The source gives the 8% prevalence, 50%-60% visual-hallucination range, multiple-seizure-type range, and propagation-dependent semiology.
findings.laterality_localization: Occipital visual/ocular signs and propagation to temporal, mesial frontal, or lateral regions; contralateral tonic direction is stated for suprasylvian spread
findings.limitations: Individual symptom frequencies and cohort denominators are not reported.
findings.locators: PDF p.9, Electroencephalography in Occipital Lobe Epilepsy, clinical manifestations paragraphs
findings.measure: 8% of focal epilepsy cases; 50%-60% elementary visual hallucinations; one-third to one-half with multiple seizure types
findings.population: Patients with occipital lobe epilepsy

findings.claim: Occipital interictal EEG commonly involves posterior temporal regions; bilateral independent, bilateral synchronous, or diffuse epileptiform activity was reported in 30%-50% of cases, occipital-restricted epileptiform activity in 8%-18%, and ictal onset restricted to the occipital lobe in less than 20%. Invasive recordings showed spread from occipital regions to mesial temporal structures, the supplementary motor area, or dorsolateral frontal convexity before generalization.
findings.comparator: occipital-restricted versus posterior temporal, bilateral, or diffuse activity
findings.evidence_text: The source reports the bilateral/diffuse, occipital-restricted, and ictal-onset ranges and names the invasive propagation destinations.
findings.laterality_localization: Posterior temporal/occipital versus bilateral or diffuse patterns; spread from occipital to mesial temporal, supplementary motor, or dorsolateral frontal regions
findings.limitations: The source does not give denominators or uncertainty and does not quantify each propagation route.
findings.locators: PDF p.9, Occipital lobe epilepsy, interictal EEG paragraph; PDF p.10, continuation before "Surgical Evaluation"
findings.measure: 30%-50% bilateral/diffuse; 8%-18% occipital-restricted interictal activity; <20% occipital-restricted ictal onset
findings.population: Patients with occipital lobe epilepsy

findings.claim: Long-term video EEG with concurrent behavioral observation is described as useful for identifying responsiveness and language or motor function and for correlating clinical behavior with EEG findings; modified electrode placements and semi-invasive techniques are described as improving localization of interictal and ictal activity.
findings.evidence_text: The source describes simultaneous behavior and EEG recording as an aid to identifying clinical function and localizing or lateralizing seizures.
findings.laterality_localization: Clinical behavior and modified/semi-invasive recordings assist localization and lateralization; no fixed direction is reported
findings.limitations: No performance measure or comparative denominator is reported.
findings.locators: PDF p.10, Surgical Evaluation, long-term video EEG paragraph; PDF p.11, opening Surgical Evaluation paragraph
findings.population: Patients undergoing epilepsy surgical evaluation
findings.source_term: clinical behavior during long-term video EEG

findings.claim: Interictal epileptiform abnormalities may extend beyond the cortex from which the clinical seizure originates, yet the chapter states that interictal activity generally provides more reliable localization than ictal EEG because ictal activity spreads outside the onset zone. In a temporal lobe series, a single anteromesial temporal interictal spike focus accurately predicted temporal onset when surface ictal EEG was focal, regional, or lateralized; prediction was less accurate with multiple temporal foci or a predominant mid-to-posterior temporal focus.
findings.evidence_text: The source contrasts the wider field of interictal abnormalities with their stated localization reliability and identifies anteromesial temporal focus as the more accurate context.
findings.laterality_localization: Anteromesial temporal focus versus mid-to-posterior or multiple temporal foci; surface ictal focal/regional/lateralized patterns are the comparator context
findings.limitations: The source does not quantify the accuracy difference or state the study denominator.
findings.locators: PDF p.11, Surgical Evaluation, paragraph beginning "The extent of interictal epileptiform abnormalities"
findings.population: Patients with temporal lobe epilepsy
findings.source_term: interictal epileptiform focus versus ictal onset

findings.claim: The first recorded seizure was representative of subsequent seizures in 68% of cases and predicted the ultimate clinical localization in 91% of patients with TLE; a nonlocalized initial seizure, especially during sleep, was more likely to be followed by nonlocalizing seizures.
findings.comparator: localized/representative versus nonlocalized initial seizure, including sleep context
findings.evidence_text: The source reports the 68% representativeness and 91% TLE-localization prediction values and qualifies nonlocalized initial seizures, particularly in sleep.
findings.laterality_localization: Ultimate clinical localization in TLE; nonlocalized first seizure predicts continued nonlocalizing pattern
findings.limitations: The source does not provide denominators or uncertainty and combines related series statements.
findings.locators: PDF p.11, Surgical Evaluation, paragraph beginning "The number of seizures needed"
findings.measure: 68% representative of subsequent seizures; 91% predictive of ultimate clinical localization in TLE
findings.population: Patients with temporal lobe epilepsy and related surgical-evaluation series
findings.source_term: first recorded seizure as a representative seizure

findings.claim: A minimum of four seizures was required to identify 100% of 18 patients whose ictal patterns arose independently from both temporal regions.
findings.comparator: fewer than four seizures versus at least four seizures for identifying independent bilateral temporal patterns
findings.evidence_text: The source explicitly states that four seizures were needed to identify all 18 patients with independent patterns from both temporal regions.
findings.laterality_localization: Independent onset from both temporal regions
findings.limitations: The source does not report the performance of each lower seizure count or uncertainty.
findings.locators: PDF p.11, Surgical Evaluation, paragraph on the number of seizures needed
findings.measure: 100% (18/18) identified with a minimum of four seizures
findings.population: 18 patients with ictal patterns arising independently from both temporal regions
findings.source_term: minimum seizure count for independent bilateral temporal patterns

findings.claim: In a series of medically refractory focal epilepsy not limited to the temporal lobe, 21%-38% of scalp-recorded seizures were correctly localized and fewer than one-half were correctly lateralized when depth recordings were used to define the epileptogenic zone.
findings.comparator: correct scalp localization versus correct scalp lateralization against depth-defined zone
findings.evidence_text: The source reports separate scalp correct-localization and less-than-half correct-lateralization results when depth recordings defined the zone.
findings.laterality_localization: Scalp localization and lateralization compared with a depth-recording-defined epileptogenic zone
findings.limitations: The source does not report denominators or uncertainty.
findings.locators: PDF p.11, Surgical Evaluation, paragraph on medically refractory focal epilepsy and depth recordings
findings.population: Medically refractory focal epilepsy not limited to the temporal lobe
findings.source_term: scalp-recorded seizures in extratemporal focal epilepsy

findings.analysis_unit: source-defined interictal sharp-wave observations and single-case seizure observations
findings.claim: In Case Study 1, a right-handed woman had recurrent unusual-odor auras without initial loss of consciousness, later seizures with loss of awareness, oral/manual automatisms, unintelligible speech, left-hand automatisms, right-arm dystonic posturing, and head version to the right. Interictal sharp waves were maximal at the left sphenoidal electrode in 90% of the source-defined observations versus 5% at the left anterior temporal and 5% at the right sphenoidal electrode, and ictal rhythmic delta followed by repetitive spiking was maximal in the left temporal region; the chapter's discussion interpreted the combined history and testing as left mesial temporal lobe epilepsy.
findings.comparator: left versus right temporal/sphenoidal recording maxima
findings.evidence_text: The case narrative links an olfactory aura, right-sided motor signs, and left temporal EEG findings, and the discussion explicitly interprets them as left mesial temporal epilepsy.
findings.laterality_localization: Right arm dystonia and right head version with left temporal interictal/ictal abnormalities; source discussion concludes left mesial temporal localization
findings.limitations: This is one illustrative case; the source-defined 90%/5%/5% observation denominator is not stated, and the source's imaging and neuropsychological evidence is not expanded here.
findings.locators: PDF p.12, Case Study 1, history and seizure description; PDF p.12, Case Study 1, interictal and ictal EEG paragraph; PDF p.12, Case Study 1, Discussion
findings.measure: Interictal sharp-wave maximal-amplitude distribution reported as 90% left sphenoidal, 5% left anterior temporal, and 5% right sphenoidal
findings.population: Single illustrative case, 31-year-old right-handed woman with poorly controlled seizures
findings.source_term: Case Study 1 olfactory aura, dystonic posturing, and left temporal findings

findings.claim: In Case Study 2, a man had sudden facial distortion, rhythmic jerking of both lower extremities, vocalization with impaired consciousness, and later right-arm clonic seizures; recorded seizures included sudden tonic upper-extremity posturing, vocalization, facial distortion, and one rightward head version followed by generalized tonic-clonic activity. Interictal abnormalities were bilateral frontal but higher in amplitude on the left, while ictal scalp EEG was nonlateralized or obscured by movement artifact; invasive recording showed onset over multiple contacts of the frontal convexity anterior to the precentral gyrus with rapid spread to temporal and mesial frontal regions.
findings.evidence_text: The case combines frontal motor/vocal semiology with bilateral frontal interictal activity, nonlateralized ictal scalp EEG, and anterior frontal invasive onset with rapid spread.
findings.laterality_localization: Bilateral frontal abnormalities with greater left amplitude; invasive onset over anterior frontal convexity with rapid temporal and mesial frontal spread; rightward head version occurred in one seizure
findings.limitations: This is one illustrative case with substantial movement artifact; the chapter's imaging and surgical outcome are not used as independent semiology findings.
findings.locators: PDF p.12, Case Study 2, presenting seizure semiology; PDF p.13, Case Study 2, recorded seizures and EEG; PDF p.13, Case Study 2, invasive localization and Discussion
findings.population: Single illustrative case, 36-year-old right-handed man with poorly controlled seizures and prior head trauma
findings.source_term: Case Study 2 frontal seizure semiology and invasive localization

findings.analysis_unit: source-defined regional discharge observations and 12 seizures
findings.claim: In Case Study 3, a woman experienced multicolored bright stars moving in the left visual field for about 30 seconds followed by headache, later eye blinking, vocalization, and unresponsiveness, sometimes with secondary generalized tonic-clonic activity. Video EEG showed frequent multiregional discharges maximal in the right parieto-occipital region (65%), left parieto-occipital region (25%), and right temporal region (10%); ten seizures had fast activity over the right hemisphere and two had generalized posteriorly predominant rhythmic activity. The discussion stated that the left visual aura and right occipital polyspikes suggested right occipital lobe epilepsy, while further invasive evaluation was needed to delineate the zone.
findings.comparator: right versus left parieto-occipital and right temporal maxima; right-hemisphere fast activity versus generalized posterior rhythmic activity
findings.denominator: 12 for the seizure-activity comparison; NOT_REPORTED for the regional discharge-maxima percentages
findings.evidence_text: The case links a left visual-field aura with right parieto-occipital discharges and explicitly limits the localization to a suggestion pending invasive evaluation.
findings.laterality_localization: Left visual-field aura and right parieto-occipital/right-hemisphere EEG findings; source discussion suggests right occipital origin but states that invasive evaluation was required
findings.limitations: This is one illustrative case; the denominator for the 65%/25%/10% regional maxima is not stated, MRI was normal, and the patient declined further evaluation.
findings.locators: PDF p.14, Case Study 3, clinical history and video-EEG findings; PDF p.14, Case Study 3, Discussion
findings.measure: Discharge maxima 65% right parieto-occipital, 25% left parieto-occipital, 10% right temporal; 10/12 seizures with right-hemisphere fast activity and 2/12 with posteriorly predominant generalized rhythmic activity
findings.numerator: 10 and 2 for the seizure-activity comparison; NOT_REPORTED for the regional discharge-maxima percentages
findings.population: Single illustrative case, 23-year-old ambidextrous woman with recurrent seizures
findings.source_term: Case Study 3 left visual-field aura and right occipital findings

sources.source_report_limitations: The chapter is a scanned educational source with no usable fresh page text; all 16 pages were reviewed from the authorized page images. Page 16 is an upside-down continuation of the reference list and contains no additional semiology or localization claim. Pages 14-16 contain references and case material; the cited papers themselves were not reviewed, so reference markers in the chapter are retained as attribution rather than treated as independently verified evidence. The chapter mixes review-synthesized series with illustrative cases and reports heterogeneous units (patients, seizures, cases, and source-defined observations). Many percentages lack numerators, denominators, confidence limits, or a fully specified cohort, and silence is not interpreted as a negative finding. Illustrative EEG figures were not promoted to separate findings when the surrounding text did not add a distinct semiology, localization, or lateralization claim.
sources.source_report_methods_population: This is an educational chapter rather than a single primary cohort. The general text synthesizes source-cited series involving focal epilepsy, temporal/mesial temporal epilepsy, and frontal, parietal, or occipital epilepsy, and separately presents three illustrative case observations. The source uses patients, cases, seizures, and source-defined observations as analysis units; no common cohort, eligibility rule, comparator, reference standard, or chapter-wide denominator is reported. The report retains the source's unit and missingness for each finding and does not infer denominators from percentages.
sources.source_report_summary: Scanned educational chapter 34, "Focal Epilepsy and Surgical Evaluation," by Nancy Foldvary, DO. The chapter discusses clinical semiology and EEG correlates of focal epilepsy involving temporal, frontal, parietal, and occipital regions, with implications for localization and lateralization during surgical evaluation; it also includes three illustrative cases.

findings.citation: Lesser RP, Lüders H, Klem G, Dinner DS, Morris HH, Hahn J. Cortical afterdischarge and functional response thresholds: results of extraoperative testing. Epilepsia 1984;25:615–21 [2]; Kellinghaus C, Lüders HO. The symptomatogenic zone: general principles. In: Lüders HO, editor. Textbook of epilepsy surgery. 2008. p. 425–31 [3]
findings.claim: The review states that seizure symptomatology reflects activation of specific brain regions by ictal discharge; the symptomatogenic zone is generally near, though not necessarily immediately near, the epileptogenic zone, and sequential signs can reveal propagation patterns. Multiple symptomatogenic zones may be activated simultaneously and obscure one another, while different onset regions can evolve to a common symptomatogenic zone such as the SSMA.
findings.evidence_text: The review links sequential ictal signs to propagation and cautions that simultaneous activation or convergent pathways can produce variable or misleading semiology.
findings.laterality_localization: localization to the symptomatogenic network and relationship to the epileptogenic zone; no fixed laterality
findings.limitations: The review notes that the sign itself may not identify the onset site when propagation or network convergence dominates.
findings.locators: PDF p.1, section 2 General principles of ictal symptomatology; PDF p.1, abstract
findings.population: focal epilepsy and presurgical evaluation

findings.citation: Sperling MR, O'Connor MJ. Auras and subclinical seizures: characteristics and prognostic significance. Ann Neurol 1990;28:320–8 [4]; Palmini A, Gloor P. The localizing value of auras in partial seizures: a prospective and retrospective study. Neurology 1992;42:801–8 [5]
findings.claim: As first ictal symptoms, auras provide important localizing and lateralizing information about the relationship between the symptomatogenic and epileptogenic zones. They are reported by most patients with temporal and parieto-occipital epilepsies, are associated with favorable outcome after temporal lobectomy, and were reported to localize the most likely lobe of origin as well as EEG and imaging.
findings.comparator: EEG and imaging for lobe-of-origin localization
findings.evidence_text: The review calls auras important first ictal symptoms and compares their lobe-of-origin value with EEG and imaging.
findings.laterality_localization: most likely lobe of seizure origin and relationship between symptomatogenic and epileptogenic zones
findings.limitations: The review does not provide a common cohort size or denominator for these cross-study statements.
findings.locators: PDF p.2, section 3.1 Auras; PDF p.2, Table 1
findings.measure: Qualitative association with surgical outcome; localizing value reported as comparable to EEG and imaging
findings.population: patients with temporal or parieto-occipital epilepsy and temporal-lobectomy candidates

findings.citation: Rona S. Auras: localizing and lateralizing value. In: Lüders HO, editor. Textbook of epilepsy surgery. 2008. p. 432–42 [61]
findings.claim: Somatosensory auras arising from SI involve discrete body parts contralateral to the ictal discharge; SII produces similar symptoms that may be bilateral or ipsilateral to the seizure focus; and SSMA symptoms are poorly localized and primarily involve contralateral proximal body parts. The source table likewise lists SI and SSMA as mainly contralateral and SII as ipsilateral when unilateral.
findings.evidence_text: The text distinguishes discrete contralateral SI symptoms from bilateral or ipsilateral SII symptoms and poorly localized SSMA symptoms.
findings.laterality_localization: SI contralateral to ictal discharge; SII bilateral or ipsilateral to focus; SSMA primarily contralateral proximal body parts
findings.limitations: Electrical-stimulation findings and clinical seizure observations are presented together without a single common analysis unit.
findings.locators: PDF p.2, section 3.1 Auras; PDF p.2, Table 1
findings.population: patients with focal epilepsy; electrical-stimulation and semiology observations

findings.citation: Manford M, Fish DR, Shorvon SD. An analysis of clinical seizure patterns and their localizing value in frontal and temporal lobe epilepsies. Brain 1996;119:17–40 [6]
findings.claim: Well-localized somatosensory auras that evolve to motor features are usually associated with a perirolandic epileptogenic zone close to the symptomatogenic zone, whereas illusions of swelling, shrinking, or movement of body parts are often elicited by activation of the nondominant inferior parietal lobe or TPO junction.
findings.evidence_text: Motor evolution is linked to perirolandic localization, while body-part illusions are linked to nondominant inferior parietal or TPO activation.
findings.laterality_localization: perirolandic region; nondominant inferior parietal lobe or TPO junction
findings.limitations: The review does not state denominators for either association.
findings.locators: PDF p.2, section 3.1 Auras
findings.phase: aura with evolution to motor features; ictal sensory illusion
findings.population: patients with focal epilepsy and electrical-stimulation observations
findings.source_term: well-localized somatosensory auras and somatosensory illusions

findings.citation: Rona S. Auras: localizing and lateralizing value. In: Lüders HO, editor. Textbook of epilepsy surgery. 2008. p. 432–42 [61]
findings.claim: Simple visual auras with static, flashing, or moving lights suggest activation of the primary visual cortex and contiguous visual association areas, whereas complex visual auras involving people, scenes, objects, or illusions suggest the temporo-occipital junction or basal temporal cortex.
findings.evidence_text: The review contrasts elementary lights with complex scenes and objects as clues to different visual regions.
findings.laterality_localization: primary visual cortex and contiguous visual association areas for simple visual auras; temporo-occipital junction or basal temporal cortex for complex visual auras
findings.limitations: The review does not state a common cohort or denominator.
findings.locators: PDF p.2, section 3.1 Auras; PDF p.2, Table 1
findings.population: patients with focal epilepsy and electrical-stimulation observations

findings.citation: Rona S. Auras: localizing and lateralizing value. In: Lüders HO, editor. Textbook of epilepsy surgery. 2008. p. 432–42 [61]
findings.claim: Visual phenomena lateralized to one hemi-field as an early ictal manifestation are highly suggestive of onset in the contralateral occipital lobe. Symptoms restricted to the lower or upper quadrant are reported to localize to the contralateral supra- or infracalcarine fissure, respectively.
findings.evidence_text: An early hemi-field symptom is linked to contralateral occipital onset, with lower and upper quadrant symptoms assigned to opposite supra- and infracalcarine regions.
findings.laterality_localization: one hemi-field or quadrant is interpreted relative to the contralateral occipital lobe and supra- or infracalcarine fissure
findings.limitations: No frequency or denominator is reported.
findings.locators: PDF p.2, section 3.1 Auras
findings.population: patients with focal epilepsy
findings.source_term: lateralized visual phenomena and visual field auras

findings.citation: Richer F, Martinez M, Cohen H, Saint-Hilaire JM. Visual motion perception from stimulation of the human medial parieto-occipital cortex. Exp Brain Res 1991;87:649–52 [7]
findings.claim: Stimulation of the precuneus, posterior cingulum, or mesial parieto-occipital region produces blurry vision or visual motions, and visual distortions such as micropsia, macropsia, metamorphopsia, and palinopsia suggest activation near the geniculostriate radiation.
findings.evidence_text: The review links blurry or moving vision to posterior medial regions and distortions to the geniculostriate-radiation vicinity.
findings.laterality_localization: precuneus, posterior cingulum, mesial parieto-occipital region, or tissue near the geniculostriate radiation
findings.limitations: The source combines stimulation findings with a localization inference and gives no frequency.
findings.locators: PDF p.2, section 3.1 Auras
findings.population: electrical-stimulation observations in patients with epilepsy
findings.source_term: visual motion, blurry vision, and visual distortions

findings.citation: Rona S. Auras: localizing and lateralizing value. In: Lüders HO, editor. Textbook of epilepsy surgery. 2008. p. 432–42 [61]
findings.claim: Simple auditory auras such as ringing or buzzing are associated with the primary auditory cortex, while complex voices, music, hallucinations, or illusions are associated with auditory association areas in the temporo-occipital cortex. Although auditory information has bilateral innervation, the contralateral ear is better represented in auditory cortex.
findings.evidence_text: The source contrasts simple ringing or buzzing with complex voices or music and notes the stronger contralateral-ear representation.
findings.laterality_localization: primary auditory cortex for simple symptoms; temporo-occipital auditory association cortex for complex symptoms; contralateral ear has better cortical representation
findings.limitations: No frequency, denominator, or laterality performance estimate is reported.
findings.locators: PDF p.2, section 3.1 Auras; PDF p.2, Table 1
findings.population: patients with focal epilepsy and electrical-stimulation observations

findings.citation: Kahane P, Hoffmann D, Minotti L, Berthoz A. Reappraisal of the human vestibular cortex by cortical electrical stimulation study. Ann Neurol 2003;54:615–24 [8]
findings.claim: Vertiginous auras with sensations of rotation or movement are usually associated with visual or auditory symptoms and a symptomatogenic zone near the visual and auditory association areas at the temporoparietal junction. Electrical stimulation readily elicits vestibular or rotatory sensations from a lateral temporoparietal region spanning the Sylvian fissure, including the parietal operculum and middle and posterior superior and middle temporal gyri.
findings.evidence_text: The review places vertiginous symptomatology near visual and auditory association cortex and describes a stimulation-defined lateral temporoparietal region.
findings.laterality_localization: temporoparietal junction and lateral temporoparietal cortex above and below the Sylvian fissure
findings.limitations: The review does not provide a common clinical denominator.
findings.locators: PDF p.2, section 3.1 Auras; PDF p.2, Table 1
findings.population: patients with focal epilepsy and electrical-stimulation observations

findings.citation: Bancaud J, Talairach J. Clinical semiology of frontal lobe seizures. Adv Neurol 1992;57:3–58 [9]; Hausser-Hauw C, Bancaud J. Gustatory hallucinations in epileptic seizures: electrophysiological, clinical and anatomical correlates. Brain 1987;110:339–59 [10]; Rona S. Auras: localizing and lateralizing value. 2008. p. 432–42 [61]
findings.claim: Olfactory auras are typically unpleasant and often associated with gustatory phenomena; stimulation of the amygdala, olfactory bulb, insula, or posterior orbitofrontal region can produce olfactory sensations or illusions. Gustatory auras can be difficult to distinguish from olfactory disturbances, and stimulation of the parietal operculum or mesiobasal temporal regions can produce gustatory hallucinations.
findings.evidence_text: The text identifies several stimulated olfactory and gustatory regions and says the two symptom types may be hard to separate clinically.
findings.laterality_localization: amygdala, olfactory bulb, insula, posterior orbitofrontal region, parietal operculum, or mesiobasal temporal region; table classifies these auras as generally nonlateralizing
findings.limitations: The table's NonLAT label is a source summary and is not accompanied by a performance estimate.
findings.locators: PDF p.2, section 3.1 Auras; PDF p.2, Table 1
findings.population: patients with focal epilepsy and electrical-stimulation observations

findings.claim: Autonomic auras include cardiorespiratory, gastrointestinal, genitourinary, and cutaneous sensations and are attributed to activation of the insular cortex, anterior cingulum, SSMA, or amygdala; the source notes that these areas share a subcortical relay station with the hypothalamus.
findings.evidence_text: The review groups several visceral and cutaneous sensations under autonomic auras and identifies four cortical regions.
findings.laterality_localization: insular cortex, anterior cingulum, SSMA, or amygdala; source table classifies autonomic auras as nonlateralizing
findings.limitations: The source does not provide a single autonomic-aura cohort or frequency estimate.

findings.citation: Henkel A, Noachtar S, Pfander M, Lüders HO. The localizing value of the abdominal aura and its evolution: a study in focal epilepsies. Neurology 2002;58:271–6 [12]; Kotagal P, Lüders HO, Williams G, Nichols TR, McPherson J. Psychomotor seizures of temporal lobe onset: analysis of symptom clusters and sequences. Epilepsy Res 1995;20:49–67 [13]
findings.claim: Abdominal auras are described as the most common autonomic aura and are localized to the anterior insula, frontal operculum, mesial temporal structures, and SSMA. In isolation they carry a reported 74% probability of TLE, rising to 98% when they evolve into an automotor component; when combined with vomiting they suggest an epileptogenic zone in the nondominant temporal lobe.
findings.comparator: Isolated abdominal aura versus abdominal aura evolving to automotor component; with versus without vomiting
findings.evidence_text: The review gives 74% for isolated abdominal auras and 98% when an automotor component develops, and links vomiting to nondominant temporal onset.
findings.laterality_localization: anterior insula, frontal operculum, mesial temporal structures, and SSMA; vomiting-associated abdominal aura suggests nondominant temporal onset
findings.limitations: The source does not report the numerators, denominators, or analysis unit underlying the probabilities.
findings.locators: PDF p.3, section 3.1 Auras; PDF p.2, Table 1
findings.measure: 74% probability of TLE in isolation; 98% probability when evolving to automotor component
findings.phase: isolated aura versus evolution to automotor component; vomiting-associated aura
findings.population: patients with focal epilepsy; review-reported abdominal-aura series
findings.uncertainty: Source reports probabilities only; no confidence interval or statistical test reported

findings.citation: Remillard GM, Andermann F, Testa GF, et al. Sexual ictal manifestations predominate in women with temporal lobe epilepsy: a finding suggesting sexual dimorphism in the human brain. Neurology 1983;33:323–30 [14]
findings.claim: Orgasmic auras, defined as erotic thoughts or feelings, sexual arousal, and orgasm sometimes accompanied by a viscerosensory phenomenon, were observed more often in women with right TLE.
findings.comparator: Women with right versus other temporal-lobe onset
findings.evidence_text: The review defines orgasmic auras and reports that they were observed more often in women with right TLE.
findings.laterality_localization: right temporal lobe, as a group association
findings.limitations: The review provides no count or denominator for the sex- and laterality-specific observation.
findings.locators: PDF p.3, section 3.1 Auras
findings.measure: More frequent in women with right TLE; no percentage reported
findings.population: women with temporal lobe epilepsy
findings.uncertainty: More often, as stated by the source; no statistical uncertainty reported

findings.citation: Calleja J, Carpizo R, Berciano J. Orgasmic epilepsy. Epilepsia 1988;29:635–9 [15]
findings.claim: Genital auras are often painful or unpleasant and associated with fear; the symptomatogenic zone is the postcentral parasagittal region, but bilateral symptoms can arise from SII activation.
findings.evidence_text: The source places genital aura localization in the postcentral parasagittal region and notes an SII alternative for bilateral symptoms.
findings.laterality_localization: postcentral parasagittal region; bilateral symptoms may reflect SII activation
findings.limitations: No frequency or denominator is reported.
findings.locators: PDF p.3, section 3.1 Auras
findings.population: patients with focal epilepsy

findings.citation: Fish DR, Gloor P, Quesney FL, Olivier A. Clinical responses to electrical brain stimulation of the temporal and frontal lobes in patients with epilepsy: pathophysiological implications. Brain 1993;116:397–414 [11]; Rona S. Auras: localizing and lateralizing value. 2008. p. 432–42 [61]
findings.claim: Psychic auras include emotional symptoms and familiarity distortions; the symptomatogenic zone is generally temporal neocortex or mesial temporal structures, except that forced thoughts are generally observed in FLE. Fear is associated with amygdala, hippocampal, mesial frontal, or temporal-neocortical activation, and Table 1 lists fear as nonlateralizing.
findings.evidence_text: The review places most psychic auras in temporal structures, identifies forced thoughts as a frontal exception, and describes fear-related activation.

findings.citation: Stefan H, Schulze-Bonhage A, Pauli E, et al. Ictal pleasant sensations: cerebral localization and lateralization. Epilepsia 2004;45:35–40 [16]; Rona S. Auras: localizing and lateralizing value. 2008. p. 432–42 [61]
findings.claim: Pleasant emotional auras such as euphoria or satisfaction are associated with the mesiobasal temporal area; multisensorial hallucinations require mesiobasal temporal, lateral temporal, or TPO activation; and out-of-body experiences are produced by stimulation near the temporoparietal junction.
findings.evidence_text: The review links pleasant sensations, multisensorial hallucinations, and out-of-body experiences to distinct temporal or temporoparietal regions.
findings.laterality_localization: mesiobasal temporal area; lateral temporal region; TPO or temporoparietal junction

findings.population: patients with focal epilepsy and electrical-stimulation observations

findings.citation: Rona S. Auras: localizing and lateralizing value. In: Lüders HO, editor. Textbook of epilepsy surgery. 2008. p. 432–42 [61]
findings.claim: Cephalic auras are nonvertiginous head sensations that can arise from the amygdala, entorhinal cortex, or lateral temporal neocortex but often have little localizing value, whereas whole-body auras are generalized body sensations that may be elicited by SII and SSMA stimulation.
findings.evidence_text: The review contrasts nonspecific cephalic sensations with generalized whole-body sensations and gives their source regions.
findings.laterality_localization: amygdala, entorhinal cortex, lateral temporal neocortex, SII, or SSMA; table classifies the cephalic/whole-body category as nonlateralizing

findings.citation: Baumgartner C, Podreka I, Olbrich A, et al. Epileptic negative myoclonus: an EEG-single-photon emission CT study indicating involvement of premotor cortex. Neurology 1996;46:753–8 [17]; Rona S. Auras: localizing and lateralizing value. 2008. p. 432–42 [61]
findings.claim: Myoclonic seizures are usually generalized or bilateral but can be focal; unilateral myoclonic seizures are generated from the primary motor or premotor cortex contralateral to the seizure. Negative myoclonus is brief muscle atonia during contraction, and negative epileptic myoclonus is rarely observed in perirolandic epilepsy.
findings.comparator: Generalized or bilateral versus unilateral myoclonus; positive versus negative myoclonus
findings.evidence_text: The review associates unilateral myoclonus with contralateral motor or premotor regions and says perirolandic negative epileptic myoclonus is rare.
findings.laterality_localization: unilateral myoclonus contralateral to the primary motor or premotor source; table lists contralateral lateralization when unilateral
findings.limitations: The duration ranges are definitions; no prevalence denominator is supplied for the rare observation.

findings.measure: Myoclonic duration shorter than 400 ms; negative myoclonus 20–400 ms; prevalence of perirolandic negative myoclonus not reported
findings.population: patients with focal or generalized epilepsy
findings.uncertainty: Usually or rarely, as stated by the source; no statistical uncertainty reported

findings.citation: Noachtar S, Arnold S. Simple motor seizures: localizing and lateralizing value. In: Lüders HO, editor. Textbook of epilepsy surgery. 2008. p. 450–61 [18]; Manford M, Fish DR, Shorvon SD. An analysis of clinical seizure patterns and their localizing value in frontal and temporal lobe epilepsies. Brain 1996;119:17–40 [6]
findings.claim: Clonic activity reflects propagation over the motor cortex when it spreads from distal to proximal regions. In FLE it tends to occur early with consciousness preserved; in TLE it usually involves the face or upper extremity after an automotor phase; parietal-origin seizures are typically preceded by somatosensory disturbance, occipital-origin seizures by visual auras or versive head/eye movements, and SSMA seizures by bilateral clonic activity with tonic posturing.
findings.comparator: FLE versus TLE versus parietal, occipital, or SSMA seizure origin
findings.evidence_text: The source uses the timing and accompanying semiology of clonic activity to distinguish frontal, temporal, parietal, occipital, and SSMA patterns.
findings.laterality_localization: motor-cortex propagation; parietal, occipital, temporal, frontal, or SSMA origin according to preceding signs and seizure context
findings.limitations: The statements are narrative patterns rather than a single measured comparison.
findings.locators: PDF p.3, section 3.2 Simple motor seizures; PDF p.2, Table 1
findings.measure: Clonic contractions recur at 0.2–5 per second; no frequency of localization patterns reported
findings.population: patients with focal epilepsy and focal epilepsy subgroups
findings.uncertainty: Source-stated typical patterns; no statistical uncertainty reported

findings.citation: Rona S. Auras: localizing and lateralizing value. 2008. p. 432–42 [61]
findings.claim: Tonic seizures involve sustained contraction with posturing; although proximal muscles are often affected bilaterally, clearly unilateral tonic seizures strongly support seizure origin in the contralateral hemisphere.
findings.comparator: Bilateral or asymmetric tonic activity versus clearly unilateral tonic activity
findings.evidence_text: The review says unilateral tonic seizures support contralateral seizure origin while proximal tonic activity may be bilateral.
findings.laterality_localization: unilateral tonic posturing contralateral to seizure origin

findings.citation: Chee MW, Kotagal P, Van Ness PC, Gragg L, Murphy D, Lüders HO. Lateralizing signs in intractable partial epilepsy: blinded multiple-observer analysis. Neurology 1993;43:2519–25 [19]
findings.claim: Sustained forced turning of the head or eyes, usually with same-side mouth deviation and head hyperextension, is contralateral to the hemisphere of seizure onset when it occurs immediately before a GTCS. In temporal lobe seizures version occurs later while consciousness is impaired, unlike the earlier pattern described in FLE.
findings.evidence_text: The source relates pre-GTCS version to the contralateral onset hemisphere and distinguishes its timing in frontal versus temporal seizures.
findings.laterality_localization: direction of version contralateral to seizure-onset hemisphere before GTCS
findings.limitations: No performance estimate is reported in this passage.

findings.population: patients with focal epilepsy; temporal and frontal lobe epilepsy

findings.citation: Ryvlin P, Minotti L, Demarquay G, et al. Nocturnal hypermotor seizures, suggesting frontal lobe epilepsy, can originate in the insula. Epilepsia 2006;47:755–65 [21]; Wieser HG, Hajek M. Frontal lobe epilepsy. Compartmentalization, presurgical evaluation, and operative results. Adv Neurol 1995;66:297–318 discussion 318–9 [22]; Dobesberger J, Walser G, Embacher N, et al. Gyratory seizures revisited: a video-EEG study. Neurology 2005;64:1884–7 [23]
findings.claim: Hypermotor seizures with rapid, violent proximal-limb and trunk movements originate primarily in the frontal lobe and less commonly in the temporal lobe, posterior cortex, or insula. Ventromedial frontal seizures have more hypermotor features, while dorsolateral frontal seizures more often show head/eye version and complex gestural automatisms; sexual-quality hypermotor movements and rare body-axis rotation of at least 180 degrees suggest frontal origin. Rotation is usually contralateral to the epileptogenic zone when preceded by version and usually ipsilateral when not preceded by version.
findings.comparator: Ventromedial versus dorsolateral frontal seizures; rotation preceded versus not preceded by version
findings.evidence_text: The review identifies frontal predominance, a ventromedial/dorsolateral distinction, and opposite rotation directions depending on preceding version.
findings.laterality_localization: primarily frontal origin; rotation direction relative to the epileptogenic zone depends on preceding version
findings.limitations: The table labels hypermotor seizures nonlateralizing even though the narrative describes localization and conditional rotation direction.
findings.locators: PDF p.3, section 3.3 Complex motor seizures; PDF p.2, Table 1
findings.measure: Body-axis rotation of at least 180 degrees in rare cases; no prevalence reported
findings.phase: ictal motor; rotation with or without preceding version
findings.population: patients with focal epilepsy
findings.uncertainty: Primarily, less commonly, rarely, and usually, as stated by the source

findings.citation: Lüders H, Acharya J, Baumgartner C, et al. Semiological seizure classification. Epilepsia 1998;39:1006–13 [20]; Jobst BC, Siegel AM, Thadani VM, Roberts DW, Rhodes HC, Williamson PD. Intractable seizures of frontal lobe origin: clinical characteristics, localizing signs, and results of surgery. Epilepsia 2000;41:1139–52 [24]
findings.claim: Automotor seizures consist of repetitive, stereotyped, semipurposeful oral, lingual, or distal-limb behaviors. Awareness is generally impaired except in seizures restricted to the nondominant temporal lobe; prolonged homogeneous perseverative, complex-gesture, and upper-limb automatisms characterize TLE, whereas frontal automatisms are more hyperkinetic and irregular, involve proximal limbs, and genital manipulations are rare in frontal and temporal seizures.
findings.evidence_text: The source contrasts oral, gestural, perseverative temporal automatisms with hyperkinetic proximal frontal automatisms and states that awareness is usually impaired.
findings.laterality_localization: nondominant temporal restriction can preserve awareness; temporal versus frontal pattern provides localization

findings.citation: Unnwongse K, Wehner T, Bingaman W, Foldvary-Schaefer N. Gelastic seizures and the anteromesial frontal lobe: a case report and review of intracranial EEG recording and electrocortical stimulation case studies. Epilepsia March 18 2010 Epub [25]
findings.claim: Brief laughter or grimacing with or without subjective mirth strongly suggests a hypothalamic hamartoma, although intracranial EEG and electrical-stimulation studies have identified the symptomatogenic zone in anteromesial frontal and basal temporal regions in isolated cases.

findings.citation: Fogarasi A, Janszky J, Tuxhorn I. Autonomic symptoms during childhood partial epileptic seizures. Epilepsia 2006;47:584–8 [26]
findings.claim: In children younger than 3–4 years with TLE, tonic, clonic, or myoclonic movements may be bilateral and symmetric and resemble generalized epilepsy, and automatisms are less elaborate and restricted to the orobuccal region. After age 6, TLE manifestations are similar to adults; very young posterior-cortex epilepsy more often presents with decreased motor activity or hypomotor seizures.

findings.citation: Rona S. Auras: localizing and lateralizing value. 2008. p. 432–42 [61]
findings.claim: Dialeptic seizures with altered consciousness, staring, and minimal motor activity alone provide no useful localizing or lateralizing information and can arise from virtually any area, but an aura before the dialeptic phase and the subsequent ictal sequence can identify structures activated by the discharge. A dialeptic phase evolving into automotor behavior is common in TLE, whereas an isolated dialeptic phase has no localizing value.
findings.evidence_text: The source distinguishes isolated staring from sequences that include an aura or later automotor behavior.
findings.laterality_localization: No localization from isolated dialeptic phase; preceding aura and subsequent sequence may localize activated structures
findings.limitations: The review does not quantify the frequency of either sequence.

Heart rate increase in otherwise subclinical seizures is different in temporal versus extratemporal seizure onset: support for temporal lobe autonomic influence. Epileptic Disord 2005;7:199–204 [27]; Rona S. Auras: localizing and lateralizing value. 2008. p. 432–42 [61]
findings.claim: Ictal tachycardia, defined in the review as heart rate above 100 bpm, is reported in more than 50% of seizures and early significant tachycardia is more common in temporal than extratemporal epilepsy, particularly right MTLE. Ictal bradycardia below 60 bpm is less common and has not shown localizing or lateralizing value; ictal asystole and arrhythmia are rare and are implicated in SUDEP pathogenesis.

In adults with TLE it is more common with mesial than neocortical onset; ictal apnea is most common in infants and neonates, while ictal dyspnea and stridor are rare and occur primarily during the tonic phase of GTCSs.

J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2004;75:879–83 [28]; Fogarasi A, Janszky J, Tuxhorn I. Ictal pallor is associated with left temporal seizure onset zone in children. Epilepsy Res 2005;67:117–21 [29]; Rona S. Auras: localizing and lateralizing value. 2008. p. 432–42 [61]

findings.citation: Salanova V, Andermann F, Rasmussen T, Olivier A, Quesney LF. Parietal lobe epilepsy: clinical manifestations and outcome in 82 patients treated surgically between 1929 and 1988. Brain 1995;118:607–27 [57]; Boesebeck F, Schulz R, May T, Ebner A. Lateralizing semiology predicts the seizure outcome after epilepsy surgery in the posterior cortex. Brain 2002;125:2320–31 [56]
findings.claim: Parietal epileptogenic lesions may produce vertigo, body-image disturbance, and visual illusions or hallucinations; tonic posturing is associated with superior-parietal involvement and automatisms with inferior-parietal involvement. findings.claim: Pure insular epilepsy has a typical sequence beginning with laryngeal discomfort and thoraco-abdominal constriction or dyspnea, followed by unpleasant perioral or large-area paresthesias or warmth, dysarthria or dysphonia, and focal motor manifestations. Consciousness is not impaired in seizures restricted to the insula, and unilateral sensory symptoms and focal motor activity are usually contralateral to the epileptogenic zone.

findings.claim: Extensive connections allow insular seizures to produce visceral, motor, and somatosensory symptoms that mimic seizures from many other regions; temporal seizures virtually always invade the insula.
