findings.claim: Temporal-plus epilepsy involves the temporal lobe and a connected network including orbitofrontal region, insula, frontal or parietal operculum, and TPO junction. Hippocampal sclerosis on MRI cannot reliably differentiate pure TLE from temporal-plus epilepsy, whereas semiology distinguishes them: pure TLE more often has abdominal auras evolving to automatisms and postictal amnesia, while temporal-plus epilepsy is associated with gustatory, auditory, or vertiginous auras, version, piloerection, ipsilateral tonic signs, and postictal dysphoria.
findings.evidence_text: The source contrasts the semiology of pure TLE with temporal-plus epilepsy and cautions against relying on hippocampal sclerosis alone.
findings.laterality_localization: Temporal-plus network; ipsilateral tonic signs in temporal-plus epilepsy
findings.limitations: No quantitative diagnostic performance is reported.
findings.locators: PDF p.6, section 8.4 Temporal-plus epilepsies
findings.population: patients with pure TLE and temporal-plus epilepsy

findings.citation: Rona S. Auras: localizing and lateralizing value. In: Lüders HO, editor. Textbook of epilepsy surgery. 2008. p. 432–42 [61]
findings.claim: Table 1 lists fear as arising from the amygdala, hippocampus, and mesial frontal lobe and as nonlateralizing; it lists déjà vu or jamais vu as arising from the uncus, entorhinal cortex, and temporal neocortex and as nonlateralizing, often nondominant.
findings.evidence_text: The table preserves separate symptomatogenic zones and nonlateralizing labels for fear and déjà vu/jamais vu, including the latter's often-nondominant qualifier.
findings.laterality_localization: Fear: amygdala, hippocampus, mesial frontal lobe, nonlateralizing; déjà vu/jamais vu: uncus, entorhinal cortex, temporal neocortex, nonlateralizing and often nondominant
findings.limitations: Table 1 states typical zones and common syndromes, not a validated diagnostic performance estimate.
findings.locators: PDF p.2, Table 1
findings.population: patients with focal epilepsy
findings.source_term: fear and déjà vu or jamais vu auras in Table 1

findings.citation: Bianchin MM, Sakamoto AC. Complex motor seizures: localizing and lateralizing value. In: Lüders HO, editor. Textbook of epilepsy surgery. 2008. p. 462–78 [62]
findings.claim: Table 2 lists unilateral ear plugging as a lateralizing sign associated with the superior temporal gyrus and contralateral lateralization in TLE.
findings.evidence_text: Table 2 assigns unilateral ear plugging to the superior temporal gyrus and marks its lateralization as contralateral in TLE.
findings.laterality_localization: Superior temporal gyrus; contralateral to the seizure focus as summarized in the table
findings.limitations: The table provides no frequency, denominator, or performance estimate.
findings.locators: PDF p.5, Table 2
findings.population: patients with TLE

sources.source_report_limitations: This review is a narrative synthesis with heterogeneous cited populations, phases, reference standards, and analysis units rather than a single original dataset. Many numerical statements are given only as percentages or ranges without numerators, denominators, confidence intervals, or statistical tests, and the review does not report a common denominator across its cited studies. The source explicitly cautions that clinical history depends on patient and observer factors, video/EEG depends on reproducible signs and technical quality, and electrical stimulation may activate distant areas. Several claims are explicitly limited to one series, isolated cases, or pediatric populations. Table 1 is modified from Rona [61] and Table 2 from Bianchin and Sakamoto [62]; cited-source restatements were not independently verified against the cited papers in this review.
sources.source_report_methods_population: This is a narrative review rather than a single original cohort or systematic quantitative synthesis. The discussed populations include patients with focal epilepsy, temporal lobe epilepsy, mesial and neocortical temporal lobe epilepsy, extratemporal and posterior-cortex epilepsy, children and infants, and presurgical epilepsy-surgery candidates. The review draws on clinical history, video/EEG and electrical-stimulation observations and on cited case series and cohorts; a single review-wide analysis population, eligibility rule, reference standard, and common denominator are not reported.
sources.source_report_summary: Foldvary-Schaefer and Unnwongse's narrative review from the American Epilepsy Society 2009 Annual Course surveys the localizing and lateralizing value of auras, ictal and postictal motor signs, autonomic manifestations, speech and language findings, and semiology that distinguishes temporal from extratemporal epilepsies. It emphasizes that semiology estimates the symptomatogenic zone and its relationship to the epileptogenic zone, but must be interpreted with clinical history, video/EEG, electrical stimulation, and the other components of presurgical evaluation. The review contains two source-modified summary tables and restates findings from cited studies.

findings.claim: In MTLE, the earliest FAS manifestations are subjective cognitive, autonomic, emotional, or sensory symptoms lasting a few seconds and are highly suggestive of mesial temporal seizure onset.
findings.evidence_text: The chapter describes FAS as brief subjective cognitive, autonomic, emotional, or sensory symptoms and calls them highly suggestive of mesial temporal onset.
findings.laterality_localization: mesial temporal seizure onset; no specific hemisphere stated
findings.limitations: Qualitative review synthesis; the chapter does not establish sensitivity or specificity for individual symptoms.
findings.locators: PDF p.7, Clinical features: natural history and semiology; PDF p.7, Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy; PDF p.7, Focal aware seizures
findings.population: patients with MTLE or suspected mesial temporal seizure onset
findings.uncertainty: Source gives a duration range but no distribution or uncertainty

findings.citation: Palmini and Gloor, 1992; Sadler and Rahey, 2004; Penfield and Perot, 1963; Hogan and Kaiboriboon, 2003; Vignal et al., 2006
findings.claim: Dysmnesic manifestations are characteristic of MTLE; déjà vu has been reported as predominant in nondominant MTLE, prescience is rarely described, and the “dreamy state” may include déjà vu, strangeness or unreality, and complex auditory or visual hallucinations.
findings.evidence_text: The source links episodic-memory distortions to MTLE, identifies a nondominant déjà-vu predominance, and describes the component experiences of the “dreamy state.”
findings.laterality_localization: mesial temporal; déjà vu reported more often with nondominant MTLE
findings.limitations: The cited observations use heterogeneous definitions and do not provide a chapter-level diagnostic estimate.
findings.locators: PDF p.7, Focal cognitive seizures
findings.population: patients with MTLE and historical or cited temporal-lobe seizure observations
findings.source_term: dysmnesic manifestations, déjà vu, jamais vu, prescience, and “dreamy state”

findings.citation: Heydrich et al., 2019; Simeon et al., 2000
findings.claim: Ictal derealization was reported more frequently in MTLE in one cited study (85% of that study’s MTLE patients), while derealization and depersonalization were associated with nondominant-hemisphere involvement; depersonalization was more frequent in frontal lobe epilepsy, and another study linked it to parietal rather than frontal or temporal hypermetabolism.
findings.comparator: MTLE versus frontal lobe epilepsy; parietal versus frontal or temporal hypermetabolism
findings.evidence_text: The chapter reports 85% ictal derealization in one MTLE study but also describes frontal and parietal associations for depersonalization.
findings.laterality_localization: MTLE and nondominant hemisphere associations are reported, with alternative frontal and parietal associations
findings.limitations: The cited cohorts and analysis units are not harmonized, and the percentage denominator is not reported.
findings.locators: PDF p.8, Ictal dissociative-like experiences
findings.measure: 85% MTLE frequency for ictal derealization in the cited study; qualitative cross-localization comparisons
findings.population: cited patients with MTLE or other focal epilepsy; study denominators not reported in the chapter
findings.uncertainty: Source reports nonuniform and partly conflicting localization associations

findings.citation: French et al., 1993; Isnard et al., 2000
findings.claim: Rising epigastric sensations are common ictal gastrointestinal symptoms in the MTLE discussion, last a few seconds, have varied subjective descriptions, and may suggest insular involvement rather than uniquely localizing to mesial temporal structures.
findings.evidence_text: The source lists rising epigastric sensations as brief and variably described and notes a possible insular contribution.
findings.laterality_localization: may suggest insular involvement; no reliable side relation stated
findings.limitations: This is not presented as pathognomonic for MTLE or as an isolated localization test.
findings.locators: PDF p.8, Focal autonomic seizures; PDF p.10, Temporal plus epilepsy
findings.measure: duration of a few seconds; qualitative symptom descriptions
findings.phase: ictal focal aware or early seizure phase
findings.population: patients with temporal-lobe focal seizures
findings.uncertainty: Source uses “may suggest” and does not present a diagnostic performance estimate

findings.claim: Ictal piloerection is described as a relatively rare manifestation and has been reported on the side ipsilateral to the seizure-onset zone.
findings.evidence_text: The chapter calls ictal piloerection relatively rare and reports an ipsilateral relation to the seizure-onset zone.
findings.laterality_localization: ipsilateral to the seizure-onset zone
findings.limitations: The cited source is not independently reviewed here, and no numerator or denominator is supplied.
findings.locators: PDF p.8, Focal autonomic seizures
findings.population: patients with focal seizures; cited study population not further specified in the chapter

findings.citation: Tinuper, 2001; Garcia et al., 2001; Opherk et al., 2002
findings.claim: Ictal tachycardia and bradycardia, which may lead to ictal asystole, are described as more frequent in temporal focal seizures with impaired awareness than in extratemporal seizures, particularly when seizures originate from the left hemisphere; some studies report a slight MTLE predominance.
findings.comparator: temporal versus extratemporal; left versus other hemisphere; MTLE versus other temporal subtypes
findings.evidence_text: The source places ictal cardiac-rate abnormalities more often in temporal impaired-awareness seizures, especially left-sided cases, while qualifying the MTLE predominance as slight.
findings.laterality_localization: temporal, especially left-hemisphere, origin; slight MTLE predominance in some studies
findings.limitations: No frequency, denominator, or independent reference standard is given in the chapter.
findings.locators: PDF p.8, Focal autonomic seizures
findings.population: patients with temporal or extratemporal focal seizures with impaired awareness
findings.uncertainty: “Seem to be” and “slight predominance” indicate qualified rather than definitive associations

findings.claim: Sudden ictal fear or anxiety resembling a panic attack may highlight an amygdala seizure onset; dysphoric, euphoric, and ultimately ecstatic feelings are also described in the mesial temporal semiology spectrum.
findings.evidence_text: The chapter links sudden fear or anxiety to possible amygdala onset and lists dysphoric, euphoric, and ecstatic experiences.
findings.laterality_localization: amygdala onset; no specific hemisphere stated
findings.limitations: Emotional symptoms are not stated to be unique to amygdala or MTLE seizures.
findings.locators: PDF p.8, Focal emotional seizures
findings.phase: ictal focal aware or early seizure phase
findings.population: patients with focal temporal seizures

findings.citation: Hausser-Hauw and Bancaud, 1987; Chen et al., 2003
findings.claim: Unpleasant olfactory and gustatory hallucinations can result from seizures involving mesial temporal structures, particularly the amygdala, but are not pathognomonic because gustatory symptoms with hypersalivation and olfactory symptoms have also been reported with opercular and orbitofrontal seizures, respectively.
findings.evidence_text: The source places unpleasant smell or taste in a mesial temporal/amygdala context but gives opercular and orbitofrontal alternatives.
findings.laterality_localization: mesial temporal/amygdala association with opercular and orbitofrontal alternatives
findings.limitations: The chapter does not quantify the competing localization probabilities.
findings.locators: PDF p.8, Focal sensory seizures; PDF p.10, Temporal plus epilepsy
findings.phase: ictal focal aware or early seizure phase
findings.population: patients with focal seizures involving temporal, opercular, or orbitofrontal regions

findings.claim: Impaired awareness may follow FAS and is associated with unresponsiveness, motion arrest, and repetitive nonpurposeful automatisms; unlike highly localized FAS, it may reflect propagation to brainstem and thalamic arousal structures with depression of associative cortices.
findings.evidence_text: The chapter contrasts localized FAS with impaired-awareness seizures that include automatisms and may involve subcortical arousal networks.
findings.laterality_localization: propagation beyond localized mesial temporal discharge to subcortical arousal structures
findings.limitations: Clinical impairment of awareness is not treated as proof of a single temporal subregion.
findings.locators: PDF p.8, Focal impaired awareness seizures
findings.phase: ictal transition to focal impaired awareness
findings.population: patients with focal temporal seizures progressing from focal aware to impaired awareness
findings.source_term: focal impaired awareness seizures and automatisms

findings.claim: Ictal leaving behavior, consisting of walking or running away, has been mentioned as a possible sign of nondominant MTLE.
findings.evidence_text: The source lists walking or running away as a possible nondominant-MTLE sign.
findings.laterality_localization: possible nondominant MTLE
findings.limitations: The cited association is qualified and not independently verified here.
findings.locators: PDF p.8, Focal impaired awareness seizures
findings.population: patients with MTLE; cited report population not further specified in the chapter

findings.citation: Yen et al., 1996; Chauvire et al., 2007; Dupont et al., 2015; Horvath et al., 2009
findings.claim: Ictal vocalizations and ictal speech are reported in TLE but are not exclusive to it; comprehensible stereotyped speech, including rare second-language automatisms, suggests a nondominant-hemisphere focus, whereas the lateralizing value of vocalizations toward the dominant hemisphere remains controversial.
findings.evidence_text: The chapter distinguishes elementary vocalizations from comprehensible ictal speech and qualifies the dominant-hemisphere value of vocalizations as controversial.
findings.laterality_localization: ictal speech suggests nondominant hemisphere; dominant-hemisphere lateralization of vocalizations is controversial
findings.limitations: Speech and vocalization categories are heterogeneous and the chapter gives no pooled performance measure.
findings.locators: PDF p.8, Focal impaired awareness seizures
findings.population: patients with focal temporal seizures
findings.source_term: ictal speech, verbal automatisms, and ictal vocalizations

findings.citation: Dupont et al., 2015; R/C19emi et al., 2011
findings.claim: Secondary motor signs related to propagation outside the temporal lobe may lateralize the seizure-onset zone: unilateral dystonic posturing is usually contralateral to the focus, head or eye deviation suggests an ipsilateral focus, and other unilateral clonic or tonic movements or limb immobility usually indicate a contralateral focus.
findings.comparator: direction of different secondary motor signs relative to the seizure focus
findings.evidence_text: The source states that dystonia is usually contralateral, head/eye deviation suggests ipsilateral focus, and other unilateral motor signs usually contralateral.
findings.laterality_localization: dystonia, clonic/tonic movement, and hypokinesia contralateral; head/eye deviation ipsilateral to seizure focus
findings.limitations: These are secondary signs after propagation; head deviation is also described as earlier and faster in frontal lobe epilepsy than in TLE.
findings.locators: PDF p.8, Focal impaired awareness seizures
findings.measure: unilateral dystonic posturing reported in almost half of patients with MTLE
findings.population: patients with focal impaired awareness temporal seizures
findings.source_term: unilateral dystonic posturing, head/eye deviation, clonic or tonic movements, and hypokinesia
findings.uncertainty: Source uses “usually,” “suggests,” and “in most cases,” and attributes signs to propagation

findings.claim: During the tonic phase of a focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure, asymmetric tonic limb posturing, also called the “figure-of-4” sign, is described as contralateral to the seizure focus.
findings.evidence_text: The chapter identifies contralateral asymmetric tonic limb posturing as the lateralizing “figure-of-4” sign.
findings.laterality_localization: asymmetric tonic limb posture contralateral to seizure focus
findings.limitations: The sign occurs during a propagated focal to bilateral seizure and is not presented as a localizing sign for the exact onset subregion.
findings.locators: PDF p.9, Focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures
findings.population: patients with focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures

findings.citation: Helmstaedter et al., 1994; Pottk€amper et al., 2020
findings.claim: Postictal verbal memory impairment is suggestive of a dominant-hemisphere temporal focus, visual memory impairment of a nondominant-hemisphere focus, and postictal aphasia strongly suggests a dominant-hemisphere focus.
findings.evidence_text: The source assigns verbal memory and aphasia to dominant-hemisphere suggestion and visual memory impairment to nondominant-hemisphere suggestion.
findings.laterality_localization: verbal memory impairment and aphasia dominant hemisphere; visual memory impairment nondominant hemisphere
findings.limitations: Generic postictal manifestations after focal to bilateral seizures are distinguished from these more specific signs.
findings.locators: PDF p.9, Postictal state
findings.population: patients after focal impaired awareness or focal to bilateral seizures
findings.source_term: postictal verbal and visual memory impairment and postictal aphasia

findings.claim: Postictal hemiparesis reflects a contralateral seizure focus, whereas postictal nose wiping affects the hand ipsilateral to the seizure focus.
findings.evidence_text: The chapter gives opposite laterality relations for postictal hemiparesis and nose wiping.
findings.laterality_localization: hemiparesis contralateral; nose-wiping hand ipsilateral to seizure focus
findings.limitations: The cited source is not independently reviewed here; exact timing and diagnostic performance are not reported.
findings.locators: PDF p.9, Postictal state
findings.population: patients after focal seizures

findings.claim: Postictal coughing or sighing has no stated lateralizing value but is described as rare and quite specific for MTLE; these signs are usually absent in LTLE.
findings.evidence_text: The source separates the MTLE-specific postictal association from lateralization and notes that LTLE patients usually do not cough or sigh postictally.
findings.laterality_localization: no lateralizing value stated; association with MTLE rather than LTLE
findings.limitations: “Specific” is source wording without a reported denominator or diagnostic estimate.
findings.locators: PDF p.9, Postictal state; PDF p.9, Other signs to discriminate between LTLE and MTLE
findings.population: patients after focal impaired awareness temporal seizures

findings.claim: Focal auditory seizures are the most suggestive symptom of LTLE: elementary sounds implicate Heschl’s gyrus and primary auditory cortex, complex voices or music implicate secondary auditory cortex, and auditory illusions represent distorted perception of real sounds; unilateral auditory symptoms arise from the contralateral hemisphere, while complex verbal hallucinations and negative auditory illusions may indicate dominant-hemisphere involvement.
findings.evidence_text: The chapter classifies elementary, complex, and illusory auditory symptoms and gives their source-anatomy and hemisphere qualifications.
findings.laterality_localization: Heschl’s gyrus/primary auditory cortex for elementary symptoms; lateral superior temporal secondary auditory cortex for complex symptoms; unilateral symptoms contralateral; complex verbal or negative illusions may be dominant-hemisphere
findings.limitations: Posterior sensory symptoms may reflect propagation beyond the temporal lobe.
findings.locators: PDF p.9, Lateral temporal lobe epilepsy; PDF p.9, Focal aware seizures
findings.population: patients with LTLE

findings.claim: Visual and vestibular illusions, especially vertigo, are reported particularly in posterior LTLE, but the chapter states that they probably rely on propagation of ictal activity to occipital or parietal regions.
findings.evidence_text: The source places vertigo and other sensory illusions in posterior LTLE but attributes them probably to occipital or parietal propagation.
findings.laterality_localization: posterior lateral temporal association qualified by propagation to occipital or parietal lobe
findings.limitations: No laterality or quantitative localization estimate is reported.
findings.locators: PDF p.9, Focal aware seizures
findings.population: patients with posterior LTLE
findings.source_term: visual and vestibular illusions, including vertigo

findings.citation: Maillard et al., 2004; Foldvary et al., 1997; Hoffmann et al., 2009; O’Brien et al., 1996; Pf€ander et al., 2002
findings.claim: Relative to MTLE, LTLE is characterized in the chapter by fewer dysmnesic, emotional, rising-epigastric, dreamy-state, and olfactory/gustatory focal aware symptoms; earlier awareness loss, early clonic movements, and focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures are more common, whereas oroalimentary or gestural automatisms, ictal hyperventilation, hypersalivation, dystonic posturing, and postictal coughing or sighing favor MTLE.
findings.evidence_text: The chapter consolidates symptom absences, awareness timing, automatisms, autonomic signs, motor signs, and postictal differences between LTLE and MTLE.
findings.laterality_localization: LTLE versus MTLE subtype; motor differences are interpreted through preferential propagation to basal ganglia or motor cortex
findings.limitations: The comparisons are qualitative and are not a pooled head-to-head estimate.
findings.locators: PDF p.9, Other signs to discriminate between LTLE and MTLE
findings.population: patients with LTLE or MTLE
findings.source_term: clinical features differentiating LTLE from MTLE

findings.citation: Bartolomei et al., 1999; Kahane and Bartolomei, 2010; Maillard et al., 2004
findings.claim: Stereo-EEG recordings have identified seizures beginning almost simultaneously in mesial and lateral temporal structures; these mesio-lateral seizures can resemble MTLE clinically, but initial awareness impairment and early automatisms are more frequent than in exclusive MTL seizures, illustrating overlapping features from connected deep and neocortical structures.
findings.comparator: mesio-lateral versus exclusive MTL or LTL seizures
findings.evidence_text: The source uses stereo-EEG to describe near-simultaneous mesial and lateral onset and notes early awareness loss and automatisms in the mesio-lateral subtype.
findings.laterality_localization: near-simultaneous mesial and lateral temporal involvement; broader epileptogenic network possible
findings.limitations: The review does not provide a single operational boundary for mesio-lateral onset.
findings.locators: PDF p.9, Mesio-lateral temporal epilepsy
findings.measure: infrequent focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures; no numeric frequency reported
findings.population: patients with MTL or LTL lesions studied with stereo-EEG
findings.uncertainty: Source emphasizes overlap and the possibility that a larger network may preclude surgical management

findings.claim: In a cited drug-resistant TLE population, up to half of patients had early temporo-polar involvement on stereo-EEG and one-third of those patients had a temporo-polar seizure-onset zone; TPE itself is described as a rare TLE subtype.
findings.comparator: early temporo-polar involvement versus temporo-polar seizure-onset zone
findings.evidence_text: The chapter distinguishes early temporo-polar involvement from a temporo-polar onset zone and reports up to one-half and one-third, respectively.
findings.laterality_localization: temporo-polar cortex involvement; temporo-polar seizure-onset zone in a subset
findings.limitations: The chapter does not give the underlying cohort size or confidence interval.
findings.locators: PDF p.10, Temporal pole or temporo-polar epilepsy
findings.measure: up to 50% early temporo-polar involvement; one-third with temporo-polar seizure-onset zone
findings.phase: early ictal stereo-EEG involvement and seizure onset
findings.population: patients with drug-resistant TLE in the cited stereo-EEG cohort
findings.source_term: early temporo-polar involvement and temporo-polar seizure onset zone
findings.uncertainty: “Up to” and “one-third” are source-reported bounds; cohort denominator is not reported

findings.citation: Herlin et al., 2020; Chabardès et al., 2005
findings.claim: In a cited TPE cohort, about 80% of patients had characteristic MTLE-like seizures with rising epigastric sensation, déjà vu or fear, followed by awareness loss and gestural or swallowing automatisms; compared with MTLE, TPE-like seizures had earlier awareness loss and greater monthly frequency.
findings.evidence_text: The source reports an approximately 80% MTLE-like pattern in a TPE cohort and qualifies it by earlier awareness loss and greater monthly frequency.
findings.laterality_localization: temporo-polar seizure onset with MTLE-like regional propagation toward mesial temporal structures
findings.limitations: The cited cohort denominator and exact frequency measures are not stated.
findings.locators: PDF p.10, Temporal pole or temporo-polar epilepsy
findings.measure: about 80% with the described MTLE-like seizure pattern; earlier awareness loss and greater monthly frequency than MTLE
findings.phase: ictal focal aware to impaired awareness
findings.population: patients with TPE in the cited cohort; cohort denominator not reported
findings.uncertainty: Source reports “about 80%” and qualitative frequency/timing differences without uncertainty intervals

findings.citation: Staack et al., 2011; Herlin et al., 2020
findings.claim: Nocturnal hyperkinetic seizures mimicking frontal lobe epilepsy are reported in TPE; the chapter interprets MTLE-like and FLE-like manifestations as potentially reflecting regional propagation toward mesial temporal or frontal structures.
findings.evidence_text: The chapter notes nocturnal hyperkinetic TPE seizures that mimic FLE and explicitly relates the clinical mimicry to possible propagation.
findings.laterality_localization: temporo-polar onset with possible propagation toward mesial temporal or frontal structures
findings.limitations: No frequency or independent onset-zone validation is reported.
findings.locators: PDF p.10, Temporal pole or temporo-polar epilepsy
findings.population: patients with TPE

findings.citation: Toledano et al., 2013; Trebuchon et al., 2018; L€uders et al., 1991; Trebuchon-Da Fonseca et al., 2009
findings.claim: Aphasic focal aware seizures in dominant-hemisphere TPE are not necessarily explained by propagation through perisylvian language areas; the chapter also describes involvement of anterior temporo-basal structures, including a basal temporal language area 2–9 cm from the temporal tip and including the fusiform gyrus.
findings.comparator: anterior temporo-basal mechanism versus perisylvian propagation
findings.evidence_text: The source gives a 2–9 cm basal-temporal distance and preserves an anterior temporo-basal explanation for aphasic seizures.
findings.laterality_localization: dominant hemisphere; anterior temporo-basal/basal temporal language area as an alternative to perisylvian propagation
findings.limitations: The anatomical range is source-reported and does not establish a universal language localization boundary.
findings.locators: PDF p.10, Temporal pole or temporo-polar epilepsy
findings.measure: basal temporal language area located 2–9 cm from the temporal tip
findings.population: patients with dominant-hemisphere TPE or anterior temporo-basal lesions
findings.source_term: aphasic focal aware seizures in TPE and the basal temporal language area
findings.uncertainty: Source says the perisylvian explanation is not necessary, not that it is excluded

findings.claim: In a cited cohort of patients with temporo-polar encephaloceles, 80% of patients with left-hemisphere lesions had aphasic seizures.
findings.comparator: left-hemisphere lesion subgroup; right-sided comparison not reported
findings.evidence_text: The chapter reports aphasic seizures in 80% of the cited left-lesion subgroup.
findings.laterality_localization: left-hemisphere temporo-polar lesion; aphasic seizure association
findings.limitations: The size of the left-lesion subgroup and the corresponding right-sided rate are not reported.
findings.locators: PDF p.10, Temporal pole or temporo-polar epilepsy
findings.measure: 80% of patients with left-hemisphere lesions had aphasic seizures
findings.population: patients with temporo-polar encephaloceles and left-hemisphere lesions in the cited cohort
findings.source_term: aphasic seizures with left temporo-polar encephaloceles
findings.uncertainty: Source gives a percentage without denominator or interval

findings.citation: Ryvlin and Kahane, 2005; Kahane and Bartolomei, 2010
findings.claim: Temporal plus epilepsy describes multilobar epilepsies involving temporal structures and neighboring orbito-frontal cortex, insula, frontal or parietal operculum, or temporo-parieto-occipital junction; simultaneous temporal and extratemporal onset has been identified with intracerebral EEG, but very rapid propagation can produce similar clinical and EEG features.
findings.evidence_text: The source defines temporal plus as a multilobar network and warns that rapid propagation may mimic simultaneous extratemporal onset.
findings.laterality_localization: temporal plus neighboring extratemporal structures; simultaneous onset versus rapid propagation remains a qualification
findings.limitations: Clinical TLE signs alone do not ensure a temporal SOZ.
findings.locators: PDF p.10, Temporal “plus” epilepsy
findings.population: patients with suspected temporal plus epileptogenic networks

findings.claim: Compared with exclusive TLE, temporal plus epilepsy was more associated with gustatory hallucinations, auditory illusions or vertigo, focal impaired awareness seizures with contralateral head rotation or ipsilateral tonic motor signs, and postictal dysphoria; exclusive TLE was more associated with epigastric sensations, gestural automatisms, and postictal amnesia.
findings.evidence_text: The chapter lists the cited temporal-plus features and contrasts them with epigastric sensations, gestural automatisms, and postictal amnesia in TLE.
findings.laterality_localization: contralateral head rotation and ipsilateral tonic signs in the temporal-plus group; network-level temporal plus versus exclusive TLE
findings.limitations: The source does not establish that any listed feature independently identifies temporal plus onset.
findings.locators: PDF p.10, Temporal “plus” epilepsy
findings.population: patients with exclusive TLE or temporal plus epilepsy in the cited comparison
findings.source_term: clinical features differentiating exclusive TLE from temporal plus epilepsy

findings.citation: Fernández Torre et al., 1999; Gavaret et al., 2004; Tao et al., 2005; Lagarde and Bartolomei, 2019; Merlet et al., 1998; Ebersole, 2000; Krendl et al., 2008
findings.claim: Scalp EEG detects only a minor proportion of epileptic abnormalities generated in mesial or deep temporal structures; locally generated deep mesial IEDs may be invisible on scalp, so scalp IEDs in MTLE often reflect spread through limbic, temporo-basal, or lateral cortical circuits.
findings.comparator: deep mesial IEDs versus scalp-visible propagated IEDs
findings.evidence_text: The chapter states that deep mesial IEDs may not appear on scalp EEG and that scalp IEDs can represent propagated activity.
findings.laterality_localization: deep mesial temporal generation with scalp expression after spread through wider circuits
findings.limitations: Scalp absence cannot be interpreted as absence of deep epileptic activity.
findings.locators: PDF p.11, Localization value of interictal epileptiform discharges
findings.measure: minor proportion detected; no numerical proportion reported
findings.population: patients with MTLE or deep temporal seizure generators
findings.source_term: scalp interictal epileptiform discharges from deep mesial temporal structures
findings.uncertainty: Source states a limitation of scalp detection and does not quantify the undetected fraction

findings.citation: Williamson et al., 1993; Tatum, 2012; Barba et al., 2007; Ebersole, 1991
findings.claim: In MTLE, more than 90% of patients in the cited description had spikes or sharp waves restricted to the anterior temporal lobe; mid-temporal IEDs can indicate wider propagation, an extra-mesial generator, or LTLE, while frequent posterior or extratemporal IEDs decrease the likelihood of MTLE. Source modeling distinguishes a mesial temporal vertical dipolar field from a broader horizontal or radial frontotemporal neocortical field.
findings.comparator: anterior temporal versus mid-temporal/posterior/extratemporal IED distribution; mesial versus neocortical source model
findings.evidence_text: The source reports an anterior-temporal IED pattern in more than 90% of the cited MTLE patients and gives alternative interpretations for broader distributions.
findings.laterality_localization: anterior temporal restriction supports MTLE; mid-temporal, posterior, or extratemporal distribution weakens or broadens the mesial interpretation; modeled source may be mesial versus temporal/frontal neocortex
findings.limitations: The percentage is not accompanied by a cohort denominator or confidence interval.
findings.locators: PDF p.11, Localization value of interictal epileptiform discharges
findings.measure: more than 90% with anterior-temporal spikes or sharp waves in the cited description
findings.population: patients with MTLE, including MTLE with hippocampal sclerosis
findings.source_term: MTLE scalp IED pattern and source modeling
findings.uncertainty: Source qualifies mid-temporal activity as potentially propagated or extra-mesial and does not provide a denominator for the percentage

findings.citation: Pf€ander et al., 2002; Barba et al., 2007; Lagarde and Bartolomei, 2019
findings.claim: About one-third of LTLE patients show IEDs over anterior temporal electrodes, while most have lateral-temporal predominance; contralateral IEDs are less frequent in LTLE than MTLE (10%–20%), maximal anterior temporal or anterior temporo-basal amplitude can suggest temporopolar epilepsy, and temporal plus epilepsy more often has precentral IEDs.
findings.comparator: LTLE versus MTLE; LTLE versus temporopolar or temporal plus patterns
findings.evidence_text: The chapter contrasts LTLE’s lateral-temporal IED predominance with temporopolar anterior temporo-basal amplitude and temporal-plus precentral activity.
findings.laterality_localization: lateral temporal predominance in LTLE; contralateral IEDs in a minority of LTLE; anterior temporo-basal amplitude suggests temporopolar; precentral IEDs suggest temporal plus

findings.source_term: LTLE, temporopolar, and temporal-plus interictal EEG distributions
findings.uncertainty: Source gives approximate percentages and uses “can be suggestive” for temporopolar localization

findings.citation: Palmini et al., 1995; Epitashvili et al., 2018; Labate et al., 2004
findings.claim: Focal rhythmic or periodic low-voltage spiking on a slow background is described as highly suggestive of cortical dysplasia, whereas temporal-lobe DNETs often show IEDs discordant with the tumor’s anatomical localization.
findings.evidence_text: The source pairs a dysplasia-associated rhythmic/periodic pattern with DNET IED-anatomical discordance.
findings.laterality_localization: lesion-associated pattern may be discordant with anatomical lesion; no specific side relation stated
findings.limitations: The finding is lesion-contextual and does not provide a general temporal-lobe localization rule.
findings.locators: PDF p.12, Localization value of interictal epileptiform discharges
findings.population: patients with cortical dysplasia or temporal-lobe DNET

findings.citation: Kanner et al., 1993; Janszky et al., 2005b; Rosati et al., 2003
findings.claim: IEDs predominantly localized to the surgical side often predict good outcome, and anterotemporal IEDs accurately predicted seizure onset in the ipsilateral temporal lobe in the cited TLE description; high spike rates were associated with longer epilepsy duration, while low spike rates were proposed to correlate with less severe epilepsy.
findings.comparator: predominant surgical-side versus other IED localization; high versus low spike rate
findings.evidence_text: The chapter links surgical-side/anterior-temporal IED predominance to outcome or ipsilateral onset and qualifies spike-rate associations.
findings.laterality_localization: anterotemporal IEDs ipsilateral to seizure onset or surgical side
findings.limitations: Prognostic associations are not equivalent to an independent causal or diagnostic effect.
findings.locators: PDF p.12, Lateralizing and prognostic value of IEDs on TLE
findings.phase: interictal; prognostic relation to postsurgical outcome
findings.population: patients with TLE undergoing or considered for temporal surgery
findings.source_term: anterotemporal IED lateralization and spike-rate prognostic associations
findings.uncertainty: Source uses “often” and “proposed to correlate”; no pooled effect estimate is given

findings.citation: Halford et al., 2013; Cascino et al., 1996; Steinhoff et al., 1995; So et al., 1989; Janszky et al., 2005b; Chung et al., 1991; Holmes et al., 1996; Janszky, 2005a; Krendl et al., 2008; Lim et al., 1991
findings.claim: Bilateral temporal IEDs occur in 20%–40% of TLE descriptions and become more likely with longer EEG monitoring; although they increase the likelihood of independent bilateral seizure origin, intracranial EEG found unilateral seizure origin in the vast majority of such patients, and unilateral IED predominance was more prognostically informative than bilateral abnormality alone.
findings.comparator: bilateral versus unilateral IED predominance; bilateral IEDs versus unilateral seizure onset
findings.evidence_text: The chapter separates bilateral IED occurrence from bilateral seizure onset and emphasizes unilateral predominance and monitoring duration.
findings.laterality_localization: bilateral temporal IEDs do not establish bilateral seizure onset; unilateral predominance may retain prognostic value
findings.limitations: Percentages and “vast majority” are source-reported without a common denominator.
findings.locators: PDF p.12, Lateralizing and prognostic value of IEDs on TLE

findings.phase: interictal with relation to ictal onset and postsurgical outcome
findings.population: patients with TLE, including patients with independent bitemporal abnormalities
findings.uncertainty: Source states that etiology’s role in unilateral versus bilateral IEDs is unclear

findings.citation: Reiher et al., 1989; Blume et al., 1993; Geyer et al., 1999; Di Gennaro et al., 2003; Palmini et al., 1995; Bogdanoff et al., 1975; Gilmore and Brenner, 1981; Koutroumanidis et al., 2004
findings.claim: TIRDA consists of short trains of intermittent rhythmic 1–4 Hz activity, predominantly over anterior temporal regions; it correlates strongly with TLE and significantly with MTLE, identifies the side of MTLE with high sensitivity and specificity, and can occur without a significant structural abnormality.
findings.comparator: TIRDA versus temporal polymorphic delta or theta activity; MTLE versus other TLE
findings.evidence_text: The source defines TIRDA by frequency, duration, and anterior-temporal distribution and states that it can lateralize MTLE even without a significant lesion.
findings.laterality_localization: anterior temporal distribution and side identification in MTLE
findings.limitations: The chapter does not provide the cited sensitivity, specificity, or a single reference standard.

findings.citation: Steinhoff et al., 1995; Ebersole and Pacia, 1996; Sakai et al., 2002; Sirin et al., 2013; Malter et al., 2016; Jin and Nakasato, 2016; Foldvary et al., 2001; Pacia and Ebersole, 1997; Assaf and Ebersole, 1999
findings.claim: Ictal scalp EEG in TLE may show temporal rhythmic delta or theta-alpha activity, ipsilateral or diffuse background attenuation, focal temporal spikes or sharp waves, or less commonly rapid focal discharges; patterns from seizures initially restricted to mesial structures may be minimal, and scalp patterns are not sufficient by themselves to identify the EZ anatomically. Regular 5–9 Hz inferior-temporal rhythm is associated with temporo-mesial onset, irregular polymorphic 2–5 Hz rhythm with lateral onset, basal or polar onset with vertex activity, and temporal plus with wider frontal, temporoparietal, or central distribution.
findings.comparator: mesial versus lateral versus basal/polar versus temporal-plus ictal scalp patterns
findings.evidence_text: The chapter lists common scalp ictal patterns, the mesial/lateral frequency associations, vertex activity for basal or polar onset, and the temporal-plus wider distribution.
findings.laterality_localization: temporo-mesial, lateral, basal/polar, or temporal-plus associations as qualified by scalp distribution
findings.limitations: Scalp EEG pattern is a qualified aid and cannot by itself establish the anatomical EZ in TLE.
findings.locators: PDF p.13, Ictal scalp EEG in TLE
findings.measure: 5–9 Hz regular inferior-temporal rhythm; 2–5 Hz irregular polymorphic rhythm; other patterns qualitative
findings.population: patients with TLE undergoing ictal scalp EEG
findings.source_term: ictal scalp EEG patterns in TLE
findings.uncertainty: Source explicitly states that scalp pattern and frequency vary within the same patient and are insufficient alone for anatomical localization

findings.citation: Lee et al., 2000a; Sirin et al., 2013; Saggio et al., 2020; Monnerat et al., 2013; Malter et al., 2016; Mintzer et al., 2004; Lieb et al., 1976; Risinger et al., 1989; Napolitano and Orriols, 2010
findings.claim: Early bilateralization at seizure onset, switch of lateralization, intradischarge asynchrony, or clearly independent bilateral seizures indicate bitemporal epileptic foci and are associated with worse prognosis, whereas delayed contralateral temporal propagation is common and is not associated with poor prognosis; severe unilateral HS can even produce an ictal scalp discharge localized to the opposite temporal lobe despite excellent surgical outcomes, and about 13% of ictal scalp patterns are hemispheric or nonlocalizing.
findings.comparator: early bilateralization or independent seizures versus delayed contralateral propagation; typical versus opposite-temporal scalp localization in unilateral HS
findings.evidence_text: The chapter distinguishes early bilateral or independent activity from delayed contralateral spread and gives the 13% hemispheric/nonlocalizing estimate.
findings.laterality_localization: early bilateral/independent activity suggests bitemporal foci; delayed contralateral activity may be propagation; opposite-temporal scalp localization can occur with unilateral HS
findings.limitations: Contralateral scalp expression is not treated as proof of contralateral SOZ.
findings.locators: PDF p.13, Bitemporal ictal activity; PDF p.14, Ictal scalp EEG in TLE
findings.measure: about 13% hemispheric or nonlocalizing ictal scalp patterns
findings.phase: ictal onset, propagation, and postsurgical prognosis
findings.population: patients with TLE, MTLE-HS, or temporal surgery evaluations
findings.source_term: bitemporal ictal activity and delayed contralateral propagation
findings.uncertainty: Source distinguishes prognostic implications by timing and synchrony and reports no common denominator for the 13%

findings.citation: Diehl and L€uders, 2000; Chassoux et al., 2018; Chauvel et al., 2019; Lhatoo et al., 2016; Zijlmans et al., 2019
findings.claim: When MTLE has concordant typical semiology, EEG, and an MTL MRI lesion, noninvasive investigations may be sufficient for surgical proposal; discordant information or independent bitemporal seizures raises the need for invasive evaluation, which is used to distinguish TLE subtypes, identify possible extratemporal origin, and characterize seizure propagation through networks.
findings.evidence_text: The source frames iEEG as targeted clarification of subtype, extratemporal origin, and propagation when clinical, EEG, and MRI information is not concordant.
findings.laterality_localization: noninvasive concordance supports an MTL hypothesis; invasive EEG samples mesial, lateral, temporopolar, basal, insular, and possible extratemporal regions according to the localization hypothesis
findings.limitations: This is source guidance, not a randomized comparison of evaluation strategies.
findings.locators: PDF p.14, Invasive EEG in TLE
findings.phase: presurgical evaluation; ictal onset and propagation
findings.population: patients with drug-resistant TLE undergoing presurgical evaluation
findings.source_term: invasive EEG in TLE and SEEG implantation strategy

findings.claim: SEEG detected 25% more discharges than scalp EEG and showed broader IED distribution; synchronous activity between distant interconnected structures, multifocal independent spikes, and preferential hippocampal spread to ipsilateral entorhinal cortex, amygdala, and posterior cingulate can reveal network connectivity and propagation.
findings.comparator: SEEG versus scalp EEG; synchronous versus independent/multifocal interictal activity
findings.evidence_text: The chapter reports more SEEG-detected discharges and uses synchronous, multifocal, and hippocampal-to-network spread to interpret connectivity.
findings.laterality_localization: hippocampal activity spreads preferentially to ipsilateral entorhinal cortex and amygdala and to posterior cingulate; distant synchrony indicates network involvement
findings.limitations: Network spread does not by itself identify the seizure-onset zone.
findings.locators: PDF p.15, Interictal SEEG activity in TLE
findings.measure: 25% more discharges detected by SEEG than scalp EEG
findings.population: patients with TLE undergoing SEEG
findings.uncertainty: Source gives a percentage without denominator and describes propagation as a functional-connectivity parameter

findings.citation: Zijlmans et al., 2017; Bragin et al., 1999a, b; Jacobs et al., 2012; Engel et al., 2009; Axmacher et al., 2008; Melani et al., 2013; Staba et al., 2004; Staba et al., 2007; Lamarche et al., 2016
findings.claim: HFOs are spontaneous activity from 80–600 Hz persisting for at least four oscillations and are divided into ripples at 80–250 Hz and fast ripples at 250–600 Hz; they may mark tissue capable of generating seizures, but physiological HFOs also occur in hippocampal and neocortical regions. In TLE, hippocampal atrophy is associated with lower ripple rates, a higher fast-ripple/ripple ratio is reported with hippocampal sclerosis, and ictal HFOs correlate with temporal FDG-PET hypometabolism.
findings.comparator: pathological versus physiological HFOs; ripple versus fast-ripple activity; atrophic versus nonatrophic hippocampal regions
findings.evidence_text: The source defines HFO frequency bands and duration, preserves the physiological-HFO caveat, and summarizes TLE pathology and PET correlations.
findings.laterality_localization: HFO-generating tissue may relate to SOZ; physiological HFOs occur in hippocampal and neocortical regions, limiting simple interpretation
findings.limitations: The chapter does not establish that every HFO is pathological or that HFO removal alone proves SOZ identity.
findings.locators: PDF p.15, High-frequency oscillations in TLE; PDF p.16, High-frequency oscillations in TLE; PDF p.17, High-frequency oscillations in TLE
findings.measure: 80–600 Hz overall; ripples 80–250 Hz; fast ripples 250–600 Hz; at least four oscillations
findings.population: patients with focal epilepsy and TLE studied with iEEG or SEEG
findings.source_term: high-frequency oscillations (HFOs), ripples, and fast ripples
findings.uncertainty: Source explicitly warns that HFOs can reflect normal function and that pathology-related associations are not universal

findings.citation: Jacobs et al., 2008; Jacobs et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013
findings.claim: HFOs were suggested to be more specific than spikes for SOZ identification; in a cited study, sensitivity for SOZ identification was 52% for fast ripples, 38% for ripples, and 33% for spikes alone, and ripple co-occurrence with spikes tracked the SOZ more closely than ripples without spikes in neocortical epilepsy.
findings.comparator: fast ripples versus ripples versus spikes alone; ripples with versus without spikes
findings.evidence_text: The chapter gives the cited 52%, 38%, and 33% sensitivities and favors ripple-spike co-occurrence over isolated ripples in neocortical epilepsy.
findings.laterality_localization: HFO or HFO-plus-spike activity relative to SOZ
findings.limitations: The cited performance values are not a chapter-level pooled estimate and specificity values are not reported.
findings.locators: PDF p.16, High-frequency oscillations in TLE
findings.measure: SOZ-identification sensitivity 52% fast ripples, 38% ripples, 33% spikes alone
findings.population: patients with focal epilepsy in cited HFO/SOZ studies, including neocortical epilepsy for the co-occurrence comparison
findings.source_term: HFO specificity and sensitivity for SOZ identification
findings.uncertainty: Percentages are source-reported sensitivities without denominators or intervals; specificity is described qualitatively

findings.citation: Maillard et al., 2004; Kahane and Bartolomei, 2010; Perucca et al., 2014; Alarcon et al., 1995; Bragin et al., 2007; de Curtis and Gnatkovsky, 2009; Gnatkovsky et al., 2011; Ryvlin et al., 2002; Chabardès et al., 2005
findings.claim: On SEEG, hippocampal seizures are often associated with HYP, whereas extrahippocampal temporal or other neocortical seizures often appear as LVFD in the beta-gamma range, with or without slow depolarization; LVFD corresponds to ictal flattening on scalp EEG and its removal-associated outcome has been used to support localizing value.
findings.evidence_text: The source contrasts hippocampal HYP with extrahippocampal/neocortical LVFD and links LVFD to scalp ictal flattening and localizing outcome evidence.
findings.laterality_localization: HYP associated with hippocampal onset; LVFD associated with extrahippocampal temporal or neocortical onset; LVFD may begin in mesial and lateral structures nearly simultaneously in mesio-lateral epilepsy
findings.limitations: The patterns are not presented as infallible or independent of propagation and pathology.
findings.locators: PDF p.17, Ictal SEEG in TLE
findings.measure: beta-gamma range for LVFD; no numeric frequency supplied for HYP
findings.population: patients with TLE undergoing SEEG
findings.source_term: hypersynchronous low-frequency periodic high-amplitude spikes (HYP) and low-voltage fast discharge (LVFD)
findings.uncertainty: Source says these patterns presumably reflect different neuronal mechanisms and notes temporopolar scalp indistinguishability from MTLE-HS

findings.claim: In cited LTLE reports, patients with an SOZ limited to temporo-lateral cortices had an initial tonic discharge localized in neocortex with no propagation to medial structures in 66% of cases, and NTLE seizures were usually shorter than MTLE or mesio-lateral temporal seizures.
findings.comparator: temporo-lateral versus medial propagation; NTLE versus MTLE or MLTLE duration
findings.evidence_text: The chapter reports 66% without medial propagation for a temporo-lateral SOZ and shorter NTLE seizures relative to MTLE or MLTLE.
findings.laterality_localization: temporo-lateral neocortical SOZ without medial propagation in the cited subset
findings.limitations: The cited report population is restricted to selected SEEG cases and is not a general LTLE estimate.
findings.locators: PDF p.17, Ictal SEEG in TLE
findings.measure: no medial propagation in 66% of cases; shorter duration than MTLE or MLTLE
findings.population: patients with LTLE/NTLE and neocortical lesions or normal MRI in cited SEEG reports
findings.source_term: temporo-lateral SEEG onset without medial propagation
findings.uncertainty: Source gives a percentage without denominator and uses “usually” for duration

findings.claim: A focal delta-brush pattern at seizure onset with 1–2 Hz rhythmic delta and superimposed brief 20–30 Hz bursts was identified exclusively in cortical dysplasia, while burst suppression with 1.5-s polyspike bursts alternating with 0.5-s attenuation was found only in tuberous sclerosis complex; other ictal SEEG patterns were also seen in spread regions and did not specifically identify onset or correlate with specific anatomical lesions.
findings.comparator: cortical dysplasia versus tuberous sclerosis complex versus other pathologies; onset versus spread region
findings.evidence_text: The source gives pathology-linked delta-brush and burst-suppression patterns but explicitly limits other patterns because they also occur in spread regions.
findings.laterality_localization: pathology-associated patterns may distinguish cortical dysplasia or tuberous sclerosis but other patterns are not specific to SOZ
findings.limitations: The pattern associations are pathology-dependent and cannot be generalized to all temporal seizures.
findings.locators: PDF p.17, Ictal SEEG in TLE; PDF p.18, Ictal SEEG in TLE
findings.measure: delta brush 1–2 Hz with 20–30 Hz bursts; burst suppression 1.5 s bursts alternating with 0.5 s attenuation
findings.population: patients with TLE or focal epilepsy studied with ictal SEEG and differing pathologies
findings.uncertainty: Source states that other patterns do not specifically identify onset or correlate with specific lesions

findings.citation: Gok et al., 2013; Vinton et al., 2007
findings.claim: Interictal FDG-PET hypometabolism indicates dysfunctional cortex that may relate to the EZ, but the hypometabolic area usually extends beyond the SOZ; a cited study reported correct seizure-focus lateralization in 95% of patients with MRI lesions, 69% with equivocal MRI, and 84% with unremarkable MRI.
findings.comparator: MRI-lesional versus MRI-equivocal versus MRI-unremarkable TLE
findings.evidence_text: The chapter combines the three MRI-stratified lateralization percentages with the warning that PET hypometabolism usually exceeds the SOZ.
findings.laterality_localization: temporal hypometabolism may relate to EZ but can extend beyond SOZ; lateralization of seizure focus across MRI strata
findings.limitations: Lateralization performance and anatomical localization are distinct; the chapter does not pool or recalibrate the cited values.
findings.locators: PDF p.18, Interictal PET in TLE; PDF p.19, Interictal PET in TLE
findings.phase: interictal imaging interpreted for ictal focus
findings.population: patients with TLE stratified by MRI lesion status in the cited FDG-PET study
findings.source_term: interictal FDG-PET localizing and lateralizing value
findings.uncertainty: Percentages lack denominators and intervals; source separately limits localizing value because of extension beyond SOZ

findings.citation: Chassoux et al., 2017; Delbeke et al., 1996; Farooque et al., 2017; LoPinto-Khoury et al., 2012; Wong et al., 2010; Theodore et al., 1997; Koutroumanidis et al., 2000; Leiva-Salinas et al., 2017
findings.claim: In MTLE-HS, more restricted or strong focal anterior mesial temporal hypometabolism was associated with better surgical outcomes, while hypometabolism sparing the hippocampus, extending laterally or extratemporally, involving both hemispheres, or reflecting propagated activity was associated with less favorable or less specific localization; unilateral temporal hypometabolism with normal MRI could still have excellent outcomes after anterior temporal lobectomy.
findings.evidence_text: The source contrasts restricted anterior mesial hypometabolism with wider or bilateral patterns and preserves propagation as an alternative explanation.
findings.laterality_localization: ipsilateral anterior mesial temporal hypometabolism favorable; lateral, extratemporal, bilateral, or propagation-related extension weakens localization or prognosis
findings.limitations: Outcome associations are not evidence that PET alone identifies the SOZ.
findings.locators: PDF p.19, Interictal PET in TLE
findings.phase: interictal imaging with postsurgical outcome relation
findings.population: patients with MTLE-HS or MRI-negative/equivocal TLE undergoing presurgical evaluation
findings.source_term: spatial extent of temporal FDG-PET hypometabolism and outcome

findings.citation: Ramchuankiat et al., 2017; Rowe et al., 1991; Newton et al., 1992; Kaiboriboon et al., 2005; Blumenfeld et al., 2004
findings.claim: Ictal SPECT requires prompt injection during video-EEG; an injection latency below 35 s was reported as sufficient to avoid findings related to propagation. Focal impaired awareness seizures beginning in the temporal lobe show initial hyperperfusion of anterior temporal cortex with homolateral insula and basal ganglia; mesial temporal structures may remain hyperperfused up to 2 min postictally, whereas lateral temporal structures show hypoperfusion.
findings.comparator: mesial versus lateral temporal perfusion; prompt versus delayed injection
findings.evidence_text: The chapter gives the 35-s injection qualification and contrasts early anterior temporal/insular/basal-ganglia hyperperfusion with mesial-versus-lateral temporal patterns.
findings.laterality_localization: anterior temporal, homolateral insula, and basal ganglia hyperperfusion; mesial temporal postictal hyperperfusion versus lateral temporal hypoperfusion
findings.limitations: Perfusion maps include propagation and timing effects; the chapter does not treat them as a direct SOZ map in every seizure.
findings.locators: PDF p.20, Ictal SPECT in TLE
findings.measure: injection latency below 35 s; mesial hyperperfusion up to 2 min postictally
findings.phase: ictal onset and up to 2 min postictal
findings.population: patients with temporal-lobe focal impaired awareness seizures undergoing ictal SPECT
findings.source_term: ictal SPECT perfusion patterns in TLE
findings.uncertainty: Source says latency below 35 s was sufficient in a cited study and notes that perfusion reflects early network activity

findings.citation: Shin et al., 2002; Van Paesschen et al., 2003; Tousseyn et al., 2017; Velasco et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2000b
findings.claim: Ictal contralateral dystonic posturing is associated with hyperperfused basal ganglia in the hemisphere contralateral to the posturing, whereas ictal SPECT has lower sensitivity for temporal focal aware seizures; SPECT can show early propagation through network connectivity but is not routinely used for MTLE-HS when video-EEG and structural MRI already provide the needed localizing information and is mainly helpful for restricting areas for SEEG in MRI-normal cases.
findings.comparator: focal impaired awareness versus focal aware seizures; MTLE-HS with concordant MRI/EEG versus MRI-normal or nonlateralized cases
findings.evidence_text: The chapter links contralateral dystonia to basal-ganglia hyperperfusion, limits focal-aware sensitivity, and reserves SPECT mainly for selected nonlateralized or MRI-normal cases.
findings.laterality_localization: basal-ganglia hyperperfusion contralateral to dystonic posturing; remote hyperperfused regions may reflect connected network rather than SOZ
findings.limitations: No chapter-level sensitivity, specificity, or universal decision threshold is reported.
findings.locators: PDF p.20, Ictal SPECT in TLE; PDF p.21, Ictal SPECT in TLE
findings.measure: lower sensitivity for focal onset aware seizures; no numeric sensitivity reported
findings.phase: ictal and early propagation; presurgical decision-making
findings.population: patients with TLE undergoing ictal SPECT and presurgical evaluation
findings.source_term: ictal SPECT, dystonic posturing, focal aware seizures, and network propagation
findings.uncertainty: Source describes SPECT as supplementary and timing/network dependent, not as a universal localizer

sources.source_report_limitations: This chapter is a broad narrative review with heterogeneous cited populations, evidence roles, and reference standards. It does not provide a single systematic search, unified cohort, pooled denominator, or pooled diagnostic estimate. Many percentages are reported without numerators, denominators, confidence intervals, or the exact study population in the chapter. Several localization statements are explicitly qualified by propagation, network connectivity, pathology, timing, or uncertainty between early regional involvement and true seizure onset. Pages 21–30 are bibliography and were inspected for complete page coverage but do not add separate source-native semiology or localization claims beyond the cited attributions already retained above. No PDF page, figure, or table was blocked; figure-bearing pages were visually checked for layout-dependent MRI, EEG, PET, and SPECT content.
sources.source_report_methods_population: This source is a narrative review chapter and does not state a unified search strategy, eligibility set, enrollment cohort, or pooled analysis population. It draws on heterogeneous cited patient cohorts, seizure/event observations, imaging and EEG studies, and case reports, with emphasis on drug-resistant and presurgical temporal lobe epilepsy. Denominators, reference standards, and analysis units therefore remain study-specific; no chapter-level aggregate estimate is established.
sources.source_report_summary: Chapter 27, “Semiology, EEG, and neuroimaging findings in temporal lobe epilepsies,” by Valerio Frazzini, Louis Cousyn, and Vincent Navarro, is a narrative educational/review chapter in the 2022 Handbook of Clinical Neurology volume The Temporal Lobe. It synthesizes clinical semiology, scalp and intracranial EEG, and interictal/ictal metabolic imaging relevant to temporal seizure-onset localization and lateralization. It is not a single primary cohort or a pooled quantitative analysis; claims attributed to individual cited studies are retained as cited-study restatements.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a selected surgical cohort of patients with intractable temporal-lobe epilepsy who underwent temporal lobectomy; patients with bihemispheric speech representation were excluded. Seizures were limited to good-quality video recordings, up to four per patient, and speech testing was constrained by consciousness and seizure duration. Several findings are based on small subgroups, and the source notes limited ability to perform thorough ictal aphasia testing for isolated paraphasia. Dominant/nondominant origin and speech dominance are retained as the source’s viewpoints; no left/right equivalence is inferred. Cited-study restatements are reported as such and were not verified against the cited originals.
sources.source_report_methods_population: Thirty-five patients aged 12-39 years (mean 24.6) were selected from an epilepsy-surgery population; all had intractable temporal-lobe epilepsy and subsequently underwent temporal lobectomy. The investigators reviewed up to four good-quality videotaped seizures per patient until 100 seizures were reached; 94 were spontaneous, 3 hyperventilation-induced, and 3 Metrazol-activated. The cohort comprised 80 complex partial seizures and 20 complex partial seizures with secondary generalization; 48 seizures arose from the dominant temporal lobe in 16 patients and 52 from the nondominant temporal lobe in 19 patients. Simultaneous scalp and chronically implanted subdural EEG-video monitoring was used, speech dominance was determined by intracarotid amobarbital testing, and patients with bihemispheric speech representation were excluded. One author reviewed the videotapes without knowledge of EEG localization or eventual surgical management.
sources.source_report_summary: Gabr M, Lüders H, Dinner D, Morris H, and Wyllie E, “Speech manifestations in lateralization of temporal lobe seizures,” Annals of Neurology 1989;25:82-87. This primary empirical study evaluates the incidence, ictal/postictal timing, and dominant-versus-nondominant temporal-lobe lateralizing value of speech manifestations in 100 seizures from 35 patients with intractable temporal-lobe epilepsy.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a retrospective, single-center surgical series of drug-resistant SHE and therefore has referral and surgical-selection constraints; the source specifically notes that the high FCD type II proportion reflects surgical bias and that applicability to drug-sensitive SHE and autosomal dominant NFLE remains uncertain. The semiology analysis excluded 20 patients with unclear or widespread SOZ, and the extrafrontal subgroups were small. SOZ-overlap and incomplete-resection handling are described in Methods, but no independent general-population estimate is established. Most findings have no hemisphere or body-side direction. Figure 3 explicitly displays all SOZs on the left hemisphere for clarity, so that rendering cannot support left-sided lateralization. Table 2 and the narrative differ on autonomic manifestations in the operculoinsular subgroup; the discrepancy is retained in F006 without converting an absent table entry to zero. The article announces online supporting information, but no supporting file is part of this 11-page source package and no claim from it is used. Cited-study restatements in F012, F013, F015, F019, and F020 remain unverified against their cited sources.
sources.source_report_methods_population:
The study retrospectively identified 155 patients with drug-resistant sleep-related epilepsy from 1433 consecutive epilepsy-surgery patients treated from October 1997 through July 2015; sleep-related epilepsy required more than 90% of seizures during sleep. After exclusion of 20 patients with nocturnal temporal lobe epilepsy who did not meet confirmed SHE criteria, 135 patients comprised the SHE series. SOZ location was assigned from presurgical anatomo-electroclinical data, including stereo-EEG when performed, postoperative MRI, and postoperative Engel outcome. Six patients with overlapping frontal and extrafrontal SOZs were assigned to the principal SOZ location; seven patients with incomplete resection but confidently localized SOZs were retained using stereo-EEG; 20 patients with unclear or widespread SOZs were excluded from the semiology analysis. The semiology analysis therefore included 115 patients: 74 frontal and 41 extrafrontal, comprising 14 temporal, 18 operculoinsular, and 9 posterior cases.

Clinical descriptions came from patients and family members, and the earliest nonmotor manifestation was selected when more than one was reported. All patients had at least one typical sleep-related event captured during video-EEG and stereo-EEG monitoring when performed. Five epileptologists reviewed captured events; two independently categorized the four video-documented semiology patterns, and four reviewed discordant assignments. One semiology pattern was assigned per patient because seizures were considered stereotyped, with early motor semiology weighted more heavily than late semiology. Seventeen patients (15%) required consensus review for discordant categorization. Postictal confusion was assessed from the clinical assessment during ictal recordings. Welch-corrected unpaired t tests, two-tailed Fisher exact tests, and kappa statistics were used; significance was retained at P < 0.05.

Context reported by the source: mean seizure-onset age was 5.8 +/- 4.4 years, mean disease duration was 17.9 +/- 10.3 years, 64% had at least one seizure per night, and 90% had at least one seizure per week. An MRI-identifiable lesion was present in 88/135 patients (65%); probable focal cortical dysplasia was the most common MRI diagnosis (52%). The most common postoperative histopathologic diagnosis was FCD type II (67%). At least 2 years of postoperative outcome data were available for 127/135 patients (94%); Engel I outcome occurred in 104/127 (82%) and Engel class Ia in 86/127 (68%). Mortality outcomes were NOT_REPORTED.
sources.source_report_summary: Source role: full-length original empirical research report and retrospective single-center case series, published in Epilepsia in 2019. The article reviews 135 surgically treated, drug-resistant patients with video-EEG documented sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy (SHE) and examines whether ictal semiology patterns and early nonmotor manifestations differ by seizure-onset zone (SOZ) and can help localize seizure onset. It compares frontal SHE with temporal, operculoinsular, and posterior SHE.

sources.source_report_limitations: All 16 native pages were reviewed from the fresh per-page text, and the page renderings were checked for the title and definitions, Table 1, Figures 1-26, Tables 2-3, references, and translated summaries; no page was blocked, and no rotation, clipping, table-layout, figure, or missing-text issue changed interpretation. The source describes a predominantly white, middle-class Rochester population and a 50-year record-based cohort in which diagnostic terminology was not constant. Classification was based primarily on historical documentation and the study neurologist's diagnostic impression; EEG was not used to modify seizure-type assignment. The authors note that some sources of medical care in the first 15 years were absent from the project index, that case ascertainment and medical-care use could have changed over time, and that potential underenumeration may affect time-trend interpretation. General methods and definitions are referred to a companion paper, and cited comparison studies were not separately reviewed under this source authorization. The seizure-type incidence distributions, epidemiologic definitions, tables, and age/gender/etiology/time plots were not converted into V30 findings because they do not constitute source-reported semiology-localization or lateralization claims; the document reports no body-side, reference-side, anatomical-localization, or laterality result for a semiologic phenomenon.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The Rochester Project diagnostic record system was screened for residents with records of seizures, convulsions, or epilepsy, including broad rubrics such as syncope and loss of consciousness; a neurologist reviewed potential cases, and residency was verified. Epilepsy incidence used residents at the date of epilepsy diagnosis and recurrent unprovoked seizures, whereas FUS included residents with one or more unprovoked seizures at first medical contact and used age at first seizure; a cluster within one 24-hour interval was treated as one seizure episode. Denominators were projected age- and gender-specific resident populations derived from census data and modified for Rochester epidemiology exclusions; rates were age-adjusted by the direct method to the 1970 total United States population. The study identified 880 individuals with a new diagnosis of epilepsy (418 male and 462 female) and 1,208 individuals with one or more unprovoked seizures who received medical attention while Rochester residents (584 male and 624 female). Seizure type was classified from the history using the 1981 ILAE criteria, based on the predominant type at diagnosis and the study neurologist's review of available histories; interictal EEG was not used to modify classification.
sources.source_report_summary: This is a population-based incidence study of epilepsy and unprovoked seizures among residents of Rochester, Minnesota, during 1935-1984, using the Rochester Project medical-record linkage system. It reports age-, gender-, seizure-type-, etiology-, and time-specific incidence and cumulative incidence, including comparisons between epilepsy and a first medical diagnosis of an unprovoked seizure (FUS). The paper is epidemiologic and does not report a source-specific semiologic sign, a semiology-to-localization relationship, or a lateralizing direction that meets the V30 finding definition.

sources.source_report_limitations: The document is an opinion/review rather than a primary seizure or epilepsy study and contains no ictal, postictal, seizure-frequency, or semiology cohort. Its lesion, aphasia, functional-imaging, direct-stimulation, Wada, split-brain, and unpublished-observation statements are reported at the level supplied by the review; cited sources were not independently consulted. Many claims lack study-level denominators, numerators, effect sizes, or statistical uncertainty. The model’s within-stream organization, task dependence, hemispheric differences, compensatory mechanisms, and PT/Spt parcellation are presented as hypotheses or unresolved questions in parts of the article. No individual table-cell coordinates were promoted to findings, and no inference or normalization was performed.
sources.source_report_methods_population: Narrative opinion/review; no single study cohort, eligibility rule, comparator set, or reference standard is reported for the document as a whole. The review discusses aphasia and lesion evidence, functional MRI, direct cortical stimulation, Wada and split-brain evidence, and normal speech perception, recognition, production, and auditory-motor tasks. Cited-study sample sizes, finding denominators, and effect sizes are generally not reported in this document.
sources.source_report_summary: This 2007 Nature Reviews Neuroscience OPINION by Gregory Hickok and David Poeppel is a narrative review and proposed dual-stream model of cortical speech processing. It synthesizes lesion, neuropsychological, functional-imaging, direct-stimulation, Wada/split-brain, and speech-task evidence to distinguish speech perception, speech recognition, and speech production. Its relevance to the atlas is indirect: it provides speech-related localization and lateralization constraints, but it reports no seizure or epilepsy cohort and no seizure semiology.

sources.source_report_limitations: The document is a narrative review and does not present a unified cohort, prespecified search methods, pooled estimates, or a uniform reference standard. It repeatedly summarizes cited case reports, retrospective cohorts, EMU series, stimulation studies, and functional-imaging studies with heterogeneous definitions and ascertainment. Several percentages lack exact numerators or subgroup denominators; approximate language such as “nearly,” “about,” “most,” and “or fewer” is retained rather than converted. The review explicitly notes that scalp EEG, selective invasive coverage, propagation, and method-dependent sampling can make symptom-related network involvement difficult to distinguish from seizure onset. PDF p.7 is the reference list and publisher note; no additional source-reported semiology, localization, or lateralization claim was extracted from bibliography metadata alone.
sources.source_report_methods_population: Narrative literature review; no original study population or independent patient-level analysis is reported. The review summarizes retrospective cohorts, EMU series, case series, individual cases, electrical-stimulation and functional-neuroimaging studies, and prior reviews. Populations therefore vary by finding and include patients with epilepsy, focal or temporal/occipital epilepsy, EMU admissions, painful somatosensory seizures, abdominal epilepsy, and cited literature case collections. Exact ascertainment, subgroup denominators, and reference standards are retained only where the source reports them.
sources.source_report_summary: Hwang, Goodman, and Stevens present a narrative review of epileptic ictal pain, covering cephalic, somatosensory, and abdominal presentations, their reported frequency and semiology, associated EEG and anatomic localization, pain-network evidence, and selected treatment observations. The document is a review of cited studies and case reports rather than a new patient cohort.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a single case report without a comparator or cohort-level estimate. The source reports 12 recorded seizures but does not provide a population-level diagnostic or localization accuracy measure, formal language-dominance testing, or an independent reference standard. The abstract calls the lesion a low-grade glioma, whereas Results report an IDH-R132H-negative infiltrating III grade glioma; this terminology is preserved without reconciliation. Literature claims are cited restatements or qualitative synthesis, and cited sources were not reviewed under this source-only scope. The authors explicitly state that the available literature is insufficient to establish ictal paraphasia as a strong localizing element and call for further reliable techniques.
