sources.source_report_limitations: The study is observational and did not standardize postictal testing or systematically assess awareness. Only five focal seizures with tonic-clonic evolution were recorded, none in patients with ICA/PICA, so associations with postconvulsive apnea or SUDEP risk cannot be evaluated. No intracranial EEG was recorded, respiratory-muscle EMG was not directly measured, and the MRI groups were small and require replication. The source also contains an awareness-wording ambiguity (“in any seizures, the patient was aware” conflicts with the surrounding no-awareness account) and two unresolved denominator ambiguities: the Table 2 vigilance row displays 22 PICA wake/sleep observations despite 24 PICA seizures, and the awareness paragraph describes 15 actively interrogated plus 8 untested PICA seizures while stating 24 total.
sources.source_report_methods_population: Consecutive patients older than 13 years admitted to the Epilepsy Monitoring Unit at Baggiovara Civil Hospital, Modena Academic Hospital, Italy, from April 2020 through December 2023 were studied with long-term video-EEG and cardiorespiratory polygraphy; 71 met inclusion, 2 were discarded for technical artifact, 5 focal seizures with bilateral tonic-clonic evolution were excluded, and the final analysis comprised 69 patients and 406 focal-onset seizures. MRI analyses included 22 patients with ICA/PICA, 31 patients without seizure-related breathing disorders, and 30 healthy controls; analyses adjusted for age, sex, and intracranial volume and used false-discovery-rate correction.
sources.source_report_summary: Original prospective observational research article evaluating the incidence and features of postictal central apnea (PICA) in focal-onset seizures without secondary bilateral tonic-clonic evolution and comparing subcortical MRI morphometry, with particular attention to the amygdala and seizure-onset localization.

findings.claim: Clinical signs and symptoms of focal-onset seizures can help localize the discharge origin to frontal, temporal, parietal, occipital, or insular regions, and semiology is most useful when combined with EEG and other evidence; no single sign is sufficient in isolation.
findings.evidence_text: The atlas presents semiologic findings as clinically important for seizure type and, in focal seizures, for localization and lateralization, while emphasizing that their localizing value is probabilistic and strengthened by concordant combinations.
findings.laterality_localization: lobar localization with hemispheric lateralization when supported
findings.limitations: Educational synthesis; it does not provide one uniform cohort or a single validated accuracy estimate.
findings.locators: PDF p.42; PDF p.43; PDF p.50; PDF p.52
findings.population: educational synthesis of focal-onset seizures

findings.citation: Fisher et al. ILAE 2017 classification; source Chapter 3.3 refs. 1-2
findings.claim: The source's 2017 classification separates focal-onset seizures beginning in one hemisphere, generalized-onset seizures engaging both hemispheres, focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizures, and unknown-onset seizures; focal seizures are further described by awareness and motor or nonmotor onset.
findings.evidence_text: The expanded classification includes focal aware and impaired-awareness seizures, focal motor and nonmotor manifestations, generalized motor and absence types, focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizures, unknown-onset motor or nonmotor seizures, and unclassified seizures.
findings.laterality_localization: focal one-hemisphere onset versus bilateral generalized onset versus unobserved onset
findings.limitations: This is the book's teaching presentation of classification terminology, not a new classification study.
findings.locators: PDF p.45; PDF p.46; PDF p.47; PDF p.48
findings.population: educational classification framework
findings.source_term: focal, generalized, focal-to-bilateral, and unknown-onset classification

findings.claim: During transition from focal onset to bilateral tonic-clonic activity, versive head turning, contralateral tonic or clonic activity, figure-of-four posturing with contralateral arm extension and ipsilateral arm flexion, asymmetry or asynchrony, and asymmetric termination may support focal lateralization, but each can be altered by propagation and can occur in primary generalized seizures.
findings.evidence_text: The source treats versive head turning and figure-of-four asymmetry as potentially valuable early or transitional signs, while noting that clonic asymmetry, head direction, and termination can change as the discharge spreads.
findings.laterality_localization: motor sign direction relative to the seizure-onset hemisphere
findings.limitations: Direction is time-dependent and may be misleading after rapid bilateral propagation.
findings.locators: PDF p.49; PDF p.57
findings.phase: transition to bilateral tonic-clonic and late ictal
findings.population: focal-to-bilateral and generalized tonic-clonic seizure teaching groups

findings.claim: In a selected group with proven mesial temporal origin, more than 90% of patients reported an aura; auras were more common with right than bitemporal epilepsy, epigastric aura was most common, and viscerosensory or experiential auras strongly supported temporal involvement with a trend toward right temporal association, whereas absent aura was more common with bitemporal epilepsy.
findings.comparator: right temporal versus bitemporal and temporal versus non-temporal aura profiles
findings.evidence_text: The atlas identifies epigastric, viscerosensory, and experiential phenomena as particularly useful temporal clues but does not treat any aura as completely specific.
findings.laterality_localization: mesial temporal and right-versus-bitemporal trends
findings.limitations: Selection, source-study definitions, and denominators for the reported percentage are not provided on the cited page.
findings.locators: PDF p.49
findings.measure: >90% reported aura in the selected proven mesial temporal group; other associations qualitative
findings.population: selected patients with proven mesial temporal origin and broader temporal lobe epilepsy teaching groups
findings.uncertainty: The >90% value is restricted to the selected proven mesial temporal group; the right-sided statements are described as trends.

findings.claim: Multiple sequential auras suggest a nondominant, often temporal, localization; chills or goosebumps are more common with left temporal foci and are usually ipsilateral; olfactory and gustatory auras are uncommon in mesial temporal epilepsy and are associated in the source with mesial temporal tumors; auditory aura suggests lateral temporal involvement, while cephalic, somatosensory, and visual auras more often suggest extratemporal onset.
findings.evidence_text: The source links the sensory quality and sequence of an aura to possible anatomic regions but warns that non-specific cephalic sensations and isolated aura descriptions have limited localizing precision.
findings.laterality_localization: nondominant temporal, left temporal, lateral temporal, and extratemporal directions
findings.limitations: The book does not provide a common denominator or sensitivity/specificity estimate for these subtype associations.
findings.locators: PDF p.49; PDF p.50
findings.population: temporal and extratemporal focal seizure teaching groups
findings.source_term: temporal aura subtype and motor profile

findings.claim: Oroalimentary automatisms suggest temporal involvement but are not specific; spitting, drinking, and preserved responsiveness during automatisms favor right temporal localization; manipulative automatisms alone do not lateralize, whereas nonmanipulative distal or proximal movements tend to be contralateral and may precede contralateral dystonic posturing; dystonic posturing is usually contralateral, early head turning with dystonia tends ipsilateral, late head turning is more often contralateral, and versive head turning is almost always contralateral.
findings.evidence_text: The source separates manipulative from nonmanipulative automatisms and separates early tonic head turning from late versive head turning rather than treating all repetitive limb or head movements as equivalent.
findings.laterality_localization: right temporal, contralateral dystonic or nonmanipulative limb, ipsilateral early head turn, contralateral late or versive turn
findings.limitations: The associations depend on timing, preserved responsiveness, and whether the extremity is dystonic or freely moving.
findings.locators: PDF p.50; PDF p.51
findings.population: temporal lobe epilepsy and extratemporal comparison groups
findings.source_term: temporal automatisms, dystonic posturing, and head turning

findings.claim: Ictal speech arrest is not reliably lateralizing; focal aware speech arrest may represent dominant temporal aphasia, well-formed ictal language strongly suggests a nondominant, usually right, temporal lobe, ictal jargon is associated with dominant temporal involvement, and postictal aphasia strongly supports left dominant temporal localization.
findings.evidence_text: The atlas assigns different interpretive weight to speech arrest, jargon, well-formed language, and postictal aphasia and explicitly cautions against treating them as interchangeable signs.
findings.laterality_localization: dominant left versus nondominant right temporal language networks
findings.limitations: Language dominance and seizure spread can change the apparent direction of a language sign.
findings.locators: PDF p.50; PDF p.51; PDF p.52
findings.population: temporal lobe seizure teaching groups with varied language dominance

findings.citation: Privitera MD, Morris GL, Gilliam F. Postictal language assessment and lateralization of complex partial seizures. Ann Neurol. 1991;30:391-396; source Ref. 18
findings.claim: The source restates a cited postictal language study in which all patients with right temporal seizures read a test sentence correctly within 1 minute of seizure termination, whereas patients with dominant left temporal foci had reading disruption for more than 1 minute; atypical language representation limits the generality of the lateralizing interpretation.
findings.comparator: right temporal versus dominant left temporal seizure groups
findings.evidence_text: The reported timing contrast is presented as a postictal language assessment, not as a general rule for every temporal seizure or every language-dominance pattern.
findings.laterality_localization: right temporal versus dominant left temporal
findings.limitations: The source page does not reproduce the cited study's sample size or full diagnostic criteria.
findings.locators: PDF p.51; PDF p.105; PDF p.442
findings.measure: within 1 minute versus more than 1 minute postictal reading impairment
findings.population: patients with right or dominant left temporal seizures in the cited postictal language study
findings.uncertainty: Source notes that atypical language representation requires reinterpretation of the lateralizing significance.

findings.claim: Frontal auras are less common and less specific than temporal auras; abdominal sensations can arise from orbitofrontal or cingulate regions; forced thinking suggests dorsolateral frontal involvement; preserved-awareness clonic activity is most localizing to primary motor cortex, with lower-extremity signs suggesting mesial frontal and facial signs suggesting inferior frontal involvement; supplementary sensorimotor seizures tend to be brief, clustered, nocturnal, asymmetrical tonic or postural events with proximal predominance, and may include vocalization, startle precipitation, or bilateral symptoms without loss of consciousness.
findings.evidence_text: The source differentiates primary motor, supplementary sensorimotor, and frontal subregional manifestations by timing, body distribution, awareness, and nocturnal clustering.
findings.laterality_localization: primary motor, mesial frontal, inferior frontal, dorsolateral frontal, and supplementary sensorimotor regions
findings.limitations: Frontal seizures may have minimal or absent scalp EEG and can spread rapidly, limiting noninvasive localization.
findings.locators: PDF p.51; PDF p.52; PDF p.53
findings.population: frontal lobe seizure teaching groups
findings.source_term: frontal aura, primary motor, and supplementary motor semiology

findings.claim: Supplementary sensorimotor seizures may produce ictal paralysis or other negative motor symptoms, often with no scalp EEG because of mesial frontal dipole orientation; bizarre hypermotor seizures can arise from cingulate or orbitofrontal regions or appear after extrafrontal spread, with unilateral posturing and axial rotation favoring mesial frontal origin, severe agitation favoring orbitofrontal localization, and a longer electrical-to-hypermotor latency suggesting extrafrontal onset.
findings.evidence_text: The atlas describes ictal paralysis as an uncommon but recognized seizure manifestation and treats body-axis rotation, agitation, and electrical-to-clinical latency as contextual localizing clues.
findings.laterality_localization: mesial frontal, orbitofrontal, cingulate, and extrafrontal onset or spread
findings.limitations: Visual observation and scalp EEG may both be obscured by movement and muscle artifact.
findings.locators: PDF p.52; PDF p.53
findings.population: frontal, extrafrontal, and supplementary motor seizure teaching groups
findings.source_term: supplementary negative motor and frontal hypermotor seizures

findings.claim: A parietal sensory march suggests postcentral primary sensory cortex involvement contralateral to the ictal discharge, while a sensory aura without march may arise from the second sensory area or parietal operculum; focal weakness may represent a parietal inhibitory motor seizure. Occipital seizures are suggested by elementary visual aura or a contralateral visual-field deficit, complex scenes by occipitotemporal involvement, and variable spread to temporal or frontal regions by oroalimentary or asymmetric tonic manifestations.
findings.evidence_text: The source links sensory march and elementary visual phenomena to primary cortical regions but explains that posterior quadrant seizures commonly acquire temporal or frontal semiology as they propagate.
findings.laterality_localization: contralateral postcentral or visual cortex; occipitotemporal, temporal-spread, and frontal-spread routes
findings.limitations: Scalp EEG may be misleading for parietal seizures and variable propagation can obscure occipital onset.
findings.locators: PDF p.54; PDF p.55
findings.population: posterior quadrant focal seizure teaching groups

findings.citation: Isnard et al. stereo-electroencephalographic study; source Ref. 28
findings.claim: Insular epilepsy cannot be directly analyzed with scalp video-EEG because the insula is not adequately sampled; depth electrodes established the described semiology, including laryngeal discomfort or constriction, dyspnea, perioral paresthesias, large bilateral or painful sensory symptoms, autonomic chest or abdominal sensations, dysarthria or dysphonia, muteness, and hypersalivation, with spread producing frontal, temporal, or parietal-like manifestations.
findings.evidence_text: The atlas presents early laryngeal, perioral, autonomic, and painful sensory symptoms as the more characteristic clues and treats later motor or temporal-like signs as propagation-dependent.
findings.laterality_localization: insular onset with frontal, temporal, or parietal spread
findings.limitations: The source emphasizes that noninvasive scalp recordings are inadequate for direct insular sampling.
findings.locators: PDF p.55
findings.population: insular seizure teaching groups evaluated with depth electrodes

findings.analysis_unit: individual absence seizure and EEG discharge
findings.claim: Typical generalized absence seizures are abrupt, usually lack an aura, commonly last less than 15 seconds, terminate abruptly without a postictal state, and are associated with generalized 2.5-4 Hz spike-and-wave activity; arrest, simple or perseverative automatisms, blinking, subtle myoclonus, eye or neck movements, atonic slumping, and autonomic signs may occur. Atypical absence is slower than 2.5 Hz with slower onset or recovery and more prominent motor manifestations; myoclonic absence has prominent clonic activity at approximately 2.5-3.5 Hz.
findings.comparator: typical versus atypical versus myoclonic absence
findings.evidence_text: The source combines clinical duration, abruptness, postictal recovery, motor features, and discharge frequency to distinguish absence variants.
findings.laterality_localization: generalized bilateral network; no focal direction assigned from isolated motor asymmetry
findings.limitations: The terms and thresholds are educational descriptions and not a new diagnostic validation cohort.
findings.locators: PDF p.55; PDF p.56; PDF p.299; PDF p.300
findings.measure: typical duration usually <15 seconds; typical frequency 2.5-4 Hz; atypical frequency <2.5 Hz; myoclonic absence 2.5-3.5 Hz
findings.population: typical, atypical, and myoclonic absence seizure teaching groups
findings.uncertainty: Brief discharges may have no obvious clinical correlate; active engagement may reveal subtle clinical change.

findings.claim: Generalized tonic-clonic seizures may evolve from generalized absence or myoclonic seizures; versive head turning may change direction across generalized seizures and alone does not establish focal onset. In an uncaptured tonic-clonic seizure, versive head turning, figure-of-four posture, asymmetrical or asynchronous clonus, and asymmetric termination are more frequent in focal-to-bilateral seizures but can also occur in primary generalized seizures, so none is definitive individually; generalized-onset seizures with focal evolution are described as uncommon.
findings.evidence_text: The atlas separates signs that may suggest focal onset from signs that can occur in generalized epilepsy and emphasizes the importance of observing onset before bilateral artifact and motor spread.
findings.laterality_localization: focal-to-bilateral versus generalized-onset, with direction interpreted relative to onset only when onset is known
findings.limitations: Late bilateral motor activity is an unreliable basis for retrospective onset assignment.
findings.locators: PDF p.56; PDF p.57
findings.population: generalized-onset, focal-to-bilateral, and unknown-onset tonic-clonic teaching groups
findings.source_term: generalized tonic-clonic signs, unknown-onset seizures, and focal evolution

findings.citation: Source Chapter 6.3; Baykan and Wolf, source Ref. 8
findings.claim: In juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, myoclonic seizures may be unilateral or bilateral and generalized tonic-clonic or absence seizures may coexist; EEG usually shows a normal background with generalized 3-6 Hz spike-wave or irregular polyspike activity with frontal predominance, although a minority of patients have focal or markedly lateralized fragments of generalized discharges.
findings.comparator: generalized discharge pattern versus focal or lateralized fragments
findings.evidence_text: The source explicitly warns that unilateral myoclonus or focal-appearing generalized fragments may occur within a generalized electroclinical syndrome.
findings.laterality_localization: generalized network with frontal predominance; focal-appearing fragments are recognized but not automatically assigned a focal onset
findings.limitations: No prevalence denominator for the minority statement is supplied in the source text.
findings.locators: PDF p.301; PDF p.302
findings.measure: qualitative minority statement; 3-6 Hz EEG frequency
findings.population: juvenile myoclonic epilepsy teaching groups
findings.source_term: juvenile myoclonic epilepsy and generalized EEG fragments
findings.uncertainty: Focal or lateralized fragments can complicate interpretation without proving focal epilepsy.

findings.analysis_unit: pediatric syndrome, seizure type, and EEG pattern
findings.claim: Epileptic spasms may have normal waking EEG but multifocal epileptiform activity and electrodecrement emerging in sleep, while Lennox-Gastaut syndrome is associated with multiple seizure types including tonic, atonic, tonic-clonic, and absence-type seizures, slow spike-wave complexes below 2.5 Hz, and tonic seizures with overall voltage attenuation or electrodecrement-like activity.
findings.comparator: waking versus sleep EEG; epileptic spasms versus Lennox-Gastaut electroclinical patterns
findings.evidence_text: The source uses sleep-emergent electrodecrement and syndrome-associated slow spike-wave or voltage attenuation to relate pediatric seizure types to their EEG context.
findings.laterality_localization: multifocal or generalized network; no single focal onset implied by the syndrome description
findings.limitations: These are syndrome-level teaching statements and do not establish an individual patient's onset zone.
findings.locators: PDF p.294; PDF p.296
findings.measure: slow spike-wave frequency <2.5 Hz in Lennox-Gastaut syndrome
findings.population: children with epileptic spasms or Lennox-Gastaut syndrome
findings.source_term: pediatric epileptic spasms and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome
findings.uncertainty: EEG expression is age- and state-dependent and can be absent or less conspicuous while awake.

findings.claim: Rasmussen encephalitis produces focal seizures and hemiparesis from one hemisphere, with affected-hemisphere slowing and localized interictal discharges that may progress to epilepsia partialis continua and electrographic seizures, followed by possible contralateral discharges and spread. Self-limited centrotemporal seizures commonly have nocturnal unilateral face sensory or clonic symptoms with central-to-midtemporal sleep-activated discharges, whereas self-limited occipital epilepsy commonly has emesis or visual/ocular motor symptoms and posterior discharges that may extend anteriorly or appear generalized with age.
findings.evidence_text: The atlas retains clinical and EEG localization information while noting that pediatric electroclinical patterns evolve with age, sleep, and disease progression.
findings.laterality_localization: affected hemisphere in Rasmussen; central-temporal or occipital/posterior regions in self-limited focal syndromes
findings.limitations: Syndrome descriptions are not comparable cohorts and do not provide common diagnostic performance measures.
findings.locators: PDF p.296; PDF p.298; PDF p.301; PDF p.302
findings.population: pediatric Rasmussen and self-limited focal epilepsy teaching groups
findings.source_term: pediatric focal syndromes and Rasmussen encephalitis

findings.claim: Focal aware seizures, supplementary motor seizures, cingulate or orbitofrontal seizures, some temporal seizures, and neonatal or insular seizures may have no visible scalp EEG correlate; the source therefore prioritizes the first clinical change, the earliest EEG attenuation or definite rhythm, video correlation, and intracranial recording when a deep or unfavorable dipole is suspected.
findings.evidence_text: The source repeatedly separates clinical nonappearance of an EEG change from absence of an ictal generator and recommends interpreting the earliest clinical and EEG changes together.
findings.laterality_localization: deep, mesial, insular, or otherwise poorly sampled generators versus scalp-visible onset
findings.limitations: The atlas does not supply one pooled rate for scalp-negative focal seizures across regions or age groups.
findings.locators: PDF p.15; PDF p.107; PDF p.110; PDF p.111; PDF p.221; PDF p.293; PDF p.313
findings.population: focal seizures, neonatal seizures, insular seizures, and presurgical EEG teaching groups
findings.source_term: scalp EEG absence, clinical onset, and deep generators

findings.claim: F7 and F8 physically overlie inferior frontal cortex but most often record anterior temporal activity; the source recommends examining the field, with F8 plus T4 favoring anterior temporal activity and F4 plus F8 favoring inferior frontal activity, while an isolated F8 discharge is not sufficient to decide the source.
findings.evidence_text: The source presents the F7/F8 ambiguity as a field problem rather than a fixed electrode-to-lobe mapping and illustrates confirmation with referential and circumferential montages.
findings.laterality_localization: anterior temporal versus inferior frontal source beneath or around F7/F8
findings.limitations: The examples are montage-dependent and do not provide a universal electrode localization accuracy.
findings.locators: PDF p.69; PDF p.70; PDF p.90
findings.population: scalp EEG recording and localization teaching examples
findings.source_term: F7/F8 electrode ambiguity and field localization

findings.claim: Bipolar polarity reversal can localize a discharge within a chain but fails at the chain ends; average, ear, Laplacian, circumferential, and bipolar montages have different strengths and contamination risks, so focal localization should be checked across a field and with a referential montage rather than inferred from one apparent reversal.
findings.evidence_text: The source's examples show that an apparent reversal can change with reference choice and that the spatial field, not only polarity, is needed to identify the most involved region.
findings.laterality_localization: spatial field center and focal source localization
findings.limitations: These are interpretive principles and examples, not a prospective comparison of montage performance.
findings.locators: PDF p.84; PDF p.86; PDF p.87; PDF p.90
findings.population: clinical EEG interpretation teaching examples
findings.source_term: montage, polarity reversal, and reference effects

findings.citation: Source Chapters 5.4-5.5; source refs. 1-3 in Chapter 5.4
findings.claim: Consistent focal spikes, focal slowing, focal rhythmic delta, and focal attenuation can support a focal epileptogenic or structural process, but surface interictal discharges may differ from the ictal onset zone and deep or unfavorable sources may be invisible. TIRDA is described as strongly associated with seizure activity; LRDA is associated with clinical seizures even outside the temporal region; LPDs often indicate an acute lateralized structural lesion with seizure tendency and lie on an interictal-ictal continuum, with fast or rhythmic activity, short intervals, and background attenuation making an LPD pattern more ictal-appearing.
findings.evidence_text: The source links focal EEG patterns to anatomy and seizure tendency but preserves caveats about acute versus chronic lesions, scalp sampling, and the need for clinical correlation.
findings.laterality_localization: focal or lateralized region, with structural-lesion and seizure-tendency associations
findings.limitations: The statements combine educational examples and heterogeneous critical-care contexts rather than one diagnostic population.
findings.locators: PDF p.154; PDF p.156; PDF p.174; PDF p.175; PDF p.205; PDF p.208
findings.population: clinical EEG, critical-care EEG, and focal epilepsy teaching groups
findings.source_term: focal interictal patterns, periodic/rhythmic patterns, and attenuation

findings.claim: Focal ictal discharges typically evolve in frequency, morphology, voltage, and distribution; focal onset attenuation can be localizing, high-frequency beta-range onset suggests neocortical involvement near the recording electrode, hippocampal seizures usually begin in theta or sometimes alpha, and delta onset may reflect activity recorded at a distance from the seizure center.
findings.evidence_text: The source treats evolution and the earliest field as more informative for onset than the later widespread rhythmic discharge or muscle-artifact phase.
findings.laterality_localization: neocortical near-electrode onset versus hippocampal or distant-recorded onset
findings.limitations: Surface EEG frequency and field are affected by propagation, electrode coverage, reference, and artifact.
findings.locators: PDF p.205; PDF p.214; PDF p.215
findings.population: focal ictal EEG teaching examples

findings.claim: Mesial temporal seizures commonly begin in theta or alpha and a 5-Hz-or-faster rhythmic temporal pattern within 30 seconds, especially in a sphenoidal or anterior-inferomesial electrode, supports temporal localization; lateral neocortical temporal seizures more often show posterior or lateral temporal predominance, slower ictal activity, transitional sharp waves, or high-frequency beta onset, while posterior temporal discharges can be falsely localized anteriorly.
findings.comparator: mesial versus lateral neocortical versus posterior temporal patterns
findings.evidence_text: The atlas differentiates temporal subregions using discharge field, frequency, morphology, TIRDA, sphenoidal activity, and the timing of the first temporal rhythm.
findings.laterality_localization: mesial anterior-inferior temporal versus lateral or posterior temporal
findings.limitations: These are scalp and selected-depth-electrode teaching associations; widespread propagation and montage choice can obscure the earliest source.
findings.locators: PDF p.108; PDF p.214; PDF p.215; PDF p.221; PDF p.224; PDF p.225
findings.measure: 5 Hz or faster temporal rhythm within 30 seconds as a source-stated supportive criterion
findings.population: mesial, lateral neocortical, and posterior temporal epilepsy teaching groups
findings.uncertainty: The source describes supportive patterns rather than absolute criteria and notes false anterior localization in posterior temporal epilepsy.

findings.claim: Frontal seizures often spread rapidly and can be difficult to distinguish from generalized activity, but high-frequency focal fast onset can localize the epileptogenic region; parietal scalp EEG can falsely appear temporal or frontal; occipital discharges may be bilateral from volume conduction, and activity above the calcarine fissure tends to spread frontally while activity below it tends to spread temporally.
findings.evidence_text: The source explicitly warns that posterior or deep regional onset can be represented by a misleading anterior or temporal scalp pattern and that occipital seizures may evolve slowly across frequency bands.
findings.laterality_localization: frontal focal fast onset; parietal potentially misleading scalp field; occipital field and calcarine-dependent spread
findings.limitations: The described routes are source-native tendencies, not deterministic propagation maps.
findings.locators: PDF p.220; PDF p.221; PDF p.229; PDF p.230
findings.population: frontal, parietal, and occipital epilepsy EEG teaching groups
findings.source_term: frontal, parietal, and occipital ictal EEG patterns

findings.claim: Generalized spike-wave activity supports generalized epilepsy when it is appropriately generalized and clinically concordant; typical absence commonly shows abrupt synchronous 2.5-4 Hz activity, juvenile myoclonic epilepsy shows faster irregular generalized or polyspike activity, and shifting asymmetry or focal fragments can occur within generalized epilepsies without proving a focal onset.
findings.comparator: generalized pattern versus focal-appearing fragment or asymmetry
findings.evidence_text: The atlas repeatedly distinguishes a generalized network with asymmetry or fragments from a truly focal onset and uses clinical concordance to resolve ambiguous discharges.
findings.laterality_localization: generalized bilateral network with possible shifting asymmetry or focal fragments
findings.limitations: Frequency ranges and visual appearance vary with state, syndrome, montage, and recording conditions.
findings.locators: PDF p.205; PDF p.209; PDF p.212; PDF p.240; PDF p.301
findings.measure: typical absence 2.5-4 Hz; JME commonly 3-6 Hz or faster irregular polyspike activity
findings.population: generalized epilepsy and absence/JME teaching groups
findings.source_term: generalized EEG patterns with focal-appearing features
findings.uncertainty: Clinical context, sleep state, evolution, and field are required; focal fragments are not sufficient to reclassify onset.

findings.analysis_unit: status episode, EEG pattern, and clinical response
findings.citation: Beniczky et al. Unified EEG terminology and criteria for nonconvulsive status epilepticus; source Chapter 5.6 Ref. 12
findings.claim: The source organizes status epilepticus by prominent motor symptoms and coma or impaired awareness, including focal motor status, ictal paresis, adversive status, focal aware or impaired-awareness nonconvulsive status, and focal onset evolving to bilateral convulsive status; for nonconvulsive status, discharges above 2.5 Hz or slower/rhythmic patterns with clinical or EEG improvement after intravenous antiseizure medication, subtle clinical ictal signs, or spatiotemporal evolution support the diagnosis.
findings.comparator: prominent motor versus nonconvulsive status; focal versus generalized or unknown onset
findings.evidence_text: The source requires joint consideration of semiology, EEG morphology and evolution, timing of monitoring, and response to therapy, especially when the record begins after prolonged status.
findings.laterality_localization: focal, multifocal, lateralized, bilateral, or generalized status pattern
findings.limitations: The cited framework is presented educationally; the source does not validate a new threshold or treatment rule in this atlas.
findings.locators: PDF p.196; PDF p.266; PDF p.268; PDF p.269; PDF p.270; PDF p.273
findings.measure: epileptiform discharges >2.5 Hz; slower discharges require an additional electroclinical criterion in the source framework
findings.phase: ongoing ictal activity and status evolution
findings.population: clinical status epilepticus and critical-care EEG teaching groups
findings.source_term: electroclinical status epilepticus criteria and semiologic axes
findings.uncertainty: Periodic or rhythmic patterns may lie on an interictal-ictal continuum and cannot always be classified from EEG alone.

findings.claim: One recorded seizure may be sufficient when focal EEG onset and semiology are clear and concordant; otherwise additional events are needed, and presurgical monitoring commonly records three to six seizures with more events when findings conflict. The source recommends comparing the first clinical change, earliest EEG change, evolution, interictal abnormalities, and postictal signs rather than relying on a single late discharge.
findings.comparator: clear concordant event versus ambiguous or discordant events
findings.evidence_text: The atlas frames event count as dependent on the clarity and concordance of the captured onset, not as a fixed universal number.
findings.laterality_localization: concordant clinical and EEG localization/lateralization
findings.limitations: The stated event counts are educational practice guidance and do not represent a quantified diagnostic study.
findings.locators: PDF p.100; PDF p.102; PDF p.104; PDF p.105; PDF p.107; PDF p.110
findings.measure: presurgical monitoring usually 3-6 seizures; one seizure may suffice only under stated concordance conditions
findings.population: epilepsy monitoring and presurgical evaluation teaching groups
findings.uncertainty: The source explicitly recommends more events when onset, semiology, or laterality conflict.

findings.claim: The source describes nonepileptic events as often showing no electrocerebral discharge during the episode, artifact without frequency evolution, and restoration of normal background after the event; however, some cingulate, orbitofrontal, supplementary motor, focal aware, temporal, or neonatal seizures may have no scalp correlate, so nonvisualization alone does not establish a nonepileptic diagnosis.
findings.evidence_text: The source's table contrasts epileptic and nonepileptic before, during, and after EEG features, while its surrounding text preserves the important exception of scalp-negative focal seizures.
findings.laterality_localization: scalp-negative deep or poorly oriented focal generators versus nonepileptic event
findings.limitations: Differential diagnosis depends on recording a representative event and on clinical review; the source gives no universal rule from EEG absence alone.
findings.locators: PDF p.312; PDF p.313; PDF p.314; PDF p.317
findings.population: psychogenic nonepileptic event differential and focal seizure comparison groups
findings.source_term: psychogenic nonepileptic events and scalp EEG caveat

findings.analysis_unit: recorded seizure and earlier witnessed event
findings.claim: In the illustrated adult case, two recorded bilateral tonic-clonic seizures began with head deviation to the left, but the EEG began with generalized bifrontally predominant rhythmic 12 Hz activity and 4-4.5 Hz spike-and-wave activity; an earlier witnessed event reportedly turned to the right, and the case was diagnosed as adult-onset idiopathic generalized epilepsy, illustrating that head direction at onset is not by itself proof of focal epilepsy.
findings.comparator: generalized-onset versus presumed focal-onset interpretation of head turning
findings.evidence_text: The case explicitly contrasts a focal interpretation of head deviation with generalized EEG onset and changing head direction across events.
findings.laterality_localization: generalized bifrontal onset despite variable head deviation direction
findings.limitations: This is one educational patient case; the up-to-60% statement is a cited literature restatement within the case discussion.
findings.locators: PDF p.380; PDF p.381; PDF p.386
findings.measure: up to 60% of primary generalized seizures may have head deviation according to the case discussion; case-specific denominator not provided
findings.phase: ictal onset and transition to bilateral tonic-clonic activity

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a heterogeneous educational atlas with review synthesis, cited restatements, EEG teaching figures, and individual cases rather than one primary dataset. Denominators, ascertainment methods, and diagnostic reference standards vary across the cited material and are often not reproduced in the atlas text. Semiology and scalp EEG are affected by timing, propagation, montage, electrode field, artifact, sleep or age state, and deep-generator sampling. Quantitative values above remain source-native and are not recalculated or harmonized. No external links, public repository, master ledger, website, integration, promotion, or deployment artifact was accessed or changed.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The complete native PDF page set 1-473 was reviewed as one source. Per-page text was read in coherent sections with targeted consolidation of repeated headers, references, medication material, and non-in-scope management content. Renderings were additionally inspected for the vision-required pages and for selected semiology diagrams, EEG traces, montages, tables, captions, and case figures where visual field, waveform evolution, or extraction uncertainty carried scientific meaning. Populations are heterogeneous and source-native: educational descriptions, selected cited-study restatements, and distinct illustrated patient cases are kept separate below. Quantitative values are reported only when the source states them.
sources.source_report_summary: This is the complete native 473-page third edition of Atlas of EEG, Seizure Semiology, and Management (Misulis, Sonmezturk, Ess, and Abou-Khalil; Oxford University Press, 2022). It is an educational atlas and review synthesis, not a single primary cohort. The in-scope review covered seizure semiology, seizure classification, clinical and ictal EEG interpretation, localization/lateralization, ictal propagation, selected electroclinical status criteria, pediatric electroclinical syndromes, and source-native teaching cases. The 12 package pages marked NONE_REQUIRES_VISION were inspected as renderings; they were blank, section-only, or cover material and none was blocked.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a single-patient case report without a control group, population estimate, or independent reference standard. The cited background literature is reported as restatement or discussion synthesis rather than independently verified source evidence here. The authors identify intrinsic SEEG anatomical sampling as a limitation and do not exclude adjacent regions; stimulation-trial counts and most comparative statistics are not reported. All five pages and all three figures were readable; no tables or blocked page regions were present.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The report concerns one 35-year-old right-handed man with drug-resistant partial epilepsy. Long-term video-EEG captured 6 electroclinical seizures; SEEG recorded 5 stereotyped spontaneous electroclinical seizures using 11 right-hemisphere electrodes and 1 left-amygdala electrode. The report also describes high-frequency stimulation of the right amygdala and right precentral operculum. No control group or independent reference standard is reported.
sources.source_report_summary: Original single-patient case report in Epileptic Disorders (2005) describing recurrent ictal speech with altered prosody in a right-handed man with drug-resistant right mesial temporal lobe epilepsy, using video-EEG, multimodal imaging, SEEG, and intracranial stimulation to examine non-dominant frontal-opercular involvement.

sources.source_report_limitations: All 11 native pages were readable in both the packaged text and page renderings; no page is blocked. The verified package contains the main 11-page article only, while the article repeatedly refers to an online appendix for operational definitions, additional subgroup results, and additional quantitative details. The appendix was not present and was not consulted, so no appendix-specific definition, denominator, or result has been inferred. The primary cohort reports no seizure-side or hemisphere-specific result, and the primary findings therefore do not establish lateralization. Cited-study restatements and mechanistic interpretations are retained as such and were not verified against their cited sources.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The study enrolled 2632 children and adults with epilepsy at nine epilepsy-monitoring centres in the USA and UK between 2011 and 2021; 164 were lost to follow-up and 2468 participants were included in the primary follow-up analyses. There were 38 SUDEP outcomes and two near-SUDEP events. During admission, 1660 participants had seizures captured, 1432 had analysable seizures, and the report describes 1091 analysable generalised convulsive seizures and 2117 non-convulsive seizures. The primary endpoint was time to SUDEP or censoring due to other causes. Cox proportional hazards models assessed clinical and electroclinical predictors; repeated seizure predictors were aggregated to the most severe feature per patient, using the maximum for continuous features or presence for categorical features. Analyses used prolonged video-EEG, ECG, pulse oximetry, and chest/abdominal inductance plethysmography. Statistical significance in primary analyses required two-sided p<0.05 after Bonferroni correction; the report states that secondary-analysis confidence intervals were not intended for hypothesis testing. Main-text results include varying denominators and missing data, which are retained below.
sources.source_report_summary: Ochoa-Urrea et al., “Risk markers for sudden unexpected death in epilepsy: an observational, prospective, multicentre cohort study,” is an original prospective observational cohort report. Its in-scope contribution is prospective comparison of seizure manifestations and peri-ictal respiratory, cardiac, EEG, and motor signs in relation to SUDEP risk. The primary study does not report seizure-side or other direct lateralization results; localization content is limited to explicitly attributed prior claims discussed by the authors.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a small, retrospective, uncontrolled case series with history-based identification. EEG was absent at the time of palinacousis in cases 5 and 6, uncertain in case 4, and negative for electrographic seizures during case 7; extracranial EEG could not localize an exact generator in cases 2 and 3. The source reports an internal duration discrepancy for case 5 and refers to Supplemental Table E1 without including it in the locked four-page package. Literature counts, prior-study descriptions, and novelty statements are current-document syntheses or cited restatements rather than independently verified source results. Silence or absent EEG was not treated as evidence that an episode was non-ictal.
sources.source_report_methods_population: This retrospective case series included seven patients seen at The Mount Sinai Hospital epilepsy clinic or EMU between July 2009 and May 2016 who experienced palinacousis. All patients had epilepsy; EEG and MRI were performed at some point during their clinical course, and the authors reviewed those records after identifying the phenomenon by history. No comparator, uniform event-time reference standard, or inferential statistical analysis was reported.
sources.source_report_summary: Fields et al., Journal of Clinical Neurophysiology 2018;35:173-176, is a case report and case series describing seven epilepsy patients with palinacousis seen at an epilepsy clinic or epilepsy monitoring unit. It contributes case-level evidence about auditory perseveration during direct cortical stimulation, electrographic seizures, and peri- or post-ictal states, together with a narrative localization review.

findings.claim: Case 1 was a 27-year-old right-handed woman whose seizures began at age 9 with uncontrollable laughter without associated emotion, sometimes singing or whistling, and sometimes repeated vocalizations such as “it doesn’t matter” or “no, no”; she could have a nonspecific “lucidity” warning, was usually aware with possible cognitive slowing, had nocturnal predominance without postictal deficit, and had 10–25-second seizures occurring 1–4 times per day.

findings.claim: In Case 1, fronto-temporal EEG findings and the described semiology led the chapter to favor a right anterior-inferior insular or orbitofrontal focus, with MEG at the junction of the anterior insula and posterior orbitofrontal cortex; invasive recordings showed preictal spiking over orbitofrontal, opercular, and anterior-insular contacts, spread to the middle insula and anterior middle frontal gyrus, and stimulation of the anterior-inferior insula reproduced the typical aura and clinical seizure.
findings.evidence_text: Stimulation of the anterior-inferior portion of the insula produced the patient’s typical aura and clinical seizure
findings.laterality_localization: Right hemisphere; anterior-inferior/anterior insula, frontal operculum, posterior orbitofrontal cortex, with spread to middle insula and anterior middle frontal gyrus

findings.claim: In Case 2, unilateral left interictal abnormalities, centro-temporal seizure onset, right-sided sensory pain and auditory auras, and late hypermotor manifestations were interpreted as favoring a left posterior or midposterior insular and temporo-parietal opercular origin with frontal propagation rather than primary frontal onset; invasive recordings showed preictal spikes over parietal-opercular and posterior-insular contacts followed by low-voltage fast activity in the same contacts, and the patient remained seizure-free 1.5 years after left posterior insulectomy and partial parietal opercular resection.

sources.source_report_limitations: This chapter is an educational narrative synthesis rather than a systematic review or primary cohort, and its cited-study restatements were not independently checked against the cited sources. Many cited populations, subgroup sizes, numerators, denominators, and analysis units are unavailable or not re-specified; silence is not treated as a negative finding. The two cases are illustrative and have no population-level generalizability. Figure captions and implantation maps were inspected as context; no stable sign identifier or cross-document mapping was assigned.
sources.source_report_methods_population: No formal search strategy, eligibility criteria, pooled analysis, common comparator, or uniform reference standard is reported. The chapter includes two individual case observations: Case 1 is a 27-year-old right-handed woman with seizure onset at age 9, and Case 2 is a 46-year-old right-handed man with seizures since age 16. Other populations are cited literature populations as reported in individual findings, including a review of 153 patients and a 22-patient nonlesional operculo-insular series; these are not an original chapter cohort.
sources.source_report_summary: This is an educational textbook chapter and narrative review, Chapter 17, Operculo-Insular Epilepsy, by Raluca Pana and Dang Khoa Nguyen in A Practical Approach to Stereo EEG. It synthesizes cited literature on ictal semiology and localization and presents two illustrative cases; it is not a primary cohort study. The source contributes source-native semiology/localization relationships, cited-study restatements, and case-specific EEG, stimulation, and invasive findings.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a left-hemisphere post-stroke aphasia study, not an epilepsy cohort. It contains no ictal or postictal observations, seizure-onset reference standard, EEG localization, seizure count, or seizure-lateralization endpoint. All primary localization results are associations between performance and diffusion-derived QA, not causal lesion or seizure-onset claims. The connected-singing analysis lost two recordings; the less/more severe subgroup analyses used n=22 and n=21, and the post hoc analysis used n=5 versus n=6. The authors caution that the subgroup right-sided and negative associations may be false positives, did not directly quantitatively compare the nonidentical speech and singing production tasks, and did not include right-hemisphere lesion or age-matched healthy control groups. The main connected-singing tract list includes a right middle cerebellar peduncle, while the Discussion says no clear right-hemisphere association was detected and emphasizes additional right-sided effects in the less-severe subgroup; both source statements are retained without reconciliation. Cited-study rows are restatements as reported by the current document and retain the current document's missing cohort and denominator information.
sources.source_report_methods_population: Forty-five adults with chronic aphasia more than 6 months after a clinically confirmed left-hemisphere stroke were recruited in Helsinki and Turku in 2017-2019; all were Finnish native speakers, over 18 years, and had no hearing deficit, severe cognitive impairment, substance abuse, or neurological/psychiatric comorbidity. Connected spoken-language production was mean correct information units per minute across three discourse tasks; connected singing was correct words per minute while singing the familiar song Jaakko-kulta; two connected-singing recordings were lost, leaving n=43 for that analysis. Repetition used 16 identical 1-5-word phrases in spoken and melodically intoned formats, with the first attempt scored and correct words per minute calculated. Six participant-level local-connectome regression models used age and lesion volume as covariates; tract tracking used a T-score threshold of 3, 2,000 permutations, and FDR <0.0083 after Bonferroni correction.
sources.source_report_summary: Original empirical Communications Biology study using whole-brain multi-shell diffusion MRI and quantitative-anisotropy connectometry to relate white-matter pathways to spoken-language production, singing, and repetition performance in adults with chronic post-stroke aphasia. It provides indirect neuroanatomical localization/lateralization evidence for language and sung-word production, not seizure-semiology evidence.

sources.source_report_limitations:
The included sample is small (12 patients, 17 symptom-evoking cingulate stimulations) and the cingulate and other implanted structures were sampled for clinical presurgical purposes with variable spatial coverage. The authors report no clear control over subjective clinical effects, no specific quantitative assessment such as visual-analog scales, and no independent reference standard for the complex body-perception reports. The stimulation effects were rare and not equivalent to spontaneous seizure semiology; the source explicitly reports that usual seizure semiology did not contain similar signs in the included patients. The connectivity analysis used a 5-s POSTSTIM signal epoch rather than activity during HFS because of stimulation artifact, limiting temporal resolution, and its network graphs are affected by variable sampling across patients and structures.

The source contains unresolved internal reporting inconsistencies relevant to exact attribution: Section 3.1 names Patient 13 for upper-limb pain associated with a heaviness effect and Patients 11 and 14 for movement observations, whereas Table 1 contains 12 patients and Table 2 assigns the corresponding rows to Patients 11, 9, and 12; Section 3.1 describes Patient 4 pressure as upper-extremity pressure whereas Table 2 lists head/top-of-head pressure; and the prose calls the right PCC movement relationship contralateral while Table 2 labels S17 ipsilateral. These source discrepancies are retained in the affected findings rather than resolved by inference. Page 14 points to online Supporting Information, but no supplemental object is present in the locked 14-page package and no claim from it is reviewed here.
sources.source_report_methods_population:
Patients underwent phase-two invasive presurgical evaluation at the University Emergency Hospital Bucharest or Strasbourg University Hospital between 2000 and 2017. The source reviewed 110 patients whose cingulate cortex was sampled and functionally mapped and included 12 right-handed patients with body-perception changes: 8 from Bucharest and 4 from Strasbourg. All had focal drug-resistant epilepsy; the epileptogenic zone was frontal in 9 patients, temporo-basal in 1, insular-opercular in 1, and insular in 1. Patients were selected when at least one electrode sampled cingulate cortex outside the epileptogenic zone; cognitive or psychiatric comorbidity judged likely to interfere with reliable interaction was excluded. Structures and stimulation sites were selected for clinical presurgical purposes, not for this study. The source reports no visible MRI lesion in the included patients and states that the stimulated locations did not overlap the delineated epileptogenic zone in the two patients who did not undergo surgery.

Functional mapping used bipolar high-frequency stimulation at 50 Hz for 5 s through adjacent contacts with biphasic 1 ms pulses; current was gradually increased from 0.1 to 3 mA until a clinical or electrical response. Patients reported psychological or physical changes during or after stimulation. Body-representation changes were analyzed at the lowest intensity that evoked a symptom (SYM target group) and compared with typically half-intensity stimulations without a symptom (NS control group); after-discharges, auras, and seizures were excluded. Repeated trials, including 0 mA sham trials, were used for response consistency and psychogenic-event control. The separate connectivity analysis used h2 values from nonstimulated contacts in 10-s PRESTIM and 5-s POSTSTIM epochs; those network measurements are kept distinct from the semiologic findings below. No independent reference standard was reported for the subjective stimulation responses.
sources.source_report_summary: Popa et al., “Illusory own body perceptions mapped in the cingulate cortex—An intracranial stimulation study,” is an original retrospective empirical study of stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG)-guided high-frequency direct electrical stimulation in people with focal drug-resistant epilepsy. The paper reports body-perception phenomena evoked by stimulation of cingulate cortex contacts outside the epileptogenic zone, with cingulate subregion and body-side relationships, and separately reports an h2-based functional-connectivity analysis. The semiologic observations in this report are stimulation-evoked; the paper separately addresses usual seizure semiology and does not establish that the evoked phenomena are spontaneous seizure signs.

sources.source_report_limitations: The PDF is a scan with no text layer; all eight pages were represented by verified page renderings and reviewed visually, and no page was blocked. The study is a small surgical unilateral-TLE cohort with repeated seizure observations per patient. Table 1 percentages are relative to all 116 seizures, while parenthetical values are patient counts; behavior-specific denominators and confidence intervals are generally not reported. The language table likewise uses total-seizure percentages while comparing NHS and DHS groups. The source reports an internal wording/table discrepancy for unilateral automatism and uses both ictal-language and postictal-dysphasia phrasing in different sections; neither discrepancy was resolved by inference. Pages 7-8 contain the discussion tail and references; bibliography entries were not treated as findings.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The study included 19 patients with unilateral TLE who underwent anterior temporal lobectomy with amygdalohippocampectomy. Long-term video/EEG monitoring used scalp and sphenoidal electrodes; hippocampal depth electrodes were used in five patients. The epileptogenic zone was determined from ictal EEG, MRI findings including mesial temporal sclerosis, ictal SPECT, regional temporal PET, and surgical outcome; Wada-test results were used for dominant versus nondominant hemisphere classification. Two to ten seizures per patient were reviewed (mean 6.1); the cohort included 10 females and 9 males, mean age 28.7 years (range 12-43). Sixty-five seizures were classified as nondominant-hemisphere onset and 51 as dominant-hemisphere onset; 85 seizures arose from the right temporal lobe and 31 from the left. Chi-square testing was used for statistical analysis.
sources.source_report_summary: Roh, Hong, and Seo (1996) is an original empirical study of the lateralizing value of ictal behaviors in surgically treated unilateral temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE). The investigators reviewed 116 seizures in 19 patients using video/EEG and classified unilateral motor signs, ictal language, and other automatisms by their relation to EEG seizure focus, dominant or nondominant hemisphere onset, or right versus left TLE.

sources.source_report_limitations: The primary localization reference was the operated temporal side, supported by post-operative outcome rather than an independent seizure-onset standard. Group A was presumed more accurately localized because patients became seizure-free or almost so; Group B remained less valid because continuing attacks could reflect bilateral or other seizure sites. Speech dominance was presumed from left-sided resection in right-handed patients, with all but three patients right-handed, without intracarotid sodium amytal testing in doubtful cases. Tables distinguish cases from patients and speech types can overlap; the Table I overlap count conflicts with the Summary as described in F001. Several qualitative claims, including grand-mal and radiological associations, lack exact numerators and denominators. Speech arrest and vocalization were excluded by the authors. Cited-study results are retained as restatements of the current document and were not independently reviewed.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The first 100 consecutive patients with temporal lobe epilepsy operated on by anterior temporal lobectomy were studied; pre-operative documentation recorded the presence or absence and nature of speech disturbance connected with fits, and follow-up was mostly by personal interview for 2-10 years. The operated side was used as an imperfect reference for the presumed primary epileptogenic site: Group A comprised 53 patients who became seizure-free or almost so and were presumed correctly diagnosed, while Group B comprised 47 patients with continuing attacks and lower localization validity, including 30 improved patients and 17 slightly benefited or unchanged patients. Table I reports 56 left-sided and 44 right-sided resections. All patients had pre-operative psychomotor seizures and many also had grand mal attacks. All but three patients were right-handed for ordinary tasks; cerebral speech dominance was presumed from left-sided resection in right-handed persons because intracarotid sodium amytal testing had not yet been used in doubtful cases.
sources.source_report_summary: Original empirical surgical series by E. A. Serafetinides and M. A. Falconer, “Speech Disturbances in Temporal Lobe Seizures: A Study in 100 Epileptic Patients Submitted to Anterior Temporal Lobectomy” (1963). The report describes pre-operative paroxysmal dysphasia and speech automatisms, their source-native definitions and subtypes, frequency, laterality, pre-operative interictal EEG associations, and post-operative course in temporal lobe epilepsy.

findings.claim: In macaques, warping the previously published ICMS map onto INIA19 delineated two anterior oroalimentary subfields: ICMS predominantly elicited ingestive movements (chewing, mouthing, swallowing) in a dorsal anterior insular sector ventral to the frontal opercular region, whereas disgust responses (lip lifting, nose wrinkling, and in some cases initial gag; elsewhere described as mouth gaping, spitting food, or retching) clustered in the inferior/ventral anterior insula.
findings.evidence_text: The source defines the dorsal anterior field by ICMS-evoked chewing, mouthing, and swallowing and the inferior anterior field by lip-lifting, nose-wrinkling, gag-related, mouth-gaping, spitting, and retching responses.
findings.laterality_localization: Dorsal anterior insula versus inferior/ventral anterior insula; the source does not report a seizure-onset side or a body-side association for these behaviors
findings.limitations: These were high-intensity, short-train ICMS responses in macaques and cannot be treated as spontaneous seizure semiology; the paper reports no ictal observations or clinical localization validation.

findings.claim: In macaques, the ICMS-defined hand field localized to the dorsal middle insula: stimulation elicited simple contralateral hand twitches, wrist rotation or flexion, finger extension or closure, and complex goal-related movements ranging from hand-to-mouth actions to actions directed to specific body parts; the most posterior dorsal sites were intermingled with proximal-movement sites and were treated as a separate field.

findings.laterality_localization: Dorsal, predominantly middle insula; the source reports simple movements of the contralateral hand but does not define a seizure reference side or seizure-onset direction
findings.limitations: These were stimulation-evoked macaque motor responses, not spontaneous seizures; the source does not provide patient-level or seizure-level denominators, ictal timing, or clinical laterality evidence.

findings.claim: The macaque ventral middle insula was defined as an ICMS emotion-related field in which stimulation elicited lip-smacking, described as an affiliative gesture during emotionally salient social situations; intermingled stimulation sites also produced difficult-to-interpret discomfort reactions ranging from postural adjustments to psychomotor agitation. The discussion reports lip-smacking during direct eye contact with a specific experimenter and notes that the behavior can also occur during anxiety or fear.
findings.evidence_text: The source defines the ventral middle field by ICMS-evoked lip-smacking and reports intermingled discomfort reactions, including postural adjustment and psychomotor agitation; lip-smacking was elicited during direct eye contact in the cited mapping context.

findings.claim: In macaques, ICMS of the caudalmost insular region produced simple limb-muscle reactions, axial movements, and bodily tremors: proximal movements clustered in the dorsal posterior sector, axial movements occupied the ventral posterior sector, and tremors occurred across both sectors. The source also describes posterior-insula responses including tremors coupled with limb or axial movements, postural adjustments, and ventral-sector trunk rotation toward contralateral space with a gaze shift in the same direction.
findings.evidence_text: The source places proximal responses dorsally, axial responses ventrally, and tremors in both dorsal and ventral caudal insular sectors, with a ventral response described as trunk rotation toward contralateral space and gaze shift.
findings.laterality_localization: Caudal/posterior insula with dorsal proximal-movement and ventral axial-movement sectors; the source states contralateral space for the ventral trunk-rotation response without defining a seizure reference side
findings.limitations: These are electrically evoked macaque responses and may reflect recruitment of distributed networks; they do not establish spontaneous seizure semiology, seizure laterality, or clinical localization.
findings.locators: PDF p.5, Fig. 1D, E and caption; PDF p.12, §4.5.1; PDF p.15, Fig. 9A and caption; PDF p.16, §§4.5.2-4.5.3; PDF p.19, §5.4
findings.phase: Stimulation-evoked movement; not ictal or postictal
findings.population: Macaque monkeys; caudal/posterior insular ICMS field map

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a macaque anatomo-functional connectivity study, not a seizure study. The behavioral observations derive from ICMS maps, including maps from prior work, and the stimulation used a 4 mA, 50 Hz, 3-second train after a quiet baseline; the authors note that insular responses may recruit large-scale networks beyond the stimulated site. The paper contains no patients with insular seizures, no spontaneous ictal or postictal observations, no seizure-onset reference standard, and no patient or seizure denominators for the stimulation-evoked behaviors. Resting-state fMRI was acquired in sedated macaques, and tract-tracing and connectivity results provide network context rather than direct evidence of seizure expression. Bibliographic citations to human insular stimulation or seizure studies do not convert this source into a seizure study.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The paper summarizes prior macaque ICMS mapping performed with 200-microsecond biphasic pulses at 50 Hz, 4 mA, for 3 seconds; a behavior entered the dataset when two observers recognized it and it was evoked in more than 50% of trials. The present analyses used ICMS maps and insular tracer injections in two male rhesus macaques (Mk1 and Mk2), indirect tracer data from 22 additional animals, and resting-state fMRI from 12 male macaques aged 4-8 years. The authors warped the ICMS maps and injection sites onto the INIA19 macaque template and delineated six insular fields. No seizure cohort, ictal or postictal observations, or clinical localization reference standard was studied.
sources.source_report_summary: Simone et al., Progress in Neurobiology 247 (2025) 102748, is an original experimental nonhuman-primate study combining macaque intracortical microstimulation (ICMS)-defined insular field maps, tract tracing, and resting-state fMRI to characterize insular anatomo-functional networks. The functional-localization observations below are stimulation-evoked macaque behaviors; this source is not a seizure study.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a narrative review with heterogeneous cited populations and no single source cohort, unified ascertainment method, quantitative evidence table, or source-verified cited-study dataset. The review mentions that FCD may have “particular ictal changes” on EEG and that lissencephaly may have a characteristic interictal EEG appearance, but it does not name or describe those patterns; they are therefore not represented as sign-level findings. The bilateral perisylvian polymicrogyria phenotype, congenital hemiparesis, developmental delay, pseudobulbar palsy, and spastic quadruparesis are non-ictal developmental or neurological features and are not converted into seizure-atlas findings. No claim in this report establishes a body-side or hemisphere direction.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The article is a narrative review rather than a single primary cohort. The review states that it identified material through MEDLINE and Current Contents searches using MCD, malformation, epilepsy, named-gene, and related terms, supplemented by relevant articles and the author's files; only papers published in English were reviewed. The populations and designs vary across the cited reports and are often not specified in the review text. Cohort descriptors, prevalence estimates, surgery outcomes, treatment response, mortality, and developmental context are retained only as background when needed to interpret an in-scope claim, not as independent atlas findings.
sources.source_report_summary: This is a narrative clinical review by Sanjay M Sisodiya, published as Malformations of cortical development: burdens and insights from important causes of human epilepsy (Lancet Neurol 2004;3:29-38). It surveys focal cortical dysplasia, periventricular heterotopia, polymicrogyria, subcortical band heterotopia and lissencephaly, dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumours, and microdysgenesis. This report retains only source-reported seizure manifestations or statements that bear directly on epileptogenic localization; malformation taxonomy, genetics, imaging descriptors, treatment, outcomes, and general burden are not represented as findings.

sources.source_report_limitations: All 25 native pages were represented and reviewed; no page was blocked. This is an educational chapter combining review synthesis, cited-study restatements, a selected representative table, and one clinical case rather than one defined cohort. Many cited results lack denominators, response counts, effect sizes, or uncertainty estimates in the chapter, and cited sources were not independently reviewed. The source itself notes variability of stimulation responses, possible distant or systemic effects, incomplete understanding of functional networks, and difficulty interpreting memory mapping at the individual level. Table 10.1 is explicitly a selected sample; its final executive-function cell is visibly truncated to “No dis” in the rendered source and was not used for an in-scope finding. The chapter does not establish spontaneous-seizure semiology frequencies, diagnostic accuracy, or equivalence between stimulation-induced responses and spontaneous seizures.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The source describes clinical SEEG functional mapping using stimulation of sampled contacts during patient-specific tasks and summarizes cited studies involving patients with epilepsy, plus selected non-SEEG and awake-mapping studies in Table 10.1. Cited-study populations, sampling frames, analysis units, and denominators are frequently not reported in this chapter. One source-described clinical example is a 17-year-old patient with left temporo-perisylvian epilepsy and MRI-negative imaging (Fig. 10.4). The source distinguishes stimulation-induced clinical/electrophysiological responses from spontaneous seizures and treats afterdischarges as interpretation context.
sources.source_report_summary: Educational Chapter 10, “Electrical Stimulation for Functional Mapping During SEEG Exploration,” by Agnès Trébuchon and Daniel L. Drane in The Fundamentals of Stereoelectroencephalography (2025). The chapter reviews SEEG stimulation mapping and selected representative stimulation studies, with emphasis on how induced functional effects can localize functional sub-units and how they should be interpreted alongside seizure electro-clinical data. It is not a single spontaneous-seizure cohort.
